passages.text: DIVERGE v4: A Platform for Large-Scale Analysis of Functional Divergence Across Multi-Gene Families
Abstract

Gene duplication and subsequent divergence are fundamental drivers in the evolution of novel gene functions. The DIVERGE software, widely utilized for identifying amino acid residues critical to functional shifts between protein subfamilies, has been substantially upgraded to version 4 to address modern bioinformatics challenges. This major release features a modular Python package for enhanced workflow integration and a novel algorithm for scalable analysis of large gene families. Notably, we introduce DIVERGE-Chat, pioneering the application of a conversational artificial intelligence (AI) agent in the field of functional divergence, enabling intuitive, code-free exploration (https://pgx.zju.edu.cn/diverge). We have also developed a complementary interactive online web server that allows users to upload local files for interactive analysis, facilitating more flexible analysis. Furthermore, we curated phylogenetic data for 4,540 human gene families and conducted functional divergence analyses, generating a comprehensive resource accessible online. Collectively, these advancements significantly improve the accuracy, scalability, usability, and integration capabilities of functional divergence analysis, empowering broader research into protein evolution, functional specificity, and biomedical applications.
Graphical Abstract
Introduction

Gene duplication and subsequent divergence play an important part in the evolution of novel gene functions. Functional divergence is critical in generating functional variation within protein families during evolution. Understanding the functional divergence helps researchers understand how biological functions diversify within a protein family. In recent years, considerable progress has been made in developing computational tools for the analysis of functional divergence.

Compared to other programs, a distinctive feature of DIVERGE is its use of an explicit evolutionary framework that simultaneously integrates protein sequence data and phylogenetic relationships to assess functional divergence. DIVERGE is underpinned by a rigorous statistical inference framework that employs distinct statistical models to formally test for Type-I and Type-II functional divergence, respectively, thereby ensuring a robust evaluation of statistical significance. Furthermore, DIVERGE also provides an integrated statistical toolkit (see Supplementary Material) for the comprehensive analysis of functional divergence. Type-I divergence reflects site-specific evolutionary rate changes between subfamilies, whereas Type-II divergence involves shifts in site-specific amino acid properties under functional constraints. Using user-provided multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) and predefined protein subgroups, DIVERGE identifies links between evolutionary sequence patterns and functional characteristics. Specifically, DIVERGE detects site-specific functional divergence by identifying statistically significant shifts in evolutionary rates between protein subfamilies. These divergence-implicated sites, identified from MSAs alongside highly conserved positions, often serve as indicators of functionally important regions. Moreover, these functionally divergent sites are thought to contribute significantly to subfamily-specific functions within homologous protein families. They may form three-dimensional clusters constituting ligand- or protein-binding interfaces, or represent residue networks involved in allosteric regulation. Identifying these specific sites provides crucial insights into the atomic-level determinants of functional specificity. This understanding can enhance disease mechanism elucidation, inform drug discovery and therapeutic targeting strategies, and guide protein engineering efforts, such as modifying enzyme substrate specificity.

In the era of big data, reliable software for large-scale functional divergence analysis is essential for studying protein functional specificity through data-driven methods. Since its initial release, DIVERGE has gained widespread adoption and has undergone multiple updates; however, these earlier versions were constrained in handling large-scale computations due to a basic pairwise algorithm that processed only two pre-specified duplicate clusters per round. As gene family sizes increased, this limitation resulted in exponential growth in duplicate pairs and significant estimation errors (see Materials and Methods). Furthermore, despite the critical importance of functional divergence for identifying key protein residues, user-friendly tools that integrate seamlessly into contemporary computational workflows have been lacking. To address these shortcomings, we have redeveloped the DIVERGE framework in the widely used Python language, incorporating a modular API for seamless integration into analytical pipelines; these enhancements facilitate more complex functional analyses, optimize computational performance, and introduce a new, statistically robust algorithm for large-scale functional divergence analysis in multi-gene families.

Beyond algorithmic enhancements, another major update significantly improves the usability of our analysis tools. We recognized that traditional functional divergence analysis of protein families often requires laborious phylogenetic data curation. This complexity not only complicates the interpretation of predictions but also restricts access for researchers lacking expertise in bioinformatics or phylogenetics. Inspired by the rise of innovative large language models (LLMs) and dialogue systems in bioinformatics, we have developed DIVERGE-Chat, a pioneering conversational LLM-powered agentic workflow tailored for functional divergence analysis of protein families. As the first platform of its kind, DIVERGE-Chat enables zero-code exploration through intuitive dialogues, thereby democratizing access to these powerful analyses. Furthermore, we developed a complementary interactive online web server that allows users to upload local files for interactive analysis, facilitating more flexible analysis. In addition, this work includes the curation of a comprehensive resource of functional divergence analyses for 4,540 human protein families, which users can query directly from the platform.

In summary, this updated DIVERGE framework, along with DIVERGE-Chat and associated resources, addresses key limitations in functional divergence analysis by improving scalability, usability, and integration. These advancements not only facilitate more efficient research on protein evolution but also empower a broader range of scientists to uncover functional insights in the post-genomic era.
Results
The Framework of DIVERGE v4

The DIVERGE effectively addresses two key questions: whether the functional divergence between duplicate genes is statistically significant; and if so, how to identify the amino acid sites primarily responsible for these functional divergences. Type-I functional divergence arises from significant differences in evolutionary rates at specific sites between two subgroups of a protein family, indicating that the functional constraints at these positions differ between the groups. Similarly, certain positions may exhibit a subfamily-specific conservation pattern: conserved across all subfamilies but involving different amino acids in each. This Type-II divergence results from rate changes where purifying selection leads to similar conservation levels for different amino acid types across subfamilies. Another notable feature of DIVERGE is its evaluation of a Bayesian profile for each group, measuring how individual amino acid residues contribute to the functional divergences. We have re-engineered the DIVERGE software from a C desktop application into a Python package. Previous versions of DIVERGE were limited to specific platforms and faced challenges with visualization and computational scalability. To address these issues, DIVERGE v4 has been redesigned as an open-source, modular, and scalable tool, featuring 10 Python modules that handle various types of analyses related to the functional divergence of protein families. This redesign enables users to seamlessly incorporate specific DIVERGE modules into their existing computational workflows. Leveraging Python's high-performance libraries, we have enhanced DIVERGE's computational efficiency using external packages such as scikit-bio and NumPy. Additionally, to support large-scale computations, we have implemented a new algorithm called Super-Cluster, further optimizing performance. These improvements enhance cross-platform compatibility, accessibility, and flexibility, enabling users to perform complex analyses more efficiently and effectively.

Given that many users of the DIVERGE software may lack programming expertise or sufficient computational resources, we have developed a user-friendly web server that implements the algorithmic framework via our Python package architecture. The data loading processes (e.g. subfamily division) and result displays (e.g. single-site result presentation) are designed with interactive mouse-click functionality to simplify usage. Furthermore, we have streamlined the computational workflow into a user interface, thereby reducing computational complexity by requiring only a valid MSA and the corresponding phylogenetic tree to generate and access results. For users needing advanced customization capabilities, the modular Python package remains available as an alternative option. The web server is built on the Streamlit framework (see Materials and Methods), which streamlines website development, supports individual user sessions, and eliminates the limitation of queuing during analytical tasks.For those seeking maximum flexibility and integration into bespoke pipelines, the underlying Python package remains available in its modular form for expert users. The availability of these alternative interfaces ensures that the new DIVERGE platform (Fig. 1) is accessible and adaptable to a range of user needs and expertise levels.

Workflow and overview of DIVERGE v4. The diagram highlights major components and functionalities introduced in this version. a) DIVERGE v4 accepts a Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) and predefined subfamily groups as input. b) The new algorithm features a statistically enhanced method for robust, large-scale analysis of functional divergence in multi-gene families. c) Software implementation includes a redesigned modular Python package and a user-friendly interactive web server. d) The primary results generated by DIVERGE v4 include the statistical significance of functional divergence between subfamilies (sequence level) and site-specific posterior probabilities pinpointing residues potentially driving this divergence (residue level).
DIVERGE-Chat: An LLM-Powered Functional Divergence Analysis Platform

While the redesigned software framework and user-friendly web server significantly enhance the accessibility of DIVERGE, navigating complex functional divergence analysis workflows can still pose challenges for researchers without extensive bioinformatics expertise. To address this issue and further reduce the barrier to entry, we developed an innovative conversational interface powered by an LLM chatflow, named DIVERGE-Chat (Fig. 2). This agent facilitates code-free functional divergence analysis through natural language interaction. DIVERGE-Chat was developed by integrating multiple agents that support tool calls and multi-turn memory. Leveraging advanced natural language processing capabilities, DIVERGE-Chat interprets user requests expressed in a conversational manner. Based on this understanding, the agent autonomously decides on and coordinates the analysis workflow by (1) querying integrated resource modules (see Materials and Methods) to retrieve relevant, curated data on protein families and phylogenies; (2) programmatically invoking the appropriate DIVERGE computational tools to perform functional divergence analysis; and (3) systematically summarizing and analyzing the results to present key findings and their biological significance in an accessible format. All intermediate processes are presented as a chain of thought in the 'Thinking' process and culminate in the output of a complete analysis report. This interactive process enables users to efficiently explore patterns of functional divergence within protein families. Furthermore, DIVERGE-Chat facilitates more in-depth iterative exploration through its site-specific analysis capabilities: users can request follow-up analyses, including the identification and examination of specific residue positions predicted to be critical for functional divergence.

Framework and User Interface of DIVERGE-Chat: a) Workflow of the DIVERGE-Chat conversational agent for functional divergence analysis. The system uses an LLM-powered, multi-agent chatflow. User input triggers the Plan agent for task assignment. The Data Query agent retrieves data via SQL from a pre-compiled database ( vertebrate protein families). The Computation agent performs analysis using the DIVERGE Python API. Results are interpreted by the LLM, and the Check agent ensures process integrity. b) Example of the web interface allowing users to perform functional divergence analysis through dialogue and ask follow-up questions within the context of a protein family.

A critical challenge in applying general LLM agent to specialised scientific domains, such as phylogenetics, is ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the underlying data. Conventional LLM-driven searches from public databases frequently fail to retrieve the precise, high-quality protein family and phylogenetic data required for robust functional divergence analysis. To address this issue, a comprehensive Resource module has been developed to empower the DIVERGE-Chat agent with reliable domain knowledge. This curated knowledge base focuses on human and vertebrate protein families, derived from systematic processing of the PANTHER database. It encompasses 4,540 divergent human protein families, including 10,133 genes, with curated phylogenetic relationships at the vertebrate level and 215,480 protein sequences for MSA (see Materials and Methods). The agent queries this Resource module to access high-fidelity data, thereby enabling accurate responses. For functional divergence tasks, the agent invokes tools to perform Type-I, Type-II, or Super-Cluster analyses, synthesizing results into comprehensive summaries that highlight key divergence patterns. For users requesting site-specific analysis, the agent isolates relevant residue positions, applies divergence metrics, and provides detailed interpretations of site-level functional shifts. The online platform's Resource module also offers users a more direct approach, providing access to phylogenetic visualizations, divergence results, and integrated functional annotations (Gene Ontology, pathways, PANTHER protein classes) for deeper biological insights.
Super-Cluster: Divergence Profiling of Multi-Gene Families

When investigating the specific functions or functional divergence of a subfamily within a superfamily, traditional methods rely on pairwise comparisons of subfamilies, yielding numerous "one-to-one" results. This approach is highly time-consuming (see Supplementary Material), and for superfamilies with many subfamilies, it can become computationally infeasible. Additionally, the information derived from these "one-to-one" comparisons tends to be disorganized, complicating the integration of functional divergence patterns for a given subfamily and potentially leading to the omission of more complex patterns.

Here we propose an efficient method, called Super-Cluster analysis (see Materials and Methods), to tackle the challenge when the number of subfamilies  in a superfamily is large. By dividing the subfamilies into two groups in all possible ways without considering their evolutionary relationships, we can generate  Super-Cluster pairs. We hypothesize that the DIVERGE analysis of these Super-Cluster pairs can identify functional divergence sites that capture a broad spectrum of functional divergence types. Instead of relying on traditional one-to-one comparisons, we introduce a Super-Cluster functional divergence profile (Q-profile), which integrates all possible grouping patterns, allowing users to intuitively explore the functional divergence of individual subfamilies within the protein family. Compared to conventional "one-to-one" functional divergence analysis, the Super-Cluster approach not only reduces computational time but also provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of functional divergence. Furthermore, this grouping strategy utilizes sequence information from the entire protein family to calculate an overview of the functional divergence for each subfamily, thereby yielding statistically more robust results. To evaluate the performance of Super-Cluster, we first benchmarked it against several state-of-the-art methods using simulated datasets (see Supplementary Material), following an evaluation framework consistent with previous studies. Super-Cluster consistently outperformed all competing methods across key metrics, including the AUC-ROC, the AUC-PR, and the average rank of true positive sites. Furthermore, analysis of 56 real protein families with manual curation revealed that Super-Cluster successfully identifies functional divergence patterns often missed by conventional methods, particularly in scenarios where divergence is confined to a single subfamily within a large protein family (see Supplementary Table S3).
DIVERGE-Based Exploration of Subfamily Specificity in the ErbB Family

The analysis of functional divergence enhances our understanding of functional specificity within homologous protein families, which is critical for applications in biomedical and biotechnological fields. Previous studies have highlighted the significant potential of the DIVERGE algorithm in drug target discovery and elucidating disease mechanisms. A major update in the latest version of DIVERGE is the inclusion of the Super-Cluster algorithm, which enables statistically robust functional divergence analysis and facilitates a more intuitive examination of the functional divergence characteristics of specific subfamilies within a protein family. To illustrate the features and application of the new DIVERGE, we analyzed the human ErbB (Erythroblastic Leukemia Viral Oncogene Homolog) family. The ErbB family consists of four highly homologous members: EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, and ERBB4, all sharing a conserved structure comprising an intracellular tyrosine kinase domain, a transmembrane domain, and a glycosylated extracellular ligand-binding domain. Notably, ERBB3 is unique among the ErbB family members, as it is generally considered to lack tyrosine kinase activity or have impaired activity. Our Super-Cluster analysis identified a substantial number of functional divergence sites within the tyrosine kinase domain of ERBB3 (Fig. 3a), suggesting that these key residues may be responsible for locking the domain in an inactive conformation, thereby resulting in a lack of catalytic kinase activity.

Super-Cluster analysis of the ErbB family. a) Visualization of Super-Cluster analysis results: The plot displays alignment sites with posterior probabilities greater than 0.8, indicating potential functional divergence. The x-axis represents the alignment site positions. Notably, a significant number of functional divergence sites are identified in the tyrosine kinase domain of ErbB3, whereas other family members show minimal divergence in this region. b) Comparison between traditional DIVERGE analysis and Super-Cluster: This comparison illustrates that the Super-Cluster approach can replace multiple one-to-one calculations with a single, comprehensive computation. Alignment sites with posterior probabilities greater than 0.67 are visualized. The Super-Cluster approach effectively consolidates multiple calculations and identifies functional divergence sites that traditional methods may overlook.

Furthermore, we compared the results of traditional DIVERGE analysis with those of the Super-Cluster method (Fig. 3b). The results clearly demonstrate that the Super-Cluster approach can replace numerous one-to-one comparisons with a single computation, effectively identifying functional divergence sites that might be overlooked by traditional DIVERGE analysis. For example, residue position 1262 was identified as a site of potential functional divergence in the Super-Cluster analysis, with a high posterior probability . This stringent threshold corresponds to a posterior odds ratio greater than 4 (see Supplementary Material). In contrast, the conventional DIVERGE method yielded a probability below 0.6 for this position. This site corresponds to amino acid 855 in ERBB3 and 858 in EGFR. The L858R mutation in the tyrosine kinase domain of EGFR is a well-known activating mutation. With this mutation, the autoinhibitory conformation of EGFR is suppressed, rendering the receptor active even without ligand binding. Similarly, the V855A mutation in ERBB3 is also a reported oncogenic mutation, but it requires co-expression with ERBB2 to confer gain of function. MSA shows that the mutated residue is highly conserved across ERBB3 homologs in different mammalian species. It is indicated that functional divergence at this site might led to the preservation of a new function, making it a crucial site for subfamily-specific functions and contributing to the functional diversity of the protein family.

This case study demonstrates that Super-Cluster can efficiently identify subfamily-specific functional sites and provide intuitive explanations for functional divergence phenomena within large protein families, thereby offering new insights into the functional diversity of protein families. Additionally, the feasibility of implementation in a big-data environment is underscored by this case.
Discussion

In this study, we introduce DIVERGE v4, an enhanced platform for functional divergence analysis. Through algorithmic improvements (Super-Cluster), a refined modular Python architecture, an improved user experience via a web server and the novel DIVERGE-Chat interface, and robust data support utilizing curated phylogenetic resources, we have significantly advanced the platform's accuracy, scalability, usability, and integration capabilities. DIVERGE v4 not only processes large-scale datasets efficiently but also facilitates code-free exploratory analysis through DIVERGE-Chat, rendering functional divergence studies more intuitive and accessible. DIVERGE-Chat represents the first application of an LLM-powered agent in the functional divergence domain, substantially lowering the entry barrier for researchers and promoting broader recognition of the biological importance of functional divergence. A current limitation is that DIVERGE-Chat relies on our curated phylogenetic datasets, as conventional functional divergence analysis necessitates comprehensive protein family phylogenies. Consequently, a key future direction is the development of phylogeny-independent functional divergence methods to expand DIVERGE-Chat's capabilities.

Looking ahead, the field of functional divergence analysis stands at the cusp of a significant transformation with the emergence of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. Recent advances in large-scale pretrained language models and deep learning methods have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in capturing evolutionary relationships between proteins and long-range co-evolutionary patterns between residues. These models, trained on vast amounts of protein sequence data, naturally learn to encode evolutionary information and protein family relationships, making them particularly well-suited for evolution-related tasks. They are effective at decoding distant mutation coupling effects that traditional methods often struggle to identify. Moreover, these models' zero-shot inference capabilities offer promising potential for predicting functional divergence in the protein "twilight zone", where sequence similarity is too low for conventional methods to make reliable predictions.

The modular architecture and curated datasets of DIVERGE v4 provide an ideal foundation for integrating these AI-driven approaches. Integrating DIVERGE's robust statistical framework with advanced AI technologies promises enhanced sensitivity for detecting subtle patterns of functional divergence and improved predictive accuracy in challenging or low-signal cases. This integration could lead to more sophisticated analyses of protein functional divergence, particularly where traditional methods exhibit limitations. As the field continues to evolve, the flexible architecture of DIVERGE ensures its adaptability, allowing for the incorporation of new methodologies while maintaining its core strength in evolutionary analysis.
Materials and Methods
Software and Tools

All computational analyses were conducted on a workstation equipped with an Intel i5-13400 CPU (2.5 GHz) and 32 GB of RAM. The primary analytical environment was Python (v3.10.10), supported by the pandas (v1.5.3) and NumPy (v1.23.5) libraries for data manipulation and numerical operations, respectively. Multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) were generated using MAFFT (v7.520) with parameters set to -auto -anysymbol -quiet. The -auto option automatically selects an appropriate algorithm based on alignment size: L-INS-i for fewer than 200 sequences, FFT-NS-i for 200-2,000 sequences, or FFT-NS-2 for more than 2,000 sequences. All alignments utilized the BLOSUM62 scoring matrix with default gap penalties. Simulation datasets were generated using IQ-Tree (v3.0.1). For specialized analyses, the speer and subsite tools were executed using the source code provided in their original publications. The speer script was run using Perl (v5.38.2), while the subsite source code was compiled and executed using GCC (v13.1.0). Furthermore, the groupsim tool, originally developed for Python 2, was refactored for compatibility with Python 3 and run in the same Python (v3.10.10) environment.
Collection and Processing of Datasets

We utilized phylogenetic data from the PANTHER (Protein Analysis THrough Evolutionary Relationships) database and, after rigorous filtering and selection, constructed 4,540 "protein families" comprising 10,133 human genes and 215,480 protein sequences.

The PANTHER database generates fully reconciled phylogenetic trees through a combination of software-generated models and expert review, providing phylogenetically related data for thousands of protein families. As PANTHER was designed to model evolutionary sequence-function relationships on a large scale, many of the families it defines resemble extensive superfamilies, encompassing numerous subfamilies. In contrast, DIVERGE focuses more specifically on the functional divergence that occurs within individual protein families following gene duplication events. Consequently, the family definitions in DIVERGE are closer to a group of genes that evolved after the speciation of single-metazoan animals. In this study, we selected nodes from PANTHER-generated phylogenies where gene duplication events occurred and identified potential nodes for functional divergence, using these as candidate genes to construct the "protein families".

DIVERGE employs complete deletion of gaps during computation, whereas the MSAs provided by PANTHER database are generated using genomic data from 143 species. As a result, the MSA for each "protein family" tend to be lengthy and contain a significant number of gaps, leading to a reduced number of non-gap sites. When the total number of non-gap sites is low, the variance increases, leading to less accurate estimates. To mitigate this issue, we selected 19 vertebrate species for constructing the "protein families" and performed MSA on their protein sequences using the MAFFT software with default parameters. To increase the proportion of non-gap sites, we further filtered the sequences by penalizing the gap sites in the alignment. The fewer gaps in a given column, the higher the gap penalty score assigned to that column. We then applied clustering methods to exclude species sequences that significantly contributed to the overall gap count in the alignment. For phylogenetic tree construction, we extracted subtrees directly from the large phylogenetic trees of PANTHER families. These phylogenetic trees have undergone expert review, offering more accurate evolutionary relationships compared to trees constructed solely from the MSAs of the 19 selected vertebrate species.
Development of Python Package

Earlier versions of DIVERGE were desktop applications developed in C, with the graphical interface built using the Qt framework. DIVERGE v4 uses the PyBind11 library1 to bind Python with C code and implements the original DIVERGE algorithm.
DIVERGE v4 is structured into three distinct layers, each playing a crucial role in the tool's functionality and usability:

C API (Base Layer): The foundational layer of DIVERGE v4 consists of the existing C API, which provides access to the core data structures and functions. This layer is critical for the tool's performance, as it handles the computationally intensive tasks associated with evolutionary analysis.

Python Wrapper (Middle Layer): The middle layer is a C Python wrapper, created using PyBind11. This layer serves as a bridge between the C API and the high-level Python API, making the core functions accessible to Python users.

High-Level Python API (Top Layer): The topmost layer is the user-friendly Python API, designed for ease of use. It offers a set of classes that allow users to build models, run simulations, and perform analyses using Python's object-oriented programming features.
Construction of DIVERGE-Chat and DIVERGE Web Server

DIVERGE-Chat was developed as a conversational assistant for functional divergence analysis, utilizing a chatflow framework that integrated multiple agents supporting tool calls and multi-turn memory. Within this framework, each agent was designed using a role-based approach, where explicit instructions defined the responsibilities and behaviors of each LLM agent. During operation, when a user queried DIVERGE-Chat, the Plan agent leveraged the LLM to understand the user's needs and assign the appropriate agent to process the task. Specifically, the agent responsible for data querying generated SQL query statements based on natural language input, aligned with the user's requirements, to retrieve relevant data for subsequent analysis. The primary data source consisted of curated protein family phylogenetic data and associated functional annotation information, which we had previously integrated into multiple tables using PostgreSQL. While direct retrieval from public databases might offer more flexibility, querying our curated PostgreSQL database ensured that the DIVERGE-Chat utilized accurate and consistent phylogenetic data. The agent responsible for functional divergence computation primarily invoked the modular DIVERGE python API through code blocks to perform calculations. The resulting structured outputs were then summarized and analyzed by the LLM model to provide insightful interpretations of the functional divergence results. Finally, a check agent was designed to monitor key stages of the task, verifying at these points whether the user's requirements had been met, and periodically correcting the task as needed. This approach aimed to mitigate potential inaccuracies, such as hallucinations, thereby enhancing overall output reliability. To facilitate more complex or iterative exploration of functional divergence in protein families of interest, DIVERGE-Chat was designed with multi-turn memory functionality, allowing users to follow up on previous queries. Agents were configured to collaborate in a shared environment, where they could exchange information while maintaining role-specific autonomy.

Complementing the conversational interface, the DIVERGE web server was constructed using Streamlit, a Python library for building interactive web applications. This framework facilitated the creation of a dashboard that allowed users to load local files and request remote data from external resources via real-time API calls. The use of Streamlit enabled rapid development of this web application purely from Python scripts.

Algorithm of Super-Cluster

To address the challenge of analyzing functional divergence in gene families with numerous duplicate clusters, we developed the Super-Cluster method. This approach is grounded in a Finite-State Conservation model (see Supplementary Material). The model posits that at any amino acid site, each duplicate cluster can exist in one of two fundamental states: a conserved state (, low evolutionary rate) or a variable state (, high evolutionary rate). For a gene family with m clusters, the overall conservation pattern at a site can therefore be described by a binary vector . Each unique vector, which we term an S-pattern, corresponds to a distinct hypothesis of Type-I functional divergence. Under this model, clusters sharing the same state (e.g. all  or all ) are assumed to have a common evolutionary rate, while those with different states evolve independently.

The operational principle of the Super-Cluster method is to directly test for these S-patterns. Any given S-pattern inherently implies a bipartite partition of the m clusters. Our algorithm leverages this by consolidating all clusters within each part of the partition into one of two opposing 'super-clusters'. This procedure effectively reduces the complex, multi-body divergence problem into a tractable pairwise comparison, which can be robustly analyzed using established methods like DIVERGE. The detailed procedure of Super-Cluster analysis is formalized in Algorithm 1 and the algorithm can be concisely described as follows:
Partition m clusters into two groups (Super-Cluster pairs, A and B), regardless of the phylogenetic structure. There are  different partitions, e.g. , 3, and 7 for , 3, and 4, respectively.
For each Super-Cluster, the number of changes at an amino acid site, denoted by  or , is simply a sum of those over duplicate clusters included in the Super-Cluster.

For each Super-Cluster pair, perform DIVERGE Type-I analysis and record the site-specific posterior probabilities (Q -values) of being F1-sites, providing a divergence profile of the multi-gene family.

The central hypothesis is that a one-to-one correspondence exists between a specific S-pattern and the super-cluster partition that achieves the highest posterior probability of divergence. By systematically generating and analyzing all M possible non-trivial partitions, our approach can effectively pinpoint the most probable divergence pattern across the gene family and identify the key amino acid sites involved. This strategy circumvents the need for a direct multi-cluster mixture model, which is often computationally intractable for large m, by reframing the problem as a comprehensive series of well-posed pairwise tests.

passages.text: Genomic profiling of high tumor mutational load in microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer uncovers MAPK signaling pathway alterations following anti-EGFR therapy
Background
Translational studies have provided evidence that targeted therapies and chemotherapy might induce a status of adaptive mutability with an increase in the tumor mutational load.
Patients and methods

We conducted an analysis of pathogenic variants (PVs) detected by liquid biopsy (LBx)-based comprehensive genomic profiling in patients with chemo-refractory microsatellite-stable metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) pretreated with anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) within the VELO and CAVE-2 GOIM studies compared with anti-EGFR naive mCRC included in the CAPRI-2 GOIM trial.
Results

Overall, 559 patients with available samples for LBx analysis were included. EGFR pretreated tumors had significant enrichment for PVs in the MAPK signaling pathway with a median tumor mutational burden (TMB) [6 interquartile range (IQR 4-11) versus 4 (IQR 3-9), P < 0.0001]; 33.8% pretreated patients had TMB with >=10 mutations per megabase compared with 9.7% patients before first-line anti-EGFR treatment. Higher mutational load correlated with KRAS (q = 0.07), BRAFV600 (q = 0.01), ERBB2 AMP (q = 0.06) and EGFR ECD (q = 0.07) PVs. Such association was not observed in patients naive to anti-EGFR drugs. MAPK mutations were associated with higher TMB in anti-EGFR pretreated samples (beta = 4.0, P < 0.0001), but not in anti-EGFR-naive samples (beta 1.2, P = 0.4).
Conclusion
These findings might support the investigation of immunotherapy in patients with mCRC pretreated with EGFR inhibitors with high mutational load.
Highlights
Patients with mCRC pretreated with anti-EGFR therapies displayed higher TMB.
Anti-EGFR exposure might promote the development of sub-clonal alterations.
Augmented TMB was correlated with alteration in MAPK signaling.
Introduction

Metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is a malignancy characterized by several molecular alterations that promote cancer initiation, progression and invasiveness. For patients with RAS/BRAF-wild type (wt), microsatellite-stable (MSS) mCRC the addition of anti-epidermal growth factor (EGFR) inhibitors to chemotherapy is a standard of care. Despite initial antitumor activity, as for other target therapies, cancer cells will develop a mechanism of acquired resistance.

It has been shown in preclinical models of CRC that blocking EGFR signaling might cause DNA damage, stimulating adaptive mutability in cancer cells with the accumulation of genomic alterations, which become responsible for loss of responsiveness to anti-EGFR therapy. In this respect, increase in tumor mutational burden (TMB) could convert a low- into a high-immunogenic tumor microenvironment, supporting the rationale for the use of immunotherapy. Despite this biologic rationale, available clinical evidence is limited; thus, further research is needed. Recently, liquid biopsy (LBx) has emerged as a noninvasive tool, which allows researchers to obtain a dynamic portrait of the tumor molecular landscape and to detect anti-EGFR drug resistance mutations.

In this study, we carried out an exploratory analysis of pathogenic variants (PVs) identified through LBx-based comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) in a homogeneous cohort of anti-EGFR pretreated patients with MSS mCRC enrolled in the VELO and CAVE-2 GOIM studies. This cohort was compared with a cohort of anti-EGFR-naive patients from the CAPRI-2 GOIM trial. We then investigated whether specific alterations in signaling pathways were associated with higher TMB. Finally, we explored the potential impact of prior exposure to anti-EGFR monoclonal antibodies on tumor heterogeneity.
Methods
Study population
We conducted a pooled analysis of genomic data of patients enrolled in the VELO (NCT05468892), CAVE-2 GOIM (NCT05291156) and CAPRI-2 GOIM (NCT05312398).

VELO was a randomized phase II trial evaluating panitumumab plus trifluridine-tipiracil versus trifluridine-tipiracil alone as third-line therapy for RAS-wt mCRC. Patients should have obtained a partial response or complete response to first-line chemotherapy plus an anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody and an anti-EGFR free interval >=4 months during second-line therapy. Plasma samples were collected at baseline for LBx analysis.

CAVE-2 GOIM is a randomized phase II study assessing the combination of cetuximab plus avelumab compared with cetuximab as anti-EGFR rechallenge strategy in pretreated patients with circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) RAS/BRAFV600-wt MSS/mismatch repair-proficient mCRC.

CAPRI-2 GOIM trial investigates the efficacy and safety of a ctDNA biomarker-guided, cetuximab-based therapy over three treatment lines in mCRC patients with RAS/BRAF-wt tumors at start of first-line. Here we evaluated results of baseline LBx analysis before the initiation of first-line treatment.

Cases with baseline pretreatment plasma samples adequate for LBx-based ctDNA CGP by FoundationOne Liquid (F1L) CDx assay (https://www.foundationmedicine.com/test/foundationone-liquid-cdx) assessing 324 genes were considered eligible. Main exclusion criteria were (i) nonavailability of baseline plasma sample; (ii) inadequate ctDNA for LBx analysis; (iii) F1L CDx assay evaluating 78 genes; (iv) microsatellite instable (MSI) tumors; (v) withdrawal of patient consent to participate.
Genomic analyses

Only pathogenic genomic alterations detected by F1L CDx assay were included for analyses. Tumor clonality was calculated as the ratio between the detected variant allele frequency and the estimated tumor fraction (TF). Considering the potential role as mechanism(s) of resistance to anti-EGFR therapies, the following genes were included in the hyper-selection panel included RAS, BRAFV600, NF1, MAP2K1, EGFR-extracellular domain (ECD), PIK3CA exon 20, PTEN mutations, MET, FGFR1/2/3, ERBB2 amplifications (ERBB2 AMP), NTRK1/2/3, ROS1, and ALK rearrangements.
Statistical analyses

Continuous variables were reported as median and interquartile range (IQR) and compared between groups using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables were reported as frequencies and proportions and compared using Fisher's exact test. The linear association between gene alterations and an increase in TMB was calculated using ordinary least squares linear regression analysis. All tests were carried out assuming a two-sided statistical significance with an alpha level of <0.05. Family-wise error correction, where specified, was carried out using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Statistical analyses were conducted with Python software version 3.9.21.
Results

Overall, a total of 559 patients met the inclusion criteria and their data were incorporated in the current analysis (Figure 1). The study cohort includes 205 patients (36.6%) who were anti-EGFR naive and enrolled in the CAPRI-2 trial, and 354 (63.3%) patients who were candidates for anti-EGFR rechallenge therapy in the CAVE-2 and VELO trials.

We first sought to investigate the different prevalence of gene alterations between the two cohorts. In the overall study population, we observed APC (481 mutations), TP53 (394 mutations) and KRAS (141 mutations) to be the most common PVs. Previous studies have shown a potential clearance of anti-EGFR resistance PVs following exposure to chemotherapy during an anti-EGFR free interval. Comparing the two clinical settings, anti-EGFR pretreated patients who were candidates for rechallenge therapy had significant enrichment for alterations included in the MAPK signaling pathway (Figure 2A): KRAS [33.9% versus 6.0%, odds ratio (OR) 8.3, q < 0.001], EGFR ECD, 13.9% versus 1.0%, OR 15.9, q < 0.0001), MAP2K1 (13.9% versus 3.0%, OR 5.20, q = 0.003), BRAFnonV600 (7.9% versus 0.5%, q = 0.0004, OR 17.1) and NRAS (13.0% versus 3.0%, OR 4.8, q = 0.0005) (Figure 2B). This result was confirmed by conducting a pathway-level analysis. Of note, beside a slight enrichment of mutations in the TP53-pathway among pretreated tumors (77.9% versus 61.9%, OR 2.17, q = 0.0002), only mutations involving MAPK signaling were statistically significantly enriched among patients previously exposed to anti-EGFR drugs (48.3% versus 17.0%, OR 4.53, q < 0.0001) (Figure 2C). Emergence of anti-EGFR resistance PVs (RPVs) has been described in tumors that were transitioning in a genomic instability state, by favoring an increased rate of somatic mutations that are pathogenic hits in key resistance genes. Patients in the advanced treatment lines had higher median TMB [6 (IQR 4-11) versus 4 (IQR 3-9), P < 0.0001] (Figure 2D). More pretreated tumors (33.8%) than tumors that were candidates for first-line anti-EGFR treatment (9.7%) exhibited a TMB >=10 mutations per megabase (mut/Mb) (Figure 2E). This TMB value represents the diagnostic cut-off for the approved clinical indication for tumor-agnostic use of immune checkpoint inhibitors.

We next assessed whether augmented mutational load among anti-EGFR pretreated samples could be correlated with specific subgroups. A linear increase in TMB was associated with mutations in KRAS (beta = 2.91, q = 0.005), BRAFV600 (beta = 7.16, q = 0.005), BRCA2 (beta= 7.26, q = 0.005), and EGFR ECD (beta = 4.00, q = 0.058). Once stratified per treatment line, a higher TMB was reported in pretreated tumors carrying KRAS (q = 0.07), BRAFV600 (q = 0.01), ERBB2 AMP (q = 0.06) and EGFR ECD (q = 0.07) molecular alterations (Figure 2F). Nevertheless, such association was not observed among samples from patients who were naive to anti-EGFR therapies. Moreover, MAPK mutations were associated with higher TMB in samples from anti-EGFR pretreated patients (beta = 4.0, P < 0.0001), but not in samples from patients before first-line treatment of metastatic disease (beta 1.2, P = 0.4) (Figure 2G).

We next assessed the correlation between molecular hyper-selection and TMB. Overall, a higher proportion of tumors from patients who were previously exposed to anti-EGFR therapies had PVs of anti-EGFR drug resistance (56.7% versus 26.3%, OR 3.67, P < 0.0001) (Figure 2H). Tumors that exhibited PVs potentially correlated with anti-EGFR resistance (positively hyper-selected) that increased TMB compared with tumors without resistance alterations (negatively hyper-selected tumors) [median TMB, 8 (IQR 5-13) versus 4 (IQR 3-8), P < 0.0001] (Figure 2I), which was consistent among tumors not carrying RAS/BRAFV600 PVs [median TMB, 8 (IQR 4-10) versus 4 [IQR (3-8), P < 0.0001]. Once considering genes included in the hyper-selection list of genes, but not in the MAPK signaling cascade, mutated tumors (n = 47) had higher TMB compared with wild-type tumors [median TMB, 6 (IQR 4-10) versus 4 (3-8), P = 0.0006], which was consistent in samples from pretreated patients [n = 27, median TMB 9, (IQR 6-15.5) versus 4 (IQR 3-8), P < 0.0001], but not in samples from patients who were not previously exposed to anti-EGFR drugs [n = 20, 4 (IQR 1-6.5) versus 4 (3-7), P = 0.98].

We finally evaluated if previous exposure to anti-EGFR therapies could account for a distinct tumor heterogeneity. Anti-EGFR drug pretreated tumors had lower cancer cell clonality of detected PVs [47.0% (IQR 8.2-72.5) versus 59% (IQR 35.3-87.0), P < 0.0001]. Mutations in EGFR ECD (q < 0.0001), KRAS (q = 0.004), BRAFV600 (q = 0.006) and NRAS (q = 0.03) were found in tumors with lower cancer cell clonality compared with nonmutated samples. Although mutations involving EGFR ECD, KRAS, BRAFV600 and NRAS were associated with lower cancer cell clonality compared with background mutations, this was not the case for samples from patients who were not previously exposed to anti-EGFR drugs (Figure 2L). Moreover, co-occurring gene mutations in tumors carrying EGFR ECD, KRAS, BRAFV600 and NRAS had lower cancer cell clonality compared with wild-type tumors [54.7% (IQR 19.9-78.6) versus 60.0% (IQR 35.5-88.5), P = 0.01] (Figure 2M).
Discussion

Tumor heterogeneity represents a key determinant driving progression and resistance to targeted therapies. Interestingly, cancer cell resistance and progression might occur through the emergence and expansion of sub-clones that carry private mutations not found in coexisting cancer cell clones, therefore being represented at lower clonality.

In this study, we confirm that anti-EGFR drug exposure exerts a significant impact on the landscape of tumor genomic alterations in mCRC. In samples from anti-EGFR pretreated patients, we observed overall lower cancer cell clonality for KRAS/NRAS/BRAFV600 and EGFR ECD mutations compared with samples from patients who were candidates for first-line treatment (i.e. they were not previously exposed to anti-EGFR drugs). Moreover, coexisting PVs in the same sample displayed lower cancer cell clonality, underlining the potential presence of multiple clonal lineages emerging after exposure to anti-EGFR therapies and multiple lines of treatment. In a previous analysis of the CAVE-2 GOIM study we observed a correlation between the concomitant presence of sub-clonal RAS/BRAFV600 mutations and other sub-clonal PVs, suggesting that in case of a lower clonality multiple alterations were required to develop anti-EGFR resistance.

Similarly, Topham and colleagues reported in a cohort of 66 patients with chemo-refractory MSS mCRC, that after progression to anti-EGFR drugs, cancer resistance occurred via a multiplicity of concurrent sub-clonal alterations, with 21% of tumors having more >10 putative RPVs.

Although MSI or POLE/POLD-1 mCRC is characterized by a hyper-mutability state, most MSS tumors (90%-92%) display low TMB with <10 mut/Mb. Notably, we report that 33.8% of MSS anti-EGFR/chemo-refractory tumors had high mutational load. In a previous report TMB was significantly increased in plasma samples of the anti-EGFR pretreated patients compared with patients who were not pretreated with anti-EGFR drugs.

Consequently, we sought to investigate potential molecular mechanism(s) associated with increased mutational load. A correlation between KRAS/BRAFV600/EGFR ECD and BRCA2 PVs and increased TMB was reported. These findings were observed only for tumors of anti-EGFR drug treated patients, in which alterations of MAPK signaling cascade were also associated with an augmented TMB.

In this regard, a translational analysis of the IMblaze370 study showed that alterations in EGFR/MAPK signaling, but not in PI3K pathway genes, are selectively enriched in patients after anti-EGFR exposure but not following anti-angiogenic therapies in mCRC. Taken together these results suggest that MAPK alterations correlate with increased TMB only in anti-EGFR pretreated tumors. Nevertheless, it is difficult to discern if this is a causal relationship (therapy-induced genomic instability) or a secondary correlation. Further translational studies are required to clarify this association.

Emerging evidence supports the concept that a deeper molecular stratification, beside RAS/BRAF evaluation, might better select patients who could benefit from anti-EGFR inhibition. Given the overlap between MAPK signaling cascade genes and those promoting resistance to anti-EGFR therapies, we next assessed whether molecular hyper-selection could identify tumors carrying a higher mutational load. Positive hyper-selected tumors had higher TMB compared with negative hyper-selected tumors. The difference was also retained after excluding RAS/BRAFV600 PVs and MAPK alterations. Taken together, these findings underline the potential strict connection between hyper-mutability state and acquiring anti-EGFR RPVs in cancer cells treated with EGFR inhibitors.

Recently, pembrolizumab has been approved as an agnostic-therapy for the treatment of tumors with high TMB. However, limited evidence is available for mCRC. The CO.26 trial investigated the clinical activity of dual checkpoint blockade with durvalumab/tremelimumab in a cohort of pretreated patients with mCRC. A plasma TMB threshold of 28 mut/Mb was useful to identify patients who could benefit from immunotherapy. It could be argued that only clonal and more immunogenic alterations might represent a potential predictive biomarker for immunotherapy efficacy. In the CO.26 study, the authors reported a threshold of 25.9 mut/Mb for separating patients based on overall survival for sub-clonal plasma TMB. However, it should be considered that this threshold is significantly higher than the cut-off used in the KEYNOTE 158 study. Thus, the optimal cut-off to select patients with MSS mCRC that might benefit from immunotherapy combinatory strategies deserves further investigation.

In this regard, there is a rationale for immunotherapy use in MSS tumors with a mutational load induced secondary to anti-EGFR therapies. The CAVE-GOIM trial demonstrated the safety and provided signal of clinical activity for combining cetuximab with the anti-programmed death-ligand one (PD-L1) avelumab, as a rechallenge strategy in patients with refractory RAS-wt mCRC. The antitumor activity might be related to the capability of cetuximab to promote activation of natural killer cells and enhancement of antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity. In this scenario, mature results of the CAVE-2 GOIM trial will provide further evidence. The study has completed the enrollment and mature data are awaited.
Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the results presented in this study. The CAVE-2 GOIM and VELO trials initially enrolled patients with RAS-wt mCRC, who experienced clinical benefit from front-line anti-EGFR-based chemotherapy. These patients subsequently experienced disease progression and were treated with another line of therapy, ultimately becoming candidates for an anti-EGFR rechallenge strategy. However, serial plasma samples from the first to later lines of therapy were not available, and therefore, comparisons were made using a cohort of patients with RAS/BRAFV600-wt MSS, prior to treatment for metastatic disease. Moreover, matched tissue samples for patients who were candidates for anti-EGFR rechallenge were not available. However, the previous genomic analysis of CAPRI-2 GOIM trial showed a good concordance between tissue and LBx-based CGP especially in case of TF >10. Thus, in these cases LBx evaluation might represent a valuable noninvasive option for monitoring tumor molecular profiling in patients treated with tailored treatment. However, in the case of low TF (<1), LBx could not allow to identify PVs with a lower clonality or complex genomic alterations such as deletion or rearrangement of copy number variation.

Finally, for patients in the CAVE-2 GOIM and VELO trials, detailed data regarding the duration of first-line therapy, the number of anti-EGFR therapy cycles, and the maintenance strategies employed were unavailable. As a result, the potential impact of these factors on the development and clearance of PVs could not be assessed. In this context, the ongoing CAPRI-2 GOIM trial presents a unique opportunity to investigate cancer cell clonal evolution across three consecutive lines of therapy for metastatic disease in RAS/BRAFV600-wt MSS mCRC patients, through longitudinal LBx-based CGP evaluation.

passages.text: Multiomics Integration Reveals Rearing System-Induced Variations in Volatile Organic Compounds, Metabolites, and Meat Quality of Lueyang Black-Bone Chickens

Indigenous chicken breeds are favored in China for superior meat quality. We compared the breast meat of Lueyang black-bone chickens reared under free-range and cage systems at four ages (120, 150, 180, and 360 days), integrating phenotypic, metabolomic, volatilomic, and transcriptomic analyses. Free-range chickens displayed a lighter meat color and reduced intramuscular fat content. At 120 days, caged chickens exhibited a richer volatile organic compound (VOC) profile correlating with fat deposition; as fat increased in the free-range group, this correlation lessened, with elevated 2-pentylfuran, tetradecanoic acid ethyl ester, and 2-nonanol. Multiomics integration revealed that the rearing system alters the muscle metabolic O-phosphorylethanolamine in adaptive regulation of muscle development and fat deposition via the Kennedy pathway and identified TGFB2, MAP3K, PPP3CA, and PPM1A as key regulators. These findings clarify the molecular mechanisms by which free-range rearing enhances meat quality, informing indigenous poultry production.
Introduction

Over the past two decades, increasing evidence has underscored the adverse effects of conventional cage systems on poultry welfare, thereby driving a global shift toward alternative rearing methods. Notable regulatory milestones, such as the European Union's Welfare of Laying Hens Directive (Council Directive 1999/74/EC) and the Welfare of Meat Chickens Directive (Council Directive 2007/43/EC), played a key role in encouraging the transition to systems that accommodate natural behaviors like perching, nesting, and dust-bathing. -   These regulations marked a crucial turning point in rearing practices, catalyzing improvements in animal welfare standards.

Cage systems are typically associated with higher productivity, including increased weight gain and improved feed conversion rates, while alternative systems such as free-range and pasture-based farming offer notable advantages in meat quality. Free-range systems have been shown to improve meat characteristics, such as tenderness, flavor, color, and reduced fat deposition. However, they also present distinct challenges, including elevated mortality rates and reduced egg production in laying hens. Moreover, issues such as biosecurity risks arising from the dispersion of flocks, coupled with ecological concerns related to manure management and nutrient runoff, complicate the widespread adoption of free-range systems. These economic and environmental trade-offs highlight the complexity of achieving an optimal balance between animal welfare and production efficiency.

In China, traditional free-range farming remains prevalent, particularly for indigenous chicken breeds, which are renowned for their superior meat quality. The increasing consumer demand for high-quality, safety-assured food products has contributed to a willingness to pay a premium for free-range chicken. In contrast, intensively reared white-feathered broilers, which are genetically selected for high yield, often face quality-related challenges, such as the development of wooden breast muscle, spaghetti meat, and white striping. -   Despite growing interest in free-range and cage-free rearing paradigms, China currently lacks dedicated legislation and unified management standards for free-range systems, whereas intensive cage rearing, which is favored for its cost-reducing benefits, continues to predominate. This regulatory void and economic bias have constrained the expansion of free-range production. To overcome these limitations, targeted policy development and technological innovation are urgently required. Crucial areas of focus include elucidating the impacts of rearing systems on broiler growth performance, health status, and muscle-development pathways. By integrating regulatory reform with mechanistic insights into muscle biology and breed-specific adaptability, it will be possible to establish standardized, welfare-oriented free-range protocols optimized for indigenous Chinese chicken breeds, thereby aligning animal welfare objectives with production efficiency and meat quality.

Recent advances in analytical techniques, such as volatilomics and metabolomics, have provided novel insights into the metabolic pathways that influence meat quality. Metabolomics, particularly widely targeted metabolomics, integrates both untargeted and targeted approaches, offering a comprehensive metabolic profile. Volatilomics, on the other hand, focuses on the analysis of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), which are crucial for understanding meat flavor. When integrated with transcriptomics, these techniques allow for a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms that regulate meat quality, elucidating the metabolic pathways involved in the formation of key flavor compounds and fat deposition.

This study aims to investigate the molecular and metabolic differences in the breast muscle of Lueyang black-bone chickens reared in cage and free-range systems. By integrating phenotypic analysis with volatilomics, metabolomics, and transcriptomics, we seek to identify marker metabolites and regulatory pathways that mediate the observed differences in chicken meat characteristics. The findings are expected to provide a molecular foundation for enhancing poultry farming practices and optimizing production systems that balance animal welfare, efficiency, and meat quality.
Material and Methods
Ethical Statement

The experimental procedures and animal treatments were reviewed and approved by the Ethical Committee of the Experimental Animal Center at Northwest A&F University (Protocol number WAFAC1008). All animal handling was conducted in strict adherence to the Animal Ethics Procedures and Guidelines of the People's Republic of China.
Animals, Facilities, and Experimental Design

A total of 200 1 day-old female LYB chicks were obtained from Shaanxi Long Jia Agricultural Science and Technology Development Co., Ltd. The chicks were raised under standard brooding conditions until they reached 70 days of age. After routine immunization had been completed (DB6107/T 14.1-4-2020), 140 chicks with uniform body weights were randomly assigned to two rearing systems: cage-reared (CR) and free-range (FR). Each system comprised seven replicates with 10 birds per replicate. A two week preliminary trial was conducted to verify animal welfare protocols and the feasibility of the experimental procedures; no health or management issues were observed. Thereafter, the formal experiment commenced.

In the CR group, the chickens were housed in three-tiered breeding cages (50 x 45 x 35 cm) equipped with linear feeders and automatic nipple drinkers. Each cage housed a single bird, providing approximately 0.15 m2 of floor space per bird.

For the FR group, chickens were housed in indoor floor pens measuring 7 x 7 m, with a stocking density of 10 birds/m2, and were provided access to adjacent outdoor pastures (10 x 7 m). The indoor pens were equipped with natural ventilation, concrete floors, and an 80 cm-high plastic mesh barrier, while the outdoor areas were enclosed with wire mesh. Replicates were separated by fishing nets, and both indoor and outdoor areas contained perches, feeders, and plastic water tanks to ensure continuous access to feed and water. Birds were given unrestricted outdoor access from 06:00 to 18:00 daily, after which they were confined indoors until 06:00.

During the entire experimental period, feed and water were provided ad libitum, with all birds being given a basal diet formulated in accordance with the nutrient requirements for meat-type chickens as outlined in the Chinese National Standard (NY/T 33-2004). Both rearing systems were maintained under identical environmental conditions from March onward, including an indoor temperature of 20-25  C, relative humidity of 65-70%, and 16 h light/8-h dark photoperiod.
Sample Collection

At 120, 150, 180, and 360 days of age, one hen was randomly selected from each replicate for sample collection. Prior to slaughter, the birds were fasted for 12 h, with free access to water. Birds were humanely stunned using a stun bath and euthanized by severing the jugular vein and carotid artery on one side of the neck, ensuring quick and painless death. The left pectoralis major was collected for meat quality assessment, while the right pectoralis major was reserved for omics sequencing. For omics analysis, breast meat samples were collected in quintuplicate (3 g per tube), snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80  C. All sampling procedures were performed by a trained professional, with samples collected from the same position in the pectoralis major muscle for each individual.
Determination of Serum Lipid Concentrations

Blood samples (4 mL/chicken) were taken from the brachial vein and stored in anticoagulant-free vacuum tubes for determining serum biochemical indices. The blood samples were transported to our laboratory (stored in ice) and immediately centrifuged at 4,000 g for 10 min at 4  C. Levels of serum triglyceride (TG), total cholesterol (TC), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) were measured using a biochemical autoanalyzer (HITACHI 7600, Japan). Results were expressed in mmol/L.
Determination of Intramuscular Fat Content

Intramuscular fat (IMF) content of breast muscle was determined using Soxhlet petroleum ether extraction (NY/T 821-2019, section 5.6). Approximately 5 g of ground breast meat was extracted with petroleum ether (50-70  C) for 4 h. Each sample was analyzed in triplicate.
Oil Red O Staining

Intramuscular fat accumulation was assessed by using Oil Red O staining. Breast muscle samples were embedded in the OCT compound, frozen in liquid nitrogen, and sectioned into 8 mum slices. Sections were stained with 0.05% Oil Red O at room temperature for 30 min to detect lipid droplets. Photomicrographs were captured using an Olympus microscope (Olympus Corporation, Japan).
Sample Preparation for Volatile Organic Compound (VOC) Sequencing

Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were analyzed using headspace solid-phase microextraction gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (HS-SPME-GC-MS). Samples were retrieved from a -80  C freezer, ground in liquid nitrogen, and vortexed to ensure uniform mixing. Approximately 0.2 g of each sample was weighed and placed in a headspace vial. To each vial were added 0.2 g of NaCl and 20 muL of an internal standard solution (3-hexanone-2,2,4,4-D4, 10 mug/mL in n-hexane). After 5 min of equilibration at 60  C, VOCs were extracted for 15 min using a 120 mum DVB/CWR/PDMS SPME Arrow (CTC Analytics AG, Switzerland) followed by desorption at 250  C for 5 min. The desorbed analytes were analyzed by GC-MS.
GC-MS Analyses

VOCs were separated on a DB-5MS capillary column (30 m x 0.25 mm x 0.25 mum, Agilent J&W Scientific, USA) using high-purity helium (>=99.999%) as the carrier gas at a constant flow rate of 1.2 mL/min. The GC injector temperature was maintained at 250  C with a solvent delay of 3.5 min. The column temperature was programmed as follows: initial temperature of 40  C for 3.5 min, ramped at 10  C/min to 100  C, then at 7  C/min to 180  C, followed by a ramp at 25  C/min to 280  C, where it was held for 5 min.

Mass spectrometric detection was performed using an electron ionization (EI) source set at 70 eV. The ion source, quadrupole, and MS transfer line temperatures were set at 230, 150, and 280  C, respectively. Data were acquired in selected ion monitoring (SIM) mode, with specific quantification and qualification ions chosen for each compound. Quality control (QC) samples were prepared by mixing sample extracts, and one QC sample was inserted into every ten test samples to evaluate the repeatability of the analytical process.
VOC Characterization and Quantification

The mass spectrometry data of the samples were integrated, corrected, and qualitatively and quantitatively analyzed by MassHunter. VOCs were identified and quantified using a self-constructed MWDB database (MetWare Biotechnology Co., Ltd., China), which included retention times (RT) and characteristic ions derived from multispecies references, literature data, and available authentic standards. Each compound was identified by comparing its RT and mass spectral data (including one quantification ion and 2-3 qualification ions) with those in the database. A compound was confirmed if the RT matched the reference, and all selected ions were present in the sample spectrum after background subtraction. Quantitative ions were integrated and corrected for the enhanced accuracy. The VOCs with a coefficient of variation (CV) value of QC less than 0.5 were retained to obtain the final data.

The relative content of each VOC was calculated using the following formula:where Ci  is the relative content of VOC i (mug/g); Vs  is the volume of internal standard (muL); Cs  is the concentration of internal standard (mug/mL); M is the mass of the sample (g); Is  is the peak area of the internal standard; and Ii  is the peak area of VOC i.

To evaluate each VOC's contribution to chicken flavor, compounds were annotated against multiple public flavor databases: the Good Scents Company , Perflavory , the Odor Organization , and the Food FlavorLab . The relative odor activity value (rOAV) is defined as the ratio of the concentration of a single compound to its odor threshold, indicating the compound's contribution to the overall odor properties of a substance. The rOAV was calculated using the following formula:where rOAV i  is the relative odor activity value of VOC i, Ci  is the relative content of VOC (mug/g), and Ti  is the threshold of the VOC (mug/g).
Sample Peparation for Widely Targeted LC-MS/MS

Samples were retrieved from a -80  C freezer and thawed on ice. Once thawed, the samples were ground in liquid nitrogen. A 20 +- 1 mg aliquot of each sample was transferred to a centrifuge tube followed by the addition of 400 muL of a 70% methanol-water solution containing an internal standard. The tubes were oscillated at 2500 rpm for 5 min, incubated on ice for 15 min, and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4  C. The supernatant (300 muL) was transferred to a new labeled tube and stored at -20  C for 30 min. A second centrifugation was performed at 12,000 rpm for 3 min at 4  C, and 200 muL of the resulting supernatant was collected for LC-MS analysis.
LC-MS/MS Analyses

The sample extracts were analyzed using an LC-ESI-MS/MS system consisting of an ExionLC AD UPLC (SCIEX, USA) coupled with a QTRAP System mass spectrometer (SCIEX, USA). Chromatographic separation was performed on a Waters ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 C18 column (1.8 mum, 2.1 mm x 100 mm, Waters, USA) maintained at 40  C. The flow rate was set at 0.4 mL/min with an injection volume of 2 muL. The mobile phase consisted of pure water containing 0.1% formic acid (solvent A) and acetonitrile containing 0.1% formic acid (solvent B). The gradient program was as follows: starting at 5% B, increasing to 20% B over 2 min, then ramping to 60% B over the next 3 min followed by an increase to 99% B within 1 min; 99% B was held for 90 s, after which the system was re-equilibrated to 5% B within 10 s and held for 144 s.

Data acquisition was performed using a triple quadrupole-linear ion trap mass spectrometer (QTRAP LC-MS/MS System, SCIEX, USA) equipped with an electrospray ionization (ESI) Turbo Ion-Spray interface. Analyses were conducted in both positive and negative ion modes under the control of Analyst 1.6.3 software (SCIEX, USA). The ESI source parameters were set as follows: source temperature, 500  C; ion spray voltage, 5500 V in positive mode and -4500 V in negative mode; gas I (GSI), 55 psi; gas II (GSII), 60 psi; curtain gas (CUR), 25 psi. The collision gas (CAD) was set to high. Instrument tuning and mass calibration were performed by using 10 mumol/L polypropylene glycol in QQQ mode and 100 mumol/L in LIT mode. Multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) transitions were recorded for each metabolite as they eluted from the column.
Identification and Quantification of Metabolites

The mass spectrum data were processed by Software Analyst 1.6.3. The repeatability of metabolite extraction and detection can be judged by total ion current (TIC) and multipeak MRM. Qualitative analysis was based on a self-constructed target standard MWDB database (MetWare Biotechnology Co., Ltd., China) by matching RT, precursor ion pair information, and secondary spectrum data of detected metabolites. QC samples were prepared by mixing sample extracts, and one QC sample was inserted into every ten test samples to monitor a specific set of MRM transitions to evaluate the repeatability of the analytical process. Quantification was achieved via MRM using the triple quadrupole mass spectrometer. We opened the mass spectrum file under the sample machine with multiquant software to integrate and calibrate the chromatographic peaks. The peak area of each chromatographic peak represented the relative content of the corresponding substance. The CV values of the metabolites in QC samples were calculated. The metabolites with an area of >1000, signal-to-noise ratio of >3, and CV of <0.3 for each sample met the criteria. Finally, the integrated data were subjected to variance analysis for further statistical evaluation.
Strand-Specific Library Construction for RNA-seq

Total RNA was isolated and purified using the TRIzol reagent (Thermofisher, 15596018) according to the manufacturer protocol. RNA quantity and purity were assessed with a NanoDrop ND-1000 (NanoDrop, USA), and RNA integrity was examined using a Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent, USA). A concentration of >50 ng/muL, RIN value of >7.0, and >1 mug of RNA were required for downstream experiments. The mRNA with PolyA (polyadenylate) was specifically captured by two rounds of purification using oligo(dT) magnetic beads (Dynabeads Oligo (dT), cat. 25-61005, Thermo Fisher, USA). The captured mRNAs were fragmented using the Magnesium Ion Interrupter Kit (NEBNextR Magnesium RNA Fragmentation Module, cat. E6150S, USA) at high temperature, 94  C, 5-7 min. The RNA-seq library were prepared by strand-specific library construction protocol.
Transcriptome Sequencing and Data Analysis

llumina NovaseqTM 6000 (LC Bio Technology CO., Ltd., Hangzhou, China) was used for sequencing with a PE150 mode. After sequencing, the raw data were filtered to obtain high-quality clean data. The clean data were aligned to the Gallus gallus reference genome (Ensembl genome browser 110). StringTie (version 2.1.6) software was utilized for merging and assembling clean reads from each sample, as well as gene quantification to obtain the FPKM value of each gene after normalization. To identify differentially expressed genes between treatments, DESeq2 (version 1.22.2) was employed for differential expression analysis, applying a fold change (FC) threshold of >= 1.5 and adjusted p-value (q) < 0.05.
Statistical Analysis

Data were initially assessed for the normality and homogeneity of variance. Results are presented as means +- standard deviation (n = 7). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by least significant difference (LSD) post hoc tests was performed using SPSS 26.0 (SPSS Inc., USA). Additionally, orthogonal partial least-squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) and weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA), as well as correlation analyses, were performed using R version 4.4.1. OPLS-DA was implemented using the MetaboAnalyst R 4.0.0 package, and WGCNA was conducted using the WGCNA 1.73 package. Data were log2-transformed and mean-centered before analysis.
Results
Lipid Deposition Analysis of Breast Meat

The rearing system significantly influences the meat color and quality. As shown in Figure  A, the LYB chicken breast exhibited predominantly black coloration, with meat from the CR group appearing darker than that of the FR group. Our previous study demonstrated that the meat color parameters L* and the whiteness index were significantly higher in the FR group compared to the CR group, suggesting lighter meat coloration and slower melanin deposition under the free-range rearing system.

Histomorphological of breast and serum lipid profile comparisons between cage-reared (CR) and free-range (FR) chickens. (A) Histomorphological observation of chicken breast. VOC Profile of LYB Chicken Breast

Table S1 shows the specific information on the identified VOC, including qualitative and quantitative ions, relative molecular mass, and odors annotated to the flavor database. A total of 321 VOCs were identified in LYB chicken breast. These VOCs were classified into eight major categories: hydrocarbons (65, 20.25%), heterocyclic compounds (43, 13.40%), esters (37, 11.53%), ketones (35, 10.59%), alcohols (31, 9.66%), aromatics (31, 9.66%), aldehydes (19, 5.92%), and terpenoids (18, 5.61%) (Figure  A). Semiquantitative analysis using an internal standard indicated that the relative abundance of VOCs decreased in the following order: alcohols, heterocyclic compounds, aldehydes, hydrocarbons, ketones, esters, acids, and terpenoids (Figure  B).

Contribution of VOCs to Chicken Flavor

To assess the contribution of individual VOCs to chicken flavor, we calculated rOAVs. Among the 321 identified VOCs, 42 exhibited an average rOAV > 1, indicating significant contributions to the chicken flavor (Table S2). These 42 VOCs comprised 9 aldehydes, 8 alcohols, 7 esters, 6 ketones, 5 terpenoids, 3 heterocyclic compounds, 1 aromatic compound, 1 phenolic compound, 1 nitrogen compound, and 1 sulfur compound (Figure  C,D). Furthermore, annotation against multiple flavor databases further identified 111 flavor-related VOCs (Figure  E), predominantly esters, ketones, aldehydes, alcohols, terpenoids, and heterocyclic compounds. These VOCs are associated with sensory descriptors such as sweet, waxy, fruity, green, fatty, floral, woody, herbal, fresh, and citrus notes (Figure  F).
Difference Analysis of VOC in Breast Meat

OPLS-DA was used to assess the impact of the rearing systems on the chicken VOC profile. The resulting model exhibited strong explanatory power (R 2 Y > 0.5) and predictive ability (Q 2 > 0.5), with overall significance P < 0.05 (Figure S1). Differentially expressed VOCs were identified based on variable importance in projection (VIP > 1), fold change (FC > 1.5 or <0.67), and P-values (P < 0.05). There were 56, 27, 22, and 19 VOCs differentially expressed in different rearing systems at 120, 150, 180, and 360 days of age, respectively (Figure  A,B). In the FR group, the number of upregulated VOCs was 3, 2, 10, and 9 at these time points. Interestingly, we found that the differential VOCs at 120 and 150 days were mainly in the CR group. The number of differential VOCs decreased with age in the CR group, while increasing in the FR group.

Correlation Analysis of Production Performance with Breast Meat VOCs

To further investigate the relationship between VOCs and IMF, we conducted a correlation analysis between all VOCs identified at 120 days and production performance. The results revealed that most VOCs were positively correlated with IMF and abdominal fat yield but negatively correlated with breast muscle yield, meat color L*, and whiteness index (Figure  A). However, when the analysis was extended to include VOCs identified at 150, 180, and 360 days, we observed a negative correlation with both IMF and abdominal fat yield (Figure  B). This suggests that, after 120 days of age, an increase in IMF does not necessarily lead to a corresponding increase in flavor-related VOCs.
