Differential Analysis of Breast Meat Metabolites

To assess metabolite differences between the CR and FR rearing systems, we performed OPLS-DA. This supervised multivariate analysis identified metabolites significantly associated with the rearing conditions. As shown in Figure S2, the OPLS-DA score plots and permutation tests demonstrated excellent model performance (R 2 Y > 0.9, Q 2 > 0.7, and P-values <0.05), indicating high reliability and predictability in capturing the metabolic differences between the groups.

Using the criteria of VIP > 1, FC > 1.2 or <1/1.2, and P < 0.05, we identified metabolites significantly affected by the rearing systems. As shown in Figure  B, 119, 164, 89, and 196 differential metabolites were identified in the four comparison groups (CR120 vs FR120, CR150 vs FR150, CR180 vs FR180, and CR360 vs FR360, respectively). Of these, 88, 113, 44, and 137 metabolites were upregulated in the FR group (Figure  B). Figure  C is an UpSet diagram based on the differential metabolites of different comparison groups. From the perspective of the first-level classification of metabolites, amino acids and its metabolites, organic acids and its derivatives, and fatty acyls were significantly upregulated in the free-range rearing system, while the number of differentially upregulated carbohydrates and its metabolites increased significantly in the cage group after 150 days of age (Figure  D-G). The differential metabolites of each group are shown in Figure  H-K. We found that at 120, 150, and 180 days, seven metabolites were always differentially expressed under different feeding modes: 4-hydroxy-2-xoglutaric acid, Ala-Tyr, carnitine C3:1-2OH, carnitine C4-OH, cyclo(Ala-Pro), d-ornithine, and indoxylsulfuric acid. Notably, among these, 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutaric acid, Ala-Tyr, carnitine C3:1-2OH, and carnitine C4-OH were consistently affected by the rearing systems across all four time points. These metabolites indicate a sustained response to rearing systems across these time points.
Lipid Metabolites Analysis

Lipids analysis revealed that fatty acyls and glycerophospholipids were the major lipids in the LYB chicken breast (Table S3). Among these, multiple lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) and lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LPE) species exhibited significant differential expression. At 120 days, LPC(17:1/0:0) and PC(12:0/12:0) were significantly downregulated in the FR group, whereas LPE(18:3/0:0) and LPE(22:5/0:0) were significantly upregulated in the FR group. At 150 days, O-phosphorylethanolamine (OPEA) was found to be downregulated in the FR group. By 180 days, four LPC and two LPE species displayed differential expression between the two rearing systems, with LPC(16:1/0:0) and LPE(P-16:0) downregulated in the FR group, while LPC(22:4/0:0), LPC(22:6/0:0), LPC(24:6/0:0), and LPE(22:6/0:0) were upregulated in the FR group. Strand-Specific Transcriptome Sequencing

In this study, 56 samples were sequenced to obtain a comprehensive transcriptome profile, achieving an average sequencing depth of 6.22 G. After quality control and filtering, 5.70 G of valid clean data were obtained. The average Q20 and Q30 values were 99.70% and 97.30%, respectively (Supplementary Table S4). The high proportion of bases with quality scores >= 30 indicates robust sequencing quality, which is suitable for subsequent analysis. HISAT2 (ver. 2.2.1) was used to align the clean data to the Gallus gallus reference genome, achieving an average alignment rate of 87.00%. This high alignment rate suggests that the sequencing depth is sufficient to reflect gene expression levels accurately in the samples, making the clean read data suitable for further analysis (Supplementary Table S5).
Analysis of Differentially Expressed Genes

Gene quantification and differential expression analysis were performed using StringTie (version 2.1.6) for read merging, assembly, and FPKM normalization. DESeq2 (version 1.22.2) was employed for differential expression analysis, using a fold change (FC) threshold of >= 1.5 and an adjusted P-value (Q-value) of <0.05. The differential gene analysis revealed 1,350 (555 upregulated and 795 downregulated), 571 (354 upregulated and 217 downregulated), 201 (104 upregulated and 97 downregulated), and 3,691 (3,050 upregulated and 641 downregulated) differentially expressed genes in the CR120 vs FR120, CR150 vs FR150, CR180 vs FR180, and CR360 vs FR360 groups, respectively (Figure  A-D). Further examination of all differential genes identified 11 genes that were differentially expressed in different rearing systems at 120, 150, 180, 360 days of age. Among these, F3, CD164L2, PGPEP1L, SBK2, and ENSGALG00010000869 were consistently upregulated in the free-range group (Figure  E,F). The DEGs were selected for qRT-PCR analysis. The results showed that the qRT-PCR results were basically consistent with the sequencing results, indicating that the reliability of the RNA-seq results was high (Figure S3).

Weighted Gene Coexpression Network Analysis

To identify genes associated with important traits such as muscle metabolites and intramuscular fat, we performed Weighted Gene Coexpression Network Analysis (WGCNA) using FPKM values from transcriptome sequencing of 56 samples. After filtering out low-expression genes (average FPKM < 0.1), 17,921 genes remained for further analysis out of an initial 24,589 genes. A soft-thresholding power of 4 was applied, resulting in modules that conformed to a scale-free topology (Figure  A,B). Gene modules were identified through hierarchical clustering based on the dissimilarity Topological Overlap Matrix (dissTOM), with a minimum module size set to 30 genes. Modules with eigengene correlations of >0.7 were merged, yielding a total of 25 modules (Figure  C).

To explore the relationships between gene modules and phenotypic traits, including slaughter performance, serum lipid indicators, and muscle quality parameters, we conducted association analyses. The MEred module was significantly positively correlated with IMF, body weight, abdominal fat yield, meat color (a*), pH at 24 h (pH24 h), cooking loss, shear force, serum TG, and TC. Conversely, it showed significant negative correlations with breast muscle yield, meat color (L*), pH at 45 min (pH45 min), and serum HDL-C and LDL-C. The MEblack module was significantly negatively correlated with IMF, serum TC, TG, body weight, abdominal fat yield, cooking loss, and shear force, but positively correlated with serum HDL-C and LDL-C (Figure  D).

The correlation analysis between metabolites and production performance has shown that glycerophospholipid metabolites such as OPEA and LPE(22:6/0:0) are significantly positively correlated with IMF. Therefore, we further analyzed the relationship between the WGCNA gene module and glycerophospholipid metabolites. Significant associations were observed between the IMF-related modules and glycerophospholipid metabolites. Specifically, genes in the MEred module showed significant positive correlations with OPEA and LPE(22:6/0:0) while exhibiting significant negative correlations with LPC(18:1/0:0) and LPC(20:3/0:0). Conversely, genes in the MEblack module were significantly positively correlated with PC(12:0/12:0), LPC(18:1/0:0), and LPC(20:3/0:0) but negatively correlated with LPE(22:6/0:0), suggesting complex interactions between IMF-regulating genes and glycerophospholipid metabolites (Figure  E).

Furthermore, we calculated gene significance (GS) and module membership (MM) of each module and evaluated their correlations. Scatterplots illustrating the relationship between GS and MM for the traits most strongly associated with the MEred module are shown in Figure S3A-F. Corresponding scatterplots for traits linked to the MEblack module are provided in Figure S3G-K. Using thresholds of GS > 0.4 and MM > 0.8 as selection criteria, we found 97 genes significantly associated with the IMF, of which 65 genes were from the MEred module, which was significantly positively correlated with the IMF, and 32 genes were from the MEblack module, which was significantly negatively correlated with the IMF (Table S6). Additionally, scatterplots of GS and MM for the MEred and MEblack modules in relation to IMF and OPEA showed a strong correlation between GS and MM, indicating that the WGCNA-derived modules effectively capture gene sets relevant to IMF and OPEA.

Discussion

Our previous research indicated that chickens reared in a caged system exhibited higher body weight and abdominal fat deposition, whereas free-range rearing resulted in a higher breast muscle yield. Furthermore, there were significant differences in breast meat color under different rearing systems, with free-range chicken meat displaying higher lightness (L*). Histological analysis of the breast meat in this study further revealed that caged chickens exhibited more intense melanin deposition compared to free-range chickens. This result aligns with the established relationship between muscle metabolites and melanin synthesis. Studies have shown that metabolites, such as LPE 16:0 (1-palmitoyl-2-hydroxy-sn-glycerol-3-phosphoethanolamine), are involved in regulating muscle melanin deposition. Similar regulatory processes have also been confirmed in liver metabolism with respect to egg shell pigment deposition. These findings collectively suggest that the rearing system influences meat color differences through metabolite-driven regulatory mechanisms.

IMF content plays a crucial role in determining meat flavor and tenderness. While local breeds typically accumulate more IMF than commercial broilers, our study showed that free-range chickens exhibited lower IMF deposition than caged chickens across all stages of development. This phenotype was further confirmed by Oil Red O staining, which revealed fewer lipid droplets in the breast muscles of free-range chickens. Serum lipid profile analysis also supported this trend, revealing significantly higher levels of triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol (TC), and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) in caged chickens compared to those in free-range chickens. These findings are consistent with previous studies. We propose that this phenomenon results from the higher physical activity and basal metabolic rate in free-range systems, leading to increased energy expenditure and reduced lipid accumulation.

In recent years, the incidence of white striping and woody breast in commercial broilers has increased, significantly affecting the sensory characteristics of the meat. This trend is particularly concerning for consumers seeking high-quality chicken. In China, many consumers are willing to pay a premium for locally raised free-range chickens, believing that they offer superior flavor and overall quality. This shift underscores the importance of studying the regulation of chicken flavor compounds. To explore the impact of different rearing systems on chicken breast meat flavor, we focused on VOCs and their contribution to the overall flavor profile. Our study identified 321 distinct VOCs, with alcohols, heterocyclic compounds, aldehydes, hydrocarbons, ketones, esters, acids, and terpenoids accounting for 90% of the total VOCs. Previous studies have identified aldehydes and alcohols as the primary volatile components contributing to chicken meat flavor,   with hexanal and 1-octen-3-ol considered key VOC markers for chicken meat. However, our study revealed a broader VOC spectrum, with significant contributions from heterocyclic compounds and terpenoids, which were not observed in fresh chickens. Furthermore, we overlapped 111 flavor-related VOCs with 42 VOCs that exhibited an rOAV value of >1, ultimately identifying 36 key VOCs. In addition to the commonly known aldehydes and alcohols, we identified two heterocyclic compounds (2-methoxy-3-(2-methylpropyl) pyrazine and 2-pentylfuran) and five terpenoids (dl-menthol, geraniol, alpha-ionone, beta-ionone, and trans-beta-ionone), suggesting that these compounds may play an important role in the flavor of LYB chicken meat. However, further studies are needed to determine whether terpenoids and heterocyclic compounds are unique flavor compounds in LYB chicken.

Difference analysis revealed that at 120 days of age, the VOC concentrations in caged chickens were significantly higher than those in free-range chickens. Specific VOCs, such as tetradecanal, delta-dodecalactone, gamma-dodecalactone, gamma-undecanolactone, (Z)-dihydro-5-(2-octenyl)furan-2(3H)-one, and dodecanenitrile, exhibited rOAV values greater than 1 in the caged group. Correlation analysis between VOCs and IMF showed that most upregulated VOCs were positively correlated with IMF. This finding is consistent with previous studies indicating that meat with higher fat content is more likely to retain volatile compounds with fat affinity. Additionally, many of these VOCs are produced by the oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids,   confirming the decisive role of fat deposition in determining the abundance and diversity of chicken meat VOCs. Moreover, the IMF data clearly indicate that there is almost no IMF deposition in the 120 day-old free-range chickens, which is the primary reason why the VOC content in caged chickens is significantly higher than that in the free-range group.

However, when the correlation analysis was extended to 150, 180, and 360 days, the relationship between most VOCs and IMF became insignificant, and some VOCs even exhibited negative correlations with fat content. This suggests that the relationship between IMF and VOCs is more pronounced during the early growth stages of chickens. As the chickens mature, other factors may have a greater impact on the VOC profile. At 180 and 360 days, the influence of the free-range rearing system on the VOC profile gradually increased, possibly due to the promotion of plant-derived compound accumulation by environmental factors. At 180 days, we observed significant upregulation of VOCs in free-range chickens, particularly 2-pentylfuran, tetradecanoic acid ethyl ester, and 2-nonanol. The rOAV values of these VOCs were greater than 1, further indicating their importance as flavor compounds in free-range LYB chicken. Notably, 2-nonanol has a rose-like aroma and exhibits antimicrobial properties,   and 2-pentylfuran, widely present in white tea, has a bean- and dairy-like aroma.   Furthermore, tetradecanoic acid ethyl ester is widely used in the fragrance industry, highlighting its sensory relevance.

Clearly, the rearing system significantly affects the VOCs of chicken meat. During the early developmental stages (120 and 150 days), the VOC profile is primarily influenced by the IMF content, especially in caged chickens. However, during the later stages (180 and 360 days), the influence of the rearing environment on the VOC profile gradually becomes more pronounced, with free-range chickens accumulating more plant-derived VOCs. While the accumulation of these exogenous compounds is somewhat random and unstable, they still significantly impact the flavor characteristics of chicken meat. Therefore, these compounds should not be regarded as consistent or breed-specific flavor markers.

Based on the above results, it is evident that chicken meat color, IMF deposition, and flavor compounds are closely related to metabolic activities. Further exploration of muscle metabolites under different rearing systems is necessary. The metabolomic analysis of chicken breast meat revealed that LYB chicken breast primarily contains amino acids, organic acids, nucleotides, and carbohydrates, consistent with findings from studies on other chicken breeds. -   Notably, the main lipid compounds detected in breast muscle were glycerophospholipids and acylcarnitines. This distribution aligns with established observations that IMF contains an elevated phospholipid content relative to abdominal adipose tissue. Beyond serving as energy substrates, phospholipids are fundamental components of cellular membranes and participate in key signaling pathways. Given that skeletal muscle functions not only as a contractile tissue but also as an endocrine organ, requiring rapid energy mobilization during exercise, facilitating muscle repair after injury, and mediating hormone-like signaling, the high abundance of phospholipids and acylcarnitines in the breast muscle is both logical and essential for maintaining muscle homeostasis and function.

Through differential metabolite analysis, we observed higher concentrations of amino acids, organic acids, nucleotides, fatty acyls, and glycerophospholipids in free-range chickens. Skeletal muscle, as an important endocrine organ, actively participates in regulating energy balance and fat deposition. Studies have shown that physical activity can activate PGC1alpha in skeletal muscles, enhancing the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). BCAA metabolites, including isoleucine and leucine, promote muscle growth and regulate lipid deposition within muscle cells. -   In this study, upregulation of BCAA metabolites such as 3-hydroxy-2-methylbutyric acid, 2-hydroxy-4-methylpentanoic acid, isoleucine, and leucine in free-range chickens suggests that enhanced BCAA metabolism, driven by physical activity, promotes muscle protein synthesis and growth, which explains the higher breast muscle yield in free-range chickens. Simultaneously, after 150 days of age, a significant upregulation of carbohydrate metabolites was observed in the cage group, suggesting that the energy supply through carbohydrates in the cage rearing system is sufficient to support basic metabolism. This also contributes to the increased fat deposition observed in the cage group. However, it is important to note that excessive fat deposition is not a primary consumer preference.

We also observed rearing system-related differences in the expression of glycerophospholipids and acylcarnitines in chicken breast. Studies suggest that acylcarnitines may be linked to insulin resistance and diabetes development, and blood and urine levels of acylcarnitines are associated with red meat intake, mainly because red meat (especially beef and pork) contains higher levels of acylcarnitines. Chicken, with its lower acylcarnitine concentration, may therefore be more beneficial for health. Furthermore, acylcarnitines play a crucial role in the transport of fatty acids and BCAAs into the mitochondria for beta-oxidation. The upregulation of several acylcarnitines in free-range chickens suggests more active fatty acid beta-oxidation compared to caged chickens. Additionally, carnitine acetyltransferase (CrAT), a key enzyme for synthesizing medium- and short-chain acylcarnitines, is also active in BCAA oxidation products. The upregulation of medium-chain acylcarnitines in this study may be related to active BCAA metabolism, further indicating that the energy metabolism of free-range chickens undergoes adaptive changes, leading to the upregulation of metabolites, such as BCAAs and acylcarnitines.

Glycerophospholipids, especially phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), which serve as precursors for lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) and lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LPE), also exhibit differential expression across rearing systems. LPC has been shown to activate the PPARdelta pathway, promoting muscle protection and reducing inflammation, while LPE is known for its anti-inflammatory properties. The increased activity of free-range chickens may lead to higher energy expenditure, resulting in the accumulation of more phospholipids to support muscle repair and membrane remodeling. Furthermore, LPC and LPE generate fat-soluble volatile compounds during cooking, enhancing the flavor and aroma of the meat. -    This adaptive regulation of muscle metabolism not only affects muscle development and intramuscular fat deposition but also influences chicken meat flavor and quality.

We observed that differences in meat color, IMF deposition, and flavor substances, as mediated by rearing systems, were closely associated with variations in the metabolic patterns of chicken breast muscle. To investigate this further, we conducted transcriptome sequencing analysis. The results revealed that a significant number of differentially expressed genes, influenced by rearing systems, were enriched in processes related to amino acid metabolism, fatty acid metabolism, glycerophospholipid metabolism, and other key metabolic pathways.

Furthermore, these genes were found to be involved in several essential cellular processes through various signaling pathways, including MAPK, mTOR, TGF-beta, neuroactive ligand-receptor interactions, ECM-receptor interactions, cytokine-cytokine receptor interactions, calcium signaling, ErbB signaling, Wnt signaling, adipocytokine signaling, Toll-like receptor signaling, and NOD-like receptor signaling. These pathways regulate a broad spectrum of cellular activities, such as actin cytoskeleton organization, endocytosis, phagosome formation, apoptosis, tight junction formation, cellular senescence, lysosomal function, necroptosis, cell cycle regulation, and adherens junctions.

These findings suggest that the adaptive regulation of muscle metabolism, mediated by different rearing systems, plays a crucial role in modulating processes such as cell proliferation, apoptosis, and autophagy. Notably, Toll-like and NOD-like receptors appear to be central mediators through which endogenous metabolites regulate muscle development and IMF deposition. The activation of these receptors, coupled with downstream signaling cascades, such as MAPK and NF-kappaB, promotes the release of myokines and adipocytokines, ultimately regulating the function of both muscle and intramuscular fat cells.

In addition, WGCNA of the transcriptomic data identified the MEred module, which showed a significant positive correlation with IMF, body weight, abdominal fat yield, cooking loss, shear force, and serum TG and TC. Notably, the MEred module also exhibited a strong positive correlation with the OPEA and LPE(22:6/0:0), which is consistent with the previously observed correlation between metabolites and production data. OPEA, a key molecule in the Kennedy pathway, and its downstream products, lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LPE), function as ligands for G-protein-coupled receptors and Toll-like receptors, thereby activating downstream signaling that regulates inflammation and cellular functions.   These metabolites are also important intermediates in glycerophospholipid metabolism and were found to be differentially upregulated in free-range rearing systems. Previous studies suggest that OPEA could inhibit T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling by depleting diacylglycerol, an essential molecule for TCR signal transduction. Furthermore, it has been found to inhibit the proliferation, migration, and adhesion of melanoma cells. Therefore, the identification of OPEA as a key metabolite in IMF deposition provides a theoretical basis for understanding the balance between muscle development and IMF deposition in skeletal muscle. The upregulation of OPEA increases phospholipids rich in unsaturated fatty acids such as downstream LPE(22:6/0:0). The upregulation of these metabolites may activate downstream signaling pathways, which in turn affect muscle development and intramuscular fat deposition. Rearing systems mediate changes in muscle metabolism patterns in chickens, with genes such as TGFB2, MAP3K, PPP3CA, and PPM1A being associated with the differential expression of OPEA. These genes, along with OPEA, LPE(22:6/0:0), and LPE(22:5/0:0), constitute the core of the adaptive regulation of muscle metabolism. They help balance intramuscular fat deposition and muscle development through MAPK and Toll-like receptor signaling pathways. PC(12:0/12:0) containing saturated fatty acids may promote the synthesis of fatty acid metabolites and amino acids through other signaling pathways and inhibit the deposition of IMF. In subsequent research, we plan to conduct animal and cell-based experiments to further investigate OPEA's role in balancing muscle development and fat deposition. This will provide theoretical insights and scientific evidence for improving meat quality and breeding strategies for local chicken breeds.

passages.text: The receptor tyrosine kinase ErbB2/HER2 governs CDK4 inhibitor sensitivity, timing, and irreversibility of the G1/S transition

Cell cycle entry and the irreversible transition from the G1 to S phase are crucial for mammalian cell proliferation. Among the ErbB family, the ErbB2/HER2 receptor is a key driver of cancer growth. However, the quantitative mechanisms underlying the ErbB2-mediated G1/S transition remain unclarified. Here, we performed an extensive time-course analysis of high and low ErbB2-expressing breast cancer cells to describe the regulatory mechanisms of the ErbB2-mediated G1/S transition. Live-cell imaging using cell cycle reporters revealed that the G1/S transition occurs 20 h after ErbB2 activation, driven primarily by the cyclin D1/CDK4-RB axis. Hsp90 is regulated by CDK4 activity and controls the stability of ErbB2 protein in a time-dependent manner. CDK4 inhibitor treatment arrested the cell cycle in most cells; a subpopulation showed a 25-h delay in G1/S entry associated with enhanced c-Myc activation. In high ErbB2-expressing cells, CDK4 inhibition led to c-Myc overactivation, a rapid decrease in cyclin D1 expression, and cell cycle arrest. Overall, we demonstrate how ErbB2 receptor levels modulate the roles of cyclin D1 and c-Myc in the G1/S transition and suggest that variations in ErbB2 levels within breast cancer tissues confer heterogeneous sensitivity to CDK4 inhibitors, potentially complicating treatment.

The initiation of the cell cycle and subsequent transition from the G1 to S phase are regulated by a complex molecular network involving the formation of a cyclin D1/CDK4 protein complex. Understanding the regulation of the G1/S transition by mitogenic signals is fundamental for comprehending cell biology and developing cancer treatments that overcome drug resistance. For example, based on the important role of cyclin D1 overexpression in enhancing breast cancer cell proliferation, various cell cycle inhibitors targeting CDK4 have been developed to treat breast cancer.

Breast cancer can be classified into four subtypes based on the expression of estrogen receptors (ERs), progesterone receptors, and ErbB2 (HER2) receptors: luminal A (ER+ and HER2-), luminal B (ER+ and HER2+), ErbB2/HER2-positive (ER- and HER2+), and triple-negative (ER- and HER2-). CDK4 inhibitors (CDK4is) have been used to treat the luminal A subtype, but long-term administration has led to drug resistance. ErbB2 tyrosine kinase activity, commonly elevated in malignant breast cancer, increases cyclin D1 levels. Stimulation of ErbB2 receptors activates the MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT signaling pathways, leading to the rapid induction of early response genes such as c-fos and c-myc :key regulators of cyclin D1 and CDK4 expression. Both c-Myc and cyclin D1 are involved in the G1/S transition, though they appear to have distinct roles. Therefore, we hypothesized that the small population of high ErbB2-expressing cells in the luminal A subtype may contribute to CDK4i resistance by rewiring the G1/S network during the early stages of drug treatment. However, the molecular mechanisms by which ErbB2 affects the G1/S transition following CDK4i treatment remain unclear.

The G1/S transition typically involves signal-dependent and signal-independent processes, which are distinguished by the restriction (R) point. The mitogenic signal primarily regulates the expression and activation of cyclin D1/CDK4, which phosphorylates retinoblastoma protein (RB) prior to the R point. Thus, this signal-dependent process is primarily driven by the cyclin D1/CDK4-RB axis. The phosphorylation of RB (p-RB) activates E2F1, promoting the expression of its target genes, including cyclin E. Cyclin E then forms a complex with CDK2, which further phosphorylates p-RB, resulting in a fully phosphorylated state (pp-RB). pp-RB enhances E2F1 activity, creating a mitogen-independent cyclin E/CDK2-RB-E2F1 positive feedback loop. However, the expression and stability of c-Myc are modulated by external signals, and c-Myc directly influences E2F1 promoter activity. Consequently, the core machinery of cyclin E/CDK2-RB-E2F1 is considered to be indirectly regulated by mitogenic signals.

ERK controls the expression of c-Myc and cyclin D1, while AKT regulates their protein stability. However, p27 expression, which plays a crucial role in the accumulation of cyclin D1 and CDK4 during the G1 phase, is repressed by c-Myc. Since the ErbB2 receptor activates the ERK and AKT pathways at different magnitudes, different levels of ErbB2 may modulate the core machinery of the G1/S network and, consequently, the timing of cell cycle entry through modulation of cyclin D1 and c-Myc. Therefore, investigating the ratio of c-Myc to cyclin D1 at the single-cell level may elucidate their specific functions in the G1/S transition and the regulatory role of the ErbB2 receptor.

In the present study, we used representative luminal A subtype cell lines (MCF-7 and T47D), which express low levels of the ErbB1 receptor (EGFR) and high levels of the ErbB3 receptor. ErbB2 is an orphan receptor that is activated by heterodimerization with ErbB3, ErbB4, or EGFR. Stimulation with the ErbB3 ligand, heregulin (HRG) triggers the heterodimerization of ErbB2 and ErbB3, thereby activating the ERK and AKT pathways. We conducted time-course protein phosphorylation profiling after HRG stimulation, fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator (FUCCI) live-cell imaging for cell cycle dynamics, and transcriptomic/epigenetic studies to identify key transcription factors during CDK4 inhibition. We evaluated the role of ErbB2 in regulating the timing and irreversibility of the G1/S transition, revealing the molecular mechanism underlying heterogeneous CDK4 inhibitor sensitivity.
Results
G1/S transition occurs approximately 20 h after heregulin stimulation

G1/S transition occurs approximately 20 h after Heregulin stimulation.A-F, MCF-7 cells stably expressing FUCCI. A, experimental scheme for live-cell imaging using FUCCI biosensor. B, images were captured every 20 min up to 72 h in conditions with or without 10 nM HRG. The scale bar represents 100 mum. C, percentage distribution of each cell cycle phase (%) in each image; n = 3 fields per image. D, the number of nuclei increased with each passing hour relative to the cell number at 0 h n = 3 fields per image. The data are displayed as the means +- SDs. E, cell cycle phase dynamics estimated based on Geminin and PIP fluorescence for individual cells followed up to 72 h; n = 79. F, histogram of cell cycle transition times for cells that completed the cell cycle within 72 h (n = 77), based on the results in (E). Red dotted lines indicate the mean +- SEM of each transition time. In (C) and (D), *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001 (with respect to control and HRG; Welch's t test). FUCCI, fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator; HRG, heregulin.

First, we used FUCCI live-cell imaging to analyze the cell cycle dynamics in MCF-7 or T47D cells after HRG stimulation (Fig. 1A) and analyzed the distribution of each cell cycle phase in the presence or absence of HRG for up to 72 h in MCF-7 cells (Fig. 1, B-D). HRG stimulation began to significantly increase the proportion of S/G2/M-phase cells after 24 h compared to the control. The number of nuclei, serving as a proxy for cell number, increased 1.4-fold after 48 h, suggesting that HRG stimulation enhances cell proliferation. Conversely, control cells showed a gradual increase in the proportion of S/G2/M cells, but there was no increase in the number of nuclei, suggesting cell cycle arrest during the S/G2/M phase. To further examine the timing of transition for each cell cycle phase, we performed single-cell tracking and quantified the distribution of the cell cycle phases (Figs. 1E and S1, A, B). The G1/S transition occurred at 19.0 +- 7.2 h after HRG stimulation. In comparison, the S/G2 and M/G1 transitions occurred at 32.5 +- 9.3 h and 39.4 +- 8.7 h, respectively (Fig. 1F). These findings suggested that most cells entered the S phase approximately 20 h after HRG stimulation, with some intercellular variability.
CDK4 and cyclin D1 proteins are expressed in a time-dependent manner at the G1/S transition

Time-dependent expression of CDK4 and cyclin D1 in G1/S transition.A-D, dynamic changes in the expression or phosphorylation of individual proteins in MCF-7 cells stably expressing FUCCI, detected by western blotting up to 36 h after treatment with 10 nM HRG. A and B, ErbB2 pathway proteins. C and D, proteins regulating G1/S transition. Protein and phosphorylation levels were normalized relative to those of GAPDH and divided by that of the 0 h sample (0 h = 1); n = 3. The data are displayed as the means +- SEM. FUCCI, fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator; HRG, heregulin.

We further examined the signaling dynamics of the ErbB2, AKT, and ERK pathways following HRG stimulation (Fig. 2, A and B). p-ErbB2, p-AKT, and p-ERK levels decreased after peaking within 30 min, and remained present until the S/G2 transition point (32.5 +- 9.3 h). Although c-Fos protein levels peaked within 2 h and quickly returned to basal levels, p-c-Fos showed similar dynamics to those of p-ERK, a critical regulator of p-c-Fos. Following ErbB2 activation, p-AKT, p-ERK, and p-c-Fos levels remained consistent whereas c-Myc and p-c-Myc (Ser62) levels decreased around the time of the G1/S transition (19.0 +- 7.2 h).

We estimated the timing of the R point based on the dynamics of cell cycle regulatory proteins (Figs. 2, C, D and S2, A, B). The protein levels of cyclin D1 and CDK4 started to increase shortly after HRG stimulation, peaked at approximately 20 h (the G1/S transition point), and then remained consistent until the S/G2 transition (Fig. 2D), which was consistent with the trend in p-RB (Thr373) expression. p-RB (Ser807/811) showed a monotonic increase similar to cyclin E (Fig. S2, A and B), suggesting the involvement of CDK2-mediated S phase progression (Fig. S2, A and B). Since the R point occurs just before the G1/S transition, we estimated that it occurs at 12 to 16 h, when E2F1 protein levels are highly elevated. Thus, our results substantiate that cyclin D1/CDK4 maintains RB phosphorylation near the R point, which is a critical initial step toward the G1/S transition associated with HRG-induced ErbB2 activation.
A population subset enters the cell cycle even after CDK4 inhibition

A population subset enters the cell cycle even after CDK4 inhibition.A, each inhibitor (250 nM CDK4i; 600 nM AKTi; and 500 nM MEKi) was used to treat the FUCCI stably expressing MCF-7 cells 12 h after HRG stimulation. Images were acquired every 20 min from 16 to 72 h after HRG stimulation. The scale bar represents 100 mum. B, percentage distribution of each cell cycle phase (%) in the overall image at 32 h and 72 h after HRG stimulation; n = 3. The data are displayed as the means +- SD. C, increasing number of nuclei from 16 h to 72 h after HRG stimulation; n = 3. The data are displayed as the means +- SD. D, data from cells that completed the M/G1 transition within 72 h. Control, n = 96; CDK4i, n = 52; AKTi, n = 42; MEKi, n = 75. Times to G1/S (x-axis) and M/G1 (y-axis) transitions, with slope (s) and intercept (i) obtained from the regression equation. E, comparison of Pearson's coefficients using data from (D). In (B) to (C), *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001 (with respect to control and each inhibitor; Welch's t test). AKTi, AKT inhibitor; FUCCI, fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator; HRG, heregulin.

We confirmed the involvement of cyclin D1/CDK4 in the HRG-stimulated G1/S transition. Cells were treated with CDK4i at 12 h after HRG stimulation (before the R point; Fig. S3, A and B). Since ERK activates cyclin D1 expression and AKT inhibits its degradation, we used AKT inhibitor (AKTi) and MEK inhibitor (MEKi), which have comparable inhibitory effects on cyclin D1 expression (Fig. S3, A and B), as controls for CDK4is. We examined the proportions of cells in each cell cycle phase at 32 h and 72 h after HRG stimulation (Fig. 3, A and B). At 32 h, fewer cells treated with CDK4i (13.8%), AKTi (7.05%), or MEKi (13.8%) were in the S/G2/M phase compared to nontreated cells (29.2%). At 72 h, AKTi (9.85%) and MEKi (5.50%) reduced the proportion of cells in the S/G2/M phase, but CDK4i (17.7%) did not show the same level of reduction. At this time point, the number of nuclei was significantly reduced by AKTi and MEKi but not by CDK4i (Fig. 3C). To ensure accurate cell cycle analysis, we optimized CDK4i concentrations, given our preliminary findings indicating that concentrations exceeding 500 nM induced significant cell death, commencing approximately 30 h after treatment initiation (MovieS1), which would thus compromise reliable cell cycle measurements. Using the optimized 250 nM concentration, our results revealed distinct response patterns among the inhibitors, indicating that AKTi and MEKi reduced the growth of most cells, whereas a significant subpopulation of cells was unaffected by CDK4i, thus indicating that in the absence of CDK4, additional mechanisms maintain cell cycle functionality.

To investigate the distinct mechanisms associated with CDK4i, we analyzed the correlations between the times to the G1/S and M/G1 transitions up to 72 h for the different treatments (Fig. 3D). Cells nonresponsive to CDK4i showed significantly delayed G1/S transition times (49.5 +- 13.2 h), representing a delay of approximately 25 h compared to the control (24.7 +- 5.7 h), which tended to be longer than those under AKTi (39.6 +- 14.8 h) and MEKi (26.6 +- 11.5 h; Fig. 3D). We analyzed the slope (s), representing the effect on the subsequent cell cycle duration after G1/S transition, and intercept (i), representing the time to the M/G1 transition. We also performed the same analysis under low-concentration conditions where AKTi and MEKi did not show inhibition S-phase entry at the 72-h time point (Fig. S3, C and D). The results showed that CDK4i treatment exhibited lower slopes (high: s = 0.56, low: s = 0.54) and higher intercepts (high: i = 37, low: i = 36), which were markedly different from those obtained with AKTi (high: s = 1.0, i = 19; low: s = 0.97, i = 18), MEKi (high: s = 0.95, i = 17; low: s = 0.91, i = 18), and control conditions (s = 1.0, i = 17). Consequently, Pearson's correlation coefficients (R) were significantly lower for CDK4i (high: 0.76, low: 0.66) than for AKTi (high: 0.91, low: 0.96), MEKi (high: 0.95, low: 0.95), and control conditions (0.84). This observation implies that the duration of the G1/S to G2/M phase might not be uniformly controlled by CDK4i alone and that phase-specific regulation might occur.

CDK4i enhances c-Myc transcriptional activity via H3K27Ac modification.A, changes in cell-cycle distribution following CDK4 inhibition. B-H and J, MCF-7 cells stably expressing FUCCI. B, motif-enrichment analysis of H3K27Ac modifications in the promoter region. E-box sequences (CANNTG) were enriched in the promoter region at all time points in the CDK4i group compared to the control group. C, GSEA was performed using the Myc-target gene set (n = 58) obtained from the Human MSigDB Collections. Comparison between 0 to 2 h after HRG stimulation (NES = 1.6693, p = 0.004143) and near the R point (12-16 h; NES = -0.8963, p = 0.6763). D, GSEA was performed using the Myc-target gene set (C). The CDK4i condition showed a clear negative correlation between the time to G1/S transition and duration of the S/G2/M phase (Fig. 3E). We divided the cell population into early and late groups based on the median time of each G1/S transition (CDK4i, 49.5 +- 13.2 h; AKTi, 39.6 +- 14.8 h; MEKi, 26.6 +- 11.5 h; Control, 24.7 +- 5.7 h) and compared the duration of each S, G2, and M phase (Fig. S3E). The mean duration of S/G2/M differed significantly between the early (22.3 +- 7.2 h) and late (15.8 +- 2.4 h) groups, with a 6-h difference observed in the CDK4i groups. Thus, in this CDK4i-specific response, the majority of CDK4i nonresponsive cells showed a prolonged G1/S phase and shortened S/G2/M phase (Fig. 4A). We observed that CDK4i nonresponsive T47D cells (another luminal A cell line), which normally express ErbB2 at a level three times higher than MCF-7 cells (Fig. S3, F and G), also required a longer time (32.6 +- 12.2 h) to reach the G1/S transition compared to the control (21.62 +- 6.2 h; Fig. S3H).
CDK4i enhances c-Myc transcriptional activity via H3K27Ac modification

Given the distinct cell cycle kinetics observed under CDK4 inhibition (Fig. 4A), we performed transcriptome and epigenetic analyses to investigate the molecular mechanisms responsible for cell cycle regulation following CDK4 inhibition. To elucidate the changes in gene expression patterns, we added CDK4i 12 h after HRG stimulation and performed a time-course analysis of mRNA expression [0 (control), 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, and 28 h after HRG] as well as H3K27Ac and H3K4me1 modification [12 (control), 16, 20, 24, and 28 h after HRG]. First, active transcription factors were predicted at each time point using DoRothEA with RNA-seq data (Fig. S4A). mRNAs corresponding to key transcription factors, such as Myc, AP-1 family (Jun and Fos), EGR1, NFKB1, and STAT3, which are known to promote cell cycle progression, were highly upregulated 16 h after HRG stimulation.

Motif-enrichment analysis was performed to confirm the binding of these transcription factors to the promoter regions. Here, we defined the regions without overlap between the H3K27Ac and H3K4me1 peak signals as the active promoter regions. E-box sequences (CANNTG) were enriched in the promoter regions at all time points following CDK4i treatment (Figs. 4B and S4, B, C). Given that c-Myc binds to E-box sequences, we focused on its role in G1/S transition. Control cells showed lower c-Myc protein and p-c-Myc (Ser62) levels near the R point (12-16 h after HRG) than during the early time point (0-2 h after HRG; Fig. 2, A and B). In addition, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using normalized enrichment scores did not show any significant enrichment of c-Myc-target genes during 12 to 16 h (Fig. 4C). However, CDK4i induced a significant enrichment of c-Myc-target genes at 16 h after HRG stimulation, followed by a downregulation at 24 to 28 h compared to that in the control (Fig. 4D). We analyzed the temporal expression of cell cycle-related c-Myc-target genes, focusing on genes exhibiting higher abundance of H3K27Ac modifications in their promoter than in their enhancer regions (Fig. S4D). CCNE1 expression was significantly enhanced 16 h after HRG stimulation and CDK4i treatment, whereas the expression of CCND1, CDK1, CDC25A, E2F2, E2F3, and CDKN1B showed delayed upregulation during 20 to 28 h. These findings suggested that CDK4 inhibition alters H3K27Ac levels in the promoter regions of c-Myc-target genes near the R point, promoting the expression of cell cycle-related genes. Therefore, when the G1/S transition, originally regulated by the cyclin D1 and CDK4 complex, is inhibited by CDK4i, it is maintained by an alternative pathway facilitated by c-Myc activity. In addition, CDK6 upregulation is a mechanism through which cells exhibit CDK4 inhibitor resistance. If CDK6 is involved in this upregulation, a corresponding peak would be expected at 30 h, similar to the control, and cells would gradually undergo a transition to the G2/M phase. However, our results revealed that in some populations, the S phase was sustained, even at optimized concentrations (5 nM for Abemaciclib, Fig. S4, E and F). Notably, higher concentrations (50 nM Abemaciclib) induced cell death in a subset of cells (MovieS2), confirming that the optimized concentration prevents the development of cytotoxic effects, while facilitating accurate cell cycle analysis. This accordingly provides evidence to indicate that molecules other than CDK6 are involved in the sustained mechanism.

passages.text: We confirmed whether the delayed G1/S entry following CDK4i treatment was due to c-Myc activation by testing the effects of an inhibitor of c-Myc transcriptional activity (EN4). In both MCF-7 and T47D cells after 30 h, the combination of CDK4i and EN4 increased the proportion of G1-phase cells and decreased the number of S/G2/M-phase cells in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 4, E-H), while no change was observed with EN4 alone (Fig. S4, G-J). These results suggested that the transcriptional activity of c-Myc promotes the delayed G1/S entry and escape from cell cycle arrest in response to CDK4 inhibition.

To further validate these findings using clinical data, we retrospectively analyzed microarray data from patients with luminal A subtype breast cancer who received long-term (16 weeks, n = 23) or short-term (4 weeks, n = 26) CDK4/6i therapy. PCNA, a target gene for both c-Myc and E2F involved in DNA replication during G1/S transition, showed a 0.5 log2 fold change (FC) between the long-term and short-term treatment groups (Fig. 4I). PCNA mRNA expression increased after CDK4i treatment from 4 to 12 h (16-24 h after HRG) relative to the control (Fig. 4, J and K). Collectively, these findings suggested that CDK4 inhibition-induced epigenetic modifications activated c-Myc-target genes, ultimately promoting cell cycle maintenance in cancer cells (Fig. 4L).

c-Myc is known to promote G1/S transition and cell proliferation. Therefore, if the transcriptional activity of c-Myc is enhanced by CDK4i at 16 h, the time to G1/S transition is unlikely to be extended; however, the G1/S transition was prolonged in our study (Figs. 3, D, E and 4A). We found that the levels of phosphorylated ErbB2, ERK, and AKT, which induce c-Myc mRNA expression and stabilize the c-Myc protein, decreased after CDK4 inhibition, leading to a slight reduction in c-Myc protein levels (Fig. 5, A and B). Although the expression of ErbB2 was lower in MCF-7 and T47D cells than in HER2-positive cells, growth in these cell lines is mainly dependent on ErbB2-ErbB3 heterodimer activation after HRG stimulation given their low expression of EGFR and ErbB4. This finding suggested that the CDK4i-induced downregulation of the ErbB2 pathway may prolong the G1/S transition in MCF-7 and T47D cells (Figs. 3D and S3H).

To investigate this mechanism, we focused on the Hsp90-chaperone system, particularly with respect to the stability and maturation of nascent ErbB2. Since WT MCF-7 cells naturally express low ErbB2 levels, we constructed MCF-7 cells with moderate overexpression of ErbB2 (Fig. S5, A and B). After confirming the unaltered protein expression of ErbB2, PY100 (pan-tyrosine phosphorylation was used to estimate p-ErbB2 levels), and Hsp90 under CDK4i treatment (Fig. S5, C-G), we examined the colocalization patterns using Mander's and Pearson's coefficients. Compared to control conditions, CDK4i reduced the colocalization of Hsp90 with ErbB2 or PY100 (Fig. 5, C-F). No significant difference was observed in the total number of nuclei between the two groups (Fig. S5, H and I). Furthermore, proximity ligation assay (PLA) between Hsp90 and ErbB2 showed significantly reduced PLA signals under CDK4i treatment compared to control conditions, although no significant difference was observed in the total number of nuclei (Fig. 5, G and H). These results suggested that CDK4i inhibits the interaction between Hsp90 and ErbB2, leading to ErbB2 misfolding. In addition, ErbB2 protein expression was reduced 20 h after HRG stimulation under CDK4i treatment (Figs. 5, I, J and S5J); however, ErbB2 mRNA levels did not change regardless of CDK4i treatment (Fig. S5K). Therefore, we investigated whether the downregulation of ErbB2 was caused by its protein degradation using the proteasome inhibitor MG132. Upon MG132 treatment, ErbB2 protein expression remained unchanged (Fig. 5, I and J). When cycloheximide was added at 16 h after HRG stimulation and a pulse-chase assay was performed, ErbB2 protein expression was significantly reduced under CDK4i treatment, indicating that degradation via the proteasome pathway occurred (Fig. 5, K and L). This observation indicated that CDK4i disrupts the interaction between Hsp90 and ErbB2, triggering ErbB2 degradation (Figs. 5M and S5L).

To confirm this mechanism, we treated cells with the Hsp90 inhibitor, geldanamycin, at a concentration that suppressed ErbB2 expression by 40%, similar to the effect of CDK4i (Fig. S5, M and N). As a result, cell cycle progression was halted, and there was no substantial delay in the G1/S transition (Fig. S5O). The most straightforward explanation for G1/S prolongation is the direct inhibition of CDK4 activity by the CDK4i. On the other hand, our findings demonstrate that the loss of ErbB2 protein stability following CDK4i treatment may impair the regulation of rewired c-Myc-mediated G1/S transition, even though c-Myc is activated by epigenetic modifications (Fig. 5N).
High ErbB2 expression induces cell cycle arrest by repressing cyclin D1 activity via c-myc under CDK4 inhibition

We hypothesized that ErbB2 protein instability contributes to the delay in G1/S entry under CDK4i treatment and thus could be counteracted by ErbB2 overexpression. To test this hypothesis, we generated MCF-7 cells expressing varying levels of ErbB2, from moderate to high (Fig. S5, A and B), and analyzed their cell cycle phase distribution using live-cell imaging (Fig. 5O).

After CDK4i treatment, the proportion of S/G2/M-phase cells with high ErbB2 expression was significantly reduced (OE-moderate: 14.9%, OE-high: 12.5%; Fig. 5P), indicating cell cycle arrest. We examined the protein expression of cyclin D1 and p-RB, which are critical for initiating cell cycle entry (Fig. 5, A and B). We observed a significant reduction in both cyclin D1 and p-RB levels. Therefore, we investigated the cause of decreased cyclin D1 levels. The p27 protein reportedly promotes the assembly of the cyclin D1/CDK4 complex in the G1 phase, while its gene expression is inhibited by p-AKT and c-Myc. Our data revealed that p27 protein expression decreased after CDK4i treatment, whereas p-AKT and c-Myc protein levels tended to increase following treatment. By contrast, p-ERK levels remained unchanged under different conditions. These findings suggested that, in ErbB2-overexpressing cells, the enhanced p-AKT-c-Myc axis antagonizes the protein expression of p27 and cyclin D1, leading to cell cycle arrest in the absence of CDK4 activity.
