Drug resistance is closely linked to a reversible cell cycle arrest state regulated by residual survival signals. In ErbB2-overexpressing cells, a cell cycle arrest state is induced after CDK4 inhibition, but this may be reversed by survival signals from c-Myc. In CDK4i-treated cells with high ErbB2 expression, CDK4i removal increased cyclin D1, p27, and p-RB levels, while c-Myc expression and p-c-Myc (Ser62) remained unchanged (Fig. 6, A and B). We analyzed the c-Myc phosphorylation (Ser62) levels to confirm its elevated transcriptional activity in cell cycle-arrested cells. Single-cell analysis revealed that CDK4i depletion decreased the ratio of phosphorylated c-Myc (Ser62) to cyclin D1 (p-c-Myc/cyclin D1) and increased the ratio of S-phase cells from 18.7% to 47.5% (Fig. 6C). ErbB2-overexpressing cells maintained a higher p-c-Myc/cyclin D1 ratio than wild-type cells (Fig. S6A), suggesting that sustained cell cycle arrest may result from persistent c-Myc transcriptional activation.

To investigate whether blocking c-Myc transcriptional activity could prevent reversible cell cycle arrest, we treated cells with EN4 and CDK4i for 8 h, washed out the inhibitors, and analyzed cell cycle distribution at 52 h (72 h after HRG stimulation; Fig. 6, D and E). The combined treatment increased G1-phase and reduced S/G2/M-phase cell numbers, indicating impaired cell cycle re-entry. CDK4i reduced p27 (CDKN1B) mRNA levels, which were restored by cotreatment with EN4 (Fig. 6, F and G), suggesting direct c-Myc regulation of p27 gene expression. Overall, these data supported the hypothesis that, in cells overexpressing ErbB2, CDK4 inhibition promotes reversible cell cycle arrest due to an excessive increase in c-Myc transcriptional activity and a rapid decrease in cyclin D1 protein expression, which is attributed to the reduction in p27 gene and protein expression.

Given the association between stable cell cycle arrest and cellular senescence or ErbB2-induced senescence, we examined the senescence phenotype. Senescence-associated beta-galactosidase (SA-beta-Gal) staining intensity after 6 days of CDK4i treatment showed an inverse correlation with ErbB2 expression. EN4 (4 muM) enhanced SA-beta-Gal staining in WT MCF-7 cells beyond the effect of CDK4i alone but showed no additional effect in T47D or high ErbB2-expressing MCF-7 cells (Fig. 6, H and I). This finding was consistent with cell line-specific sensitivity, since 2 nM EN4 induced cell cycle arrest in WT MCF-7 cells, whereas 2 muM was required for WT T47D cells (Fig. 4, E and F). Our results suggested that ErbB2 levels modulate the irreversibility of the G1/S transition under CDK4i treatment, and the addition of a c-Myc inhibitor supports the irreversible state (Fig. 6J).
Discussion

Our findings reveal that ErbB2 receptor levels modulate the relative roles of cyclin D1 and c-Myc in the G1/S transition, ultimately providing two distinct pathways for cell cycle progression or arrest in the presence of CDK4i. Although our study confirms and extends previous observations that a subset of cells can escape CDK4/6 inhibitor-induced arrest through c-Myc activity, our work provides novel mechanistic insights into how ErbB2 expression levels specifically modulate this escape mechanism. We demonstrate that ErbB2 levels determine the relative contributions of CDK4-cyclin D1 and c-Myc pathways, with distinct temporal dynamics and reversibility patterns that have not been previously characterized in the context of ErbB2 heterogeneity within luminal A breast cancer.

Proposed model the ErbB2 receptor regulation during G1/S transition via cyclin D1 and c-Myc in CDK4i nonresponsive cells.A, in low ErbB2-expressing cells, CDK4 inhibition leads to reduced pathway activity due to ErbB2 degradation via Hsp90 dis-colocalization. This attenuates the transcriptional activity of c-Myc activated by epigenetic changes. Consequently, a subpopulation of cells unresponsive to CDK4i exhibits a delayed G1/S transition. B, in high ErbB2-expressing cells, increased AKT activity leads to increased c-Myc expression. Subsequently, the expression of p27, which is critical for the stability of cyclin D1/CDK4 during the G1 phase, is suppressed by c-Myc, resulting in cell cycle arrest after CDK4 inhibition. This arrest is reversibly maintained by the strong transcriptional activity of c-Myc, ultimately sustaining survival signals.

The luminal A subtype accounts for 30% of breast cancer cases. Although these patients typically receive standard hormone therapy, CDK4/6is are also commonly used in cases of more advanced or metastatic tumors. However, their success is limited by heterogeneous drug responses. Notably, an ErbB2-overexpressing subpopulation has been identified within luminal A breast cancer cells, which were initially characterized by low ErbB2 expression. Given that these subpopulations occur relatively infrequently, at approximately 7% of the total population, identifying differences in cell cycle regulation, especially in terms of ErbB2 expression, is critical for improving cancer treatment. Long-term CDK4i treatment, commonly used for luminal A breast cancer, activates alternative pathways, such as PI3K/AKT/mTOR, androgen receptor, and Hippo signaling, along with transcriptional reprogramming via noncoding RNAs, promoting the development of drug resistance. To mitigate this resistance, pathways that may act at the very early step of cell cycle entry must be inhibited. Accordingly, we investigated how ErbB2 levels within cells of the same luminal A subtype affect the core cell cycle regulatory network and CDK4 inhibitor sensitivity (Fig. 7, A and B). In MCF-7 cells under HRG stimulation, CDK4 RNA levels increased and remained elevated through R-point and S-phase entry, whereas CDK6 RNA levels were quite low compared to those of CDK4 and tended to decrease after HRG stimulation (Fig. S4D). Therefore, we focused on the effect of CDK4 inhibitors rather than CDK4/6 inhibitors.

The temporal dynamics of the cell cycle regulators and live-cell imaging analysis showed that the roles of cyclin D1 and c-Myc, key regulators of the G1/S transition, vary depending on the expression status of ErbB2 under CDK4i treatment. This variation ultimately affects the timing and irreversibility of the G1/S transition. In MCF-7 cells, a representative luminal A breast cancer cell line with low ErbB2 expression, the G1/S transition is normally regulated by the cyclin D1/CDK4 complex via Hsp90 (Figs. 5, C-H and S5, C-O). Although CDK inhibitors are known to sequester Hsp90 and CDK4/6, our results suggested that the function of Hsp90 is complemented by CDK4 activity and contributes to stabilizing the ErbB2 protein. This positive feedback mechanism provides valuable insights into the signal-dependent complexity of cell cycle regulation. The delayed G1/S phase transition observed in this study (Fig. 5N) can be explained by two complementary mechanisms. First, CDK4i directly inhibits CDK4 activity, blocking the canonical G1/S phase transition pathway and causing G1 phase extension. Second, CDK4i treatment resulted in the epigenetic activation of c-Myc (Fig. 4, B-D) as evidenced by increased transcriptional activity without corresponding protein level changes within the same cell line (Fig. 5, A and B). Therefore, the ErbB2-c-Myc pathway, which is normally inactive in WT cells, becomes rewired and activated after CDK4i treatment. Simultaneously, ErbB2 protein stability was reduced by the CDK4i (Fig. 5, C-M). Consequently, two opposing situations overlap: c-Myc transcriptional activity, not the protein expression itself, is somewhat insufficient to compensate for the loss of ErbB2 signal, while G1 phase extension occurs due to CDK4 inhibition. These results suggest that when the CDK4-mediated G1/S transition is compromised, weak suppression of the ErbB2-c-Myc axis may result in a delayed G1/S transition (Fig. 7A). In contrast, the excessive transcriptional activity of c-Myc observed in ErbB2 overexpression promotes cell cycle arrest by rapidly reducing cyclin D1 and p27 levels (Fig. 6, A-G). p27 expression, which recruits cyclin D1 to the nucleus during the G1 phase, is also repressed by AKT and c-Myc. Therefore, in high ErbB2-expressing MCF-7 cells with high levels of AKT and c-Myc activity, CDK4 inhibition increases free cyclin D1 levels, rendering it more susceptible to degradation. This process generates a hypophosphorylated RB state in ErbB2-overexpressing MCF-7 cells compared to WT cells, leading to cell cycle arrest due to sequestration of E2F by hypophosphorylated RB (Fig. 7B).

c-Myc regulates the cell survival pathway. In ErbB2-overexpressing MCF-7 cells, cell cycle arrest was reversible after CDK4 inhibition (Fig. 6, D and E), suggesting that the transcriptional activity of c-Myc promotes sustained cell survival in this context. Co-treatment with inhibitors targeting the transcriptional activity of c-Myc and CDK4 may be necessary to induce irreversible cell cycle arrest (Fig. 6, H and I). However, at the same concentration at which the Myc inhibitor promoted cellular senescence in WT MCF-7 cells, the percentage of senescent WT T47D and ErbB2-overexpressing cells did not change compared to that in the respective control conditions. For drug response assessments, the threshold at which c-Myc switches from supporting cell survival to inducing irreversible cell cycle arrest in relation to ErbB2 levels could inform the development of more effective molecular-targeted treatment strategies for breast cancer.

Overall, our results suggest that the relative balance between c-Myc and cyclin D1 activities offers valuable quantitative insights into the varying sensitivities of cancer cells to CDK4is. In ErbB2-positive cells, the predominance of c-Myc activity over CDK4-cyclin D1-mediated cell cycle progression results in CDK4i-induced reversible cell cycle arrest. This suggests that the c-Myc-to-cyclin D1 activity ratio serves as a predictive indicator of the treatment response. This approach does not rely solely on observable cell proliferation rates or single biomarker gene analysis.
Experimental procedures
Reagents

The MEKi PD0325901 was purchased from FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corp; CDK4 Inhibitor V was purchased from Calbiochem or Sigma-Aldrich (CAS number: 943746-57-4); Abemaciclib was purchased from Cosmo Bio. Co. (Catalog No: HY-16297A); AKTi VIII was purchased from Cayman Chemical; EN4 (Myci) was purchased from Selleck Chemicals; geldanamycin was purchased from FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corp.; blasticidin was purchased from Kaken Pharmaceutical; Lipofectamine LTX was purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific; and HRG was procured from R&D Systems.
ErbB2 overexpression

MCF-7 (American Type Culture Collection, ATCC, HTB-22) cells overexpressing full-length human ErbB2 (HER2) were established as follows: Human ErbB2 complementary DNA (cDNA) in the pCMV6-XL5 vector was purchased from OriGene (Catalog No: TC128161). The cDNA fragment was cloned into the vector pCMV-6-Neo vector (OriGene). The plasmid was then transfected into MCF-7 cells using Lipofectamine LTX (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer's protocol, and stable transfectants were selected with G418 (neomycin). Colonies derived from single cells compartmentalized in 96-well plates were isolated and examined. ErbB2 expression was examined via western blotting to group cells with moderate or high ErbB2 expression (as described below for protein extraction and immunoblotting).
Cell culture

MCF-7, ErbB2-overexpressing MCF-7, and T47D (ATCC, HTB-133) cells were cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM, Nacalai Tesque) supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS, Sigma-Aldrich) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (100 IU/ml penicillin, 100 mug/ml streptomycin; Nacalai Tesque) at 37  C in a humidified 5%-CO2 atmosphere. Cells were routinely tested using a CycleavePCR Mycoplasma Detection Kit (Takara bio, CY-232); no mycoplasma contamination was detected.
FUCCI transfection

MCF-7 and ErbB2-overexpressing MCF-7 cells stably expressing the FUCCI biosensor were generated using a PiggyBac transposase system. Lipofectamine LTX (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used to transfect the FUCCI plasmid (pPBbsr2-H2B-iRFP-P2A-mScarlet-I-hGem-P2A-PIP-tag-NLS-mNeonGreen; https://benchling.com/s/seq-LPZ1tLdpgnpJIYOG2ujR) along with hyPBase (https://benchling.com/s/seq-oGkw53b41IZqvzF5yQ9K) into MCF-7 and ErbB2-overexpressing MCF-7 cells, following the manufacturer's protocol. Cells were suspended in a drug-free medium for 48 h and treated with blasticidin (10 mug/ml) to separate those stably expressing the plasmid. Colonies derived from single cells compartmentalized in 96-well plates were selected by microscopic live-cell observation of Geminin and PIP-tag fluorescence.
Protein extraction and immunoblotting

MCF-7, T47D, and ErbB2-overexpressing (moderate or high) MCF-7 cells were seeded in six-well plates (450,000 cells/well) and cultured in 10% FBS containing DMEM for 48 h. The medium was changed to FBS-free phenol red-free DMEM (FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corp.) containing 1% penicillin-streptomycin (100 IU/ml penicillin, 100 mug/ml streptomycin; Nacalai Tesque) and 1% 100 mmol/L sodium pyruvate solution (FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corp), and the cells were cultured for 17 h. The medium were changed again, and the cells were cultured for 3 h. After administration of 10 nM HRG (R&D Systems) for 12 h, the cells were independently treated with CDK4i and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). Serum was not included under conditions where HRG was added. Total cell lysates were prepared in RIPA buffer (Nacalai Tesque, 1648834) containing protease inhibitors (11836153001, Roche Rotkreuz) and phosphatase inhibitors (Roche, 4906837001) at 4  C. Cells were vortexed for 5 min and centrifuged at 16,000g and 4  C for 15 min. The supernatant was collected and denatured by heating at 95  C with sample buffer (5x) and 2-mercaptoethanol (Nacalai Tesque, 21418-55) for 5 min. The proteins were subjected to SDS polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (Nacalai Tesque, 1306644), transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (Merck), and incubated with 10% blocking buffer (Nacalai Tesque, 03953-95) prepared in Tris-buffered saline/Tween 20 (TBS-T; T9142; Takara Bio) for 1 h at 25  C. Membranes were probed overnight with antibodies against AKT (1:1000; #4685; Cell Signaling Technology), p-AKT (Thr308; 1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology; #2965), ERK (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology; #9102), p-ERK (Thr202 Tyr204; 1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology; #4370), HER2/ErbB2 (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology; #2165), p-HER2/ErbB2 (Thr1221/1222; 1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology; #2249), p-c-Fos (Ser374; 1:1000; #ab55836; Abcam), c-Fos (1:200; #sc-166940; Santa Cruz Biotechnology), p-c-Myc (Ser62; 1:1000; Abcam; #ab51156), c-Myc (1:200; Santa Cruz; #sc-40), E2F-1 (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology; #3742), p-RB (Ser807/811; 1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology; #8516), p-RB (Thr373; 1:1000; Abcam; #ab52975), RB1 (1:1000; #SPM353; NOVUS biologicals), cyclin D1 (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology; #2978), cyclin E (1:200; Santa Cruz; #sc-247), cyclin A (1:200; Santa Cruz; #sc-271682), CDK4 (1:1000; Santa Cruz; #DSC-35), CDK2 (1:1000; Santa Cruz; #D-12), P27 Kip1 (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology; #3686), Ubiquitin (P4D1) (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology; #3936), and GAPDH (1:4000; 10494-1-AP; Proteintech) in TBS-T including 10% blocking buffer at 4  C. They were then incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies, HRP-conjugated anti-mouse IgG (1:5000; Cell Signaling Technology; #7076) and HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG (1:5000; Cell Signaling Technology; #7074), for 1 h at room temperature. The membranes were developed using a chemiluminescent HRP substrate (Merck). Protein bands were detected using an Amersham Imager 600 UV (GE Healthcare) and visualized using the ImageJ-Fiji software (v.2.14.0/1.54f, NIH).
qRT-PCR

qRT-PCR was conducted as previously described. RNA was isolated from cells using NucleoSpin RNA Plus (Catalog No. 740984.250; Macherey-Nagel) according to the manufacturer's protocol. cDNA was synthesized using ReverTra Ace qPCR RT Master Mix (TOYOBO), and quantitative PCR was performed using a KOD SYBR qPCR kit (TOYOBO) on a CFX96 Real-Time PCR System (Bio-Rad Laboratories). The DeltaDeltaCq method was used to quantify gene expression, using RPL27 expression as an internal reference. The primers used for real-time PCR are listed in Table S1.
Cell cycle analysis using the FUCCI biosensor

Cell cycle analysis was conducted as previously described. Time-lapse microscopy was performed using an IN Cell Analyzer 2500HS (GE Healthcare) equipped with a CFI S Plan Fluor ELWD dry objective lens 20x (NA: 0.45) at an excitation wavelength of 475 nm and emission wavelength of 511 nm for PIP-tag-mNeonGreen, and an excitation wavelength of 542 nm and emission wavelength of 597 nm for mScarlet-hGem. Cells were maintained at 37  C in a humidified 5%-CO2 atmosphere and imaged at 20-min intervals for 72 h. Image processing and quantification of cell cycle phase distribution were performed using ImageJ-Fiji software (v.2.14.0/1.54f, NIH). Masks of the mScarlet-hGem and PIP-tag-mNeonGreen signals were obtained by applying a fixed threshold using "Analyze Particles" and automatically counted as regions of interest. Cell cycle phases were determined in the following manner: G1 phase, PIP-tag-positive; S phase, hGem-positive; G2/M phase, PIP-tag-positive, and hGem-positive. The average brightness of mScarlet and mNeonGreen was obtained using cell-tracking software (Olympus). The threshold parameters for mScarlet and mNeonGreen were set manually for each cell line. We employed an algorithm for estimating the cell cycle phase at the single-cell level using R packages [brunnermunzel (v.1.4.1), multimode (v.1.4), rlist (v.0.4.6.1), and tidyverse (v.1.3.0)]. The duration of each cell cycle phase was obtained from the single-cell data.
Nucleus count

The number of nuclei was quantified based on the fluorescence of the FUCCI probes, and signals for a nuclear marker (histone H2B), mScarlet-hGem, and PIP-tag-mNeonGreen were used to determine cell proliferation. Image processing and nuclear ratio quantification were performed using the ImageJ-Fiji software (v.2.14.0/1.54f, NIH). Masks of the merged nuclear marker, mScarlet-hGem, and PIP-tag-mNeonGreen signals were obtained by applying a fixed threshold using "Analyze Particles" and automatically counted as regions of interest. The nuclear ratio was calculated by dividing the number of nuclei at the end of observation by that at the beginning. Thus, a nuclear ratio near 1.0 indicated potential cell cycle arrest, above 1.0 indicated cell proliferation, and below 1.0 indicated apoptosis.
Immunostaining and quantitative analysis of images

MCF-7 and ErbB2-overexpressing (moderate or high) cells were seeded in 12-well plates (200,000 cells/well) and cultured in 10% FBS containing DMEM for 48 h. The medium was changed to FBS-free phenol red-free DMEM (FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corp.) containing 1% penicillin-streptomycin (100 IU/ml penicillin, 100 mug/ml streptomycin; Nacalai Tesque) and 1% 100 mmol/L sodium pyruvate solution (FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corp.), and the cells were cultured for 17 h. The medium was changed again, and the cells were cultured for 3 h. After administration of 10 nM HRG (R&D Systems) for 12 h, the cells were independently treated with CDK4i and DMSO. Serum was not included under conditions where HRG was added. Cells were washed twice with PBS at the indicated times, fixed for 2 min with preprepared methanol at -20  C, washed twice with Blocking One (Nacalai Tesque, 03953-95), and incubated overnight at 4  C with Blocking One. The next day, cells were incubated overnight at 4  C with primary antibodies diluted in 10% goat serum (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 16210064)/Blocking One, washed five times with PBS, and incubated with fluorescent dye-conjugated secondary antibody, 2 mug/ml 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) (Nacalai Tesque, 11034-56), and 0.5 mug/ml CellMask (Thermo Fisher Scientific, H32721) for 1 h at room temperature. Cells were washed five times with PBS, and images were acquired using the IN Cell Analyzer 2500HS (GE Healthcare Life Science) at 20x magnification. At least three images were collected for each treatment, containing at least 100 cells each, for quantification using the ImageJ-Fiji software (v.2.14.0/1.54f, NIH) and CellProfiler (v.4.2.1). Colocalization analysis for Hsp90 with either ErbB2 or PY100 was performed using the "Coloc 2" plugin in the ImageJ-Fiji software. Cell fractionation was performed on CellMask-stained images using CellProfiler, and the mean intensity was calculated for p-c-Myc, cyclin D1, and DAPI in each cell. The ratio of phosphorylated c-Myc (Ser62) to cyclin D1 (p-c-Myc/cyclin D1) for each cell was plotted over the DAPI intensity. The DAPI intensity indicating the G1/S transition was determined based on the percentage of cells that were in the S/G2/M phase 24 h after HRG stimulation. In WT MCF-7 cells, 22.4% of cells were in the S/G2/M phase, at which time the DAPI intensity was 0.105. In MCF-7 cells overexpressing ErbB2 (high), 25.4% of the cells were in the S/G2/M phase, at which time the DAPI intensity was 0.0775.
In situ PLA

The procedure was performed according to the manufacturer's protocols using Duolink In Situ Detection Reagents Orange (Sigma-Aldrich, DUO92007-30RXN) and PLA probes (Anti-Rabbit MINUS; DUO92005-30RXN, Anti-Mouse PLUS; DUO92001-30RXN). WT MCF7 cells were seeded at 1 x 10 5 cells/well in 24-well glass plates (Greiner Japan; 662892). The same procedures described in the protein extraction and immunoblotting section were followed up to the addition of 10 nM HRG. Twelve hours after HRG addition, 250 nM CDK4i or DMSO (control) was added, and 4 h later (16 h after HRG stimulation), the cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 min and permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 (v/v; Nacalai Tesque) for 15 min. After washing three times with PBS, cells were incubated with blocking solution at 37  C for 1 h. The following procedures were then conducted: ErbB2 (Proteintech, PGI-60311-1-IG-150), Hsp90 (Proteintech, PGI-13171-1-AP-150), and rabbit IgG (#3900, CST) were diluted 1:500 and incubated overnight at 4  C. After washing twice with Buffer A, diluted PLA probes were added and incubated at 37  C for 1 h. After washing twice with Buffer A, ligation reaction was performed at 37  C for 30 min, and excess ligation buffer was removed by washing twice with Buffer A. Rolling circle amplification reaction was performed at 37  C for 100 min, followed by washing with Buffer B. Finally, slides were mounted using the DAPI mounting medium provided with the PLA kit.
Cycloheximide chase assay

In experiments monitoring ErbB2 protein stability, MCF-7 cells were treated with cycloheximide (100 mug/ml) at 4 h after treatment with either 250 nM CDK4i or DMSO (control), which was administered 16 h after HRG stimulation. Cell extracts collected at 16, 18, and 20 h after HRG stimulation were subjected to immunoblotting with anti-ErbB2 and anti-GAPDH antibodies. The results were normalized to the control conditions at 16 h.
Immunoprecipitation assay

ErbB2 overexpressing MCF7 cells were lysed with SDS-free RIPA buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.8, 0.15 M NaCl, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, and 0.5% Nonidet P-40). After incubation on ice for 30 min, samples were centrifuged at 16,000g for 15 min at 4  C. After centrifugation, the supernatant was collected. Subsequently, 500 ng of ErbB2 antibody (CST, #2165) was added to the supernatant and incubated overnight at 4  C. Thirty microliters of Pierce Protein A/G Agarose (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 20422) prepared as a 50% slurry in RIPA(-SDS) buffer was added and incubated for 1.5 h at 4  C. Samples were washed three times with RIPA(-SDS) buffer. After washing, samples were collected and denatured by heating at 95  C with sample buffer (5x) and 2-mercaptoethanol for 5 min.
Analysis of senescence associated beta-galactosidase-positive cells

SA-beta-gal staining was conducted as previously described. Briefly, senescent cells were stained using a Senescence beta-Galactosidase Staining Kit (#9860; Cell Signaling Technology) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Images were acquired with a BZ-9000 microscope (Keyence) at 20x magnification. The percentage of SA-beta-gal-positive cells was calculated from images using CellProfiler (v.4.2.1). The total number of cells was determined by visualizing nuclear segmentation with DAPI staining. The number of SA-beta-gal-stained cells was identified using the UnmixColors module. The percentage of SA-beta-gal-positive cells was calculated by dividing the number of SA-beta-gal-stained cells by the total number of nuclei in each field of view.
RNA-seq

FUCCI-expressing MCF-7 cells were seeded in six-well plates (450,000 cells/well) and cultured in 10% FBS containing DMEM for 48 h. The medium was changed to FBS-free phenol red-free DMEM, the cells were cultured for 17 h, the medium was changed again, and the cells were cultured for 3 h. After administration of 10 nM HRG for 12 h, the cells were independently treated with CDK4i and DMSO. Serum was not included under conditions where HRG was added. Cells were washed twice with PBS at the indicated times. Total RNA was isolated using NucleoSpin RNA Plus (Macherey-Nagel; Cat. No. 740984.250) at the specified time. Library construction and RNA-seq were performed on an Illumina sequencing platform (Rhelixa). Poly(A) RNA was prepared with a Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Module (E7490; New England Biolabs), and the sequencing library was generated using a NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs, E7760). RNA-seq was performed on a NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina) with 150-bp paired-end reads. Raw reads were quality-checked using FastQC (v.0.11.9) and trimmed using TrimGalore (v.0.6.0). Trimmed reads were mapped using STAR (v.2.7.9a) with GRCh38 as the reference genome. featureCounts (v.1.6.4) was used to construct the count matrix with the "-p -B -t exon -g gene_name" parameters. Raw counts were converted to transcripts per kilobase million and corrected using EdgeR (v.3.36.0). Principal component analysis was performed using the prcomp function in R (v.4.1.1). Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using the fgsea package (v.1.20.0) and the hallmark gene set in the Human MSigDB Collections.
ChIP-seq

FUCCI-expressing MCF-7 cells were seeded in 100-mm dishes (2,300,000 cells/dish) and cultured in 10% FBS containing DMEM for 48 h. The medium was changed to FBS-free phenol red-free DMEM, the cells were cultured for 17 h, the medium was changed, and the cells were cultured for 3 h. After administration of 10 nM HRG for 12 h, the cells were independently treated with CDK4i and DMSO. Cells were washed twice with PBS at the indicated times. Cells were fixed with 1% formaldehyde (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 5 min. Fragmented DNA was obtained using a SimpleChIP Plus Enzymatic Chromatin IP Kit (Cell Signaling Technology, 9005) and M220 Focused-ultrasonicator (Covaris). Immunoprecipitated DNA was obtained using an Auto iDeal chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-seq kit for Histones x24 (Diagenode) on an SX-8G platform (Diagenode). Next, 2 mug anti-H3K27Ac antibody (Diagenode) and 2 mug anti-H3K4me1 antibody (Diagenode) were mixed with 10 mul DiaMag Protein A-coated magnetic beads, and immunoprecipitaion reactions with DNA were performed for 12 h. De-crosslinking was conducted using 4 mul of 5 M NaCl and 1 mul of 20 mg/ml proteinase K (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 4 h at 60  C. Library construction and RNA-seq were performed using the Illumina sequencing platform (Rhelixa). A sequencing library was generated using a NEBNext Ultra II DNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (New England Biolabs, 7645). ChIP-seq was performed on the NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina) with 150-bp paired-end reads. H3K27Ac ChIP-seq and H3K4me1 data were processed using the same protocol as for RNA-seq. FastQC (v.0.11.9) was used for quality control. Trimming was performed using Trimmomatic (v.0.39) with the following parameters: ILLUMINACLIP, TruSeq2-SE; fa, 2:30:10; LEADING, 30; TRAILING, 30; SLIDINGWINDOW, 4:15; MINLEN, 30; HEADCROP, 2. Reads were mapped using Bowtie2 (v.2.4.4) with GRCh38 as the reference genome, and duplicate reads were excluded using Picard (v.2.26.6) (http://broadinstitute.github.io/picard). Bigwig files were created from the generated BAM files using deepTools (v.3.5.1; bamCoverage function). Peak regions were identified using HOMER (v.4.11) with the "-style histone -L 0 -fdr 0.00005" parameters. All detected peak regions were annotated to their nearest neighbor genes using HOMER annotatePeaks.pl (v.4.11).
Promoter and enhancer detection

Promoter regions were defined as those in the H3K27Ac peak that did not overlap with the H3K4me1 peak and were within 250-bp of the transcription start site (TSS, at the center of the peak). Enhancer regions were defined as those in the H3K27Ac peak overlapping with the H3K4me1 peak and were more than 250-bp from the TSS. The TSS was obtained from the Ensembl database using BiomaRt (v.2.50.3). The bed files containing the promoter and enhancer regions for all time points were merged, and the time-course of the coverage values for H3K27Ac ChIP-seq was calculated using HOMER annotatePeaks.pl (v.4.11). The estimated coverage values were used to detect promoters and enhancers affected by CDK4i. Promoters that gained or lost signal were defined as those with coverage values of llog2 FCl > 0.3 for inhibitor and control conditions. Enhancers that gained or lost signals were defined as those with coverage values changing by llog2 FCl > 0.3 and target gene expression changing by llog2 FCl > 0.2 in the same direction as the change in enhancer activity.
Motif analysis of ChIP-seq data

Motif analysis was performed using MEME Suite SEA (v.5.4.1). The motif files were obtained from the JASPAR 2022 database (JASPAR2022_CORE_vertebrates_nonredundant_v2). Peak regions containing motifs were detected using MEME Suite FIMO (v.5.4.1). The analysis was performed using default parameters.
Transcription factor enrichment analysis

Transcription factor analysis was conducted using DoRothEA (v.1.6.0) with the "run_viper" function. We used regulon data with "confidence" levels of A and B. Target genes were selected based on their changes in expression (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.01) between the control and inhibitor treatments at each time point.
Clinical data analysis

We used microarray gene expression data (GEO GSE93204) for biopsy samples from the NeoPalAna clinical trial (NCT01723774) to identify differentially expressed genes based on p values adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method to control the FDR in GEO2R.
Statistical analysis

Statistical analysis, data visualization, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality testing were performed in the R software (v.4.2.1; The R Foundation). For normally distributed data, the two-tailed Student's t test and Welch's two-sample t test were used after confirming equal variances using the F-test for comparisons between the two groups. Comparisons between more than two groups were performed one-way ANOVA followed by the Tukey's post hoc test. p < 0.05 was considered significant. When examining the effects of two independent factors and their interaction, two-way ANOVA was employed.
Data availability

The sequence data for RNA-seq and ChIP-seq reported in this paper have been deposited in the DNA Data Bank of Japan with accession number ESUB001718. The code is available at https://github.com/okadalabipr/HER2_Cellcycle. All other data will be made available upon reasonable request.

passages.text: DTP cells evade treatment via reversible dormancy, metabolic rewiring, enhanced DNA repair, and immune escape.

passages.text: Fatty acid oxidation and epigenetic changes support DTP survival and resistance to targeted therapies.
DTPs reshape the tumor microenvironment, promoting M2 macrophage polarization and immune suppression.
Emerging strategies target metabolism, DNA repair, and immune evasion to eliminate DTPs and prevent relapse.

Although treatments for HNSCC have improved, the cancer is still challenging because many patients tend to develop the disease again nearby and often have poor recovery. Since drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells display a wide range of types and unique genetic characteristics, nonhormonal endocrine therapies, including chemotherapy, targeted therapy and immunotherapy, are ineffective in eliminating these cells. DTP cells evade elimination by entering a reversible dormant state characterized by altered metabolism, enhanced DNA repair capacity, and modified immune escape mechanisms, all of which promote the cells' survival and treatment failure. Platinum-based chemotherapy, widely prescribed for HNSCC, reduces tumor size but fails to confer long-term benefits because of the strong treatment resistance of DTP cells. These cells also exhibit resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors by activating alternative signaling pathways. Alternative survival pathways are also activated in DTP cells when targeted therapies such as those using epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors are used. Although programmed death 1/programmed death ligand 1 inhibitors are exciting new treatments, their effect is hampered by DTP cells that affect the immune system. This review examines the ways DTP cells make HNSCC tumor cells resistant to treatment by looking at metabolic reprogramming, DNA methylation alterations and the microenvironment of the tumor. This review further explores strategies for targeting metabolic dependencies, inhibiting DNA repair, and combining therapeutic approaches, all of which can mitigate DTP cell-mediated recurrence. Advancing strategies that specifically target DTP cells could enhance HNSCC management by reducing recurrence and improving overall prognosis.

passages.text: Schematic abstract
Introduction

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is inherently multidisciplinary, comprising surgery, chemoradiation, systemic chemotherapy, and targeted or immune-based therapies, as reflected in updated clinical guidance. Nevertheless, contemporary international data show that long-term outcomes in advanced HNSCC remain unacceptably poor, with most patients experiencing recurrence or progression within five years. This persists even when chemotherapy is combined with targeted agents and immunotherapy in the recurrent and metastatic settings. Although cytotoxic chemotherapy remains the therapeutic backbone, multiple reviews conclude that survival gains are modest and that treatment-related toxicities frequently overshadow the durability of benefit. A major impediment to durable control is the presence of drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells, a tumor subpopulation capable of surviving exposure to therapeutic agents. In contrast to genetically resistant clones, DTP cells exhibit nonheritable resistance by deploying nongenetic stress-response programs that enable survival during initial therapy. These cells evade eradication by adopting a reversible, quiescent state that withstands drug-induced stress. Consequently, DTP cells persist through treatment and contribute to disease relapses and progression. Studies are required to address this form of treatment resistance in HNSCC. The literature indicates that platinum-based chemotherapy, particularly cisplatin-based chemotherapy, is a standard treatment option for HNSCC. However, therapeutic resistance is increasingly linked to drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells, which survive initial cytotoxic or targeted therapy and later drive tumor relapses. Although combining cisplatin or carboplatin with 5-fluorouracil enhances treatment response in HNSCC, the combined therapy causes side effects without improving overall survival. Furthermore, combining platinum-based therapeutic agents with 5-fluorouracil or cetuximab increases response rates, but these combinations are associated with increased toxicity and only modest survival benefits. Frizzled-7 exhibits tolerance to platinum-based therapeutic agents, tolerance makes ovarian cancer cells with stem-like features susceptible to ferroptosis, a form of regulated cell death through glutathione peroxidase 4 inhibition. Emerging evidence implicates ferroptosis control in cisplatin tolerance in HNSCC, supporting strategies that target glutathione handling and lipid peroxidation to eradicate persister populations. The Differential Sensitivity Analysis for resistant malignancies tool can be used to identify promising drugs and predictive biomarkers for treating cisplatin-resistant cancers, supporting personalized treatment strategies. The 5-nucleotidase (NT5E) protein acts as a marker to predict different cancers, including HNSCC. A high level of NT5E is associated with poor prognosis and unsuccessful immunotherapy. NT5E helps cancer-associated fibroblasts transition from epithelial to mesenchymal, which leads to the formation of an immunosuppressive area in the tumor; therefore, NT5E could be a focus for new immunotherapy aimed at cancer-associated fibroblasts. Cetuximab retains a role in selected scenarios; however, adaptive resistance limits durability, and its use is largely in combination regimens. Unfortunately, DTP cells typically adapt to EGFR-targeted treatment, reducing the duration of therapeutic benefit. While antibodies against programmed death 1 (PD-1) or programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) provide additional treatment choices, the effects of immune therapy on DTP cells are difficult to predict and vary among HNSCC patients. DTP cells in HNSCC use several adaptive mechanisms to withstand therapeutic pressure. The present review summarizes recent findings on DTP cells in HNSCC for example, their adaptive mechanisms, the challenges they pose to standard therapies, and potential strategies for targeting them. This review further explores the effects of DTP cells on treatment resistance and relapse in HNSCC to identify suitable pathways for reducing recurrence rates and improving survival outcomes. Nonheritable drug tolerance is increasingly recognized as a principal barrier to durable disease control in HNSCC, enabling small subpopulations of tumor cells to survive initial therapy and drive relapse. A focused synthesis is therefore warranted to consolidate current evidence on the biology of drug-tolerant persister states, define their convergent vulnerabilities across signaling, metabolic, DNA-damage, and immune-evasion programs, and clarify how these insights can be operationalized in the clinic. The objective of this review is to integrate contemporary data, identify actionable targets and biomarkers that enable early recognition of emerging tolerance, and delineate rational combination strategies designed to eradicate persister populations and prolong meaningful clinical benefit.

passages.text: Fig 1

HNSCC arises from the mucosal epithelium of the oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx; tobacco and alcohol remain established risk factors, while HPV16 is now recognized as a major etiologic driver in oropharyngeal cancer. This malignancy remains clinically challenging because of its biological heterogeneity, high rates of locoregional recurrence, and the frequent development of treatment resistance. A summary of current treatment strategies for HNSCC and their corresponding mechanisms is illustrated in (Fig. 1). Current therapeutic approaches include surgery for Resectable disease and, in non-surgical settings, definitive chemoradiation; in the recurrent/metastatic setting, systemic options span platinum-based chemotherapy, EGFR inhibitors, and PD-1-directed immunotherapies. Even with these advances, the prognosis for advanced HNSCC remains poor, with most patients experiencing relapse or progression, underscoring the need for biomarker-guided and multimodal strategies.

passages.text: Therapeutic pathway for HNSCC: Resectable disease: surgery with adjuvant radiotherapy or concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT). Unresectable disease: definitive CRT. Post-treatment assessment with [^18F] FDG-PET/CT guides further management. On progression, second-line options include targeted therapy (afatinib) or PD-1 inhibitors (nivolumab, pembrolizumab); later lines may use taxanes or investigational miRNA-based approaches (miR-21/miR-375). Refractory cases may pursue advanced immunotherapy and clinical-trial enrollment. This stepwise, multimodal framework integrates established and emerging therapies.

infons.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Head and Neck

passages.text: Fig 2

Current treatment regimen for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) follows an escalating care model in which therapy selection depends on disease stage, tumor respectability, response to prior interventions, and evidence of recurrence (Fig. 2). Despite technological advances, radiotherapy for head and neck cancer still carries substantial acute/late toxicity and critically 50 % loco-regional recurrence within 3 years in high-risk patients. This relapse pattern aligns with our study's premise that drug/radiation-tolerant persister (DTP) cells survive initial RT and later repopulate tumors. Targeting persister-cell biology alongside modern RT therefore represents a rational path to improve outcomes and optimize the risk-benefit profile. Standard first-line treatment typically involves surgery followed by radiotherapy or concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT), particularly in respectable cases. For unresectable tumors, chemoradiotherapy remains the primary treatment modality. Integration of 18F-FDG PET-CT imaging significantly improves response assessment, informing clinicians when further intervention or therapy escalation is warranted. Despite aggressive multimodal treatment, many patients experience disease progression and require second-line therapy. While systemic therapies such as targeted inhibitors or immune checkpoint blockade are introduced at this stage, therapeutic resistance frequently emerges, primarily due to the presence of drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells. These cells survive initial treatment by entering a reversible dormant state, exploiting metabolic and epigenetic plasticity, and often serve as a reservoir for subsequent tumor regrowth. As patients advance to third- and fourth-line therapy, options such as taxanes, experimental compounds, and microRNA (miRNA)-based strategies (miR-21 and miR-375) continue to demonstrate limited clinical efficacy. A major limitation of current therapeutic protocols is their focus on eliminating proliferative tumor cells while inadequately addressing the treatment-resistant DTP population. Consequently, heavily pretreated patients often rely on advanced immunotherapies or enrollment in clinical trials, signaling the need for precision strategies tailored to overcome resistance. A growing body of evidence suggests that incorporating DTP-targeted approaches such as inhibition of metabolic dependencies, suppression of DNA-repair pathways, and disruption of immune-evasion mechanisms may enhance therapeutic durability. Understanding how and when DTP cells evade conventional therapies is essential for designing combinatorial regimens that can improve long-term outcomes in HNSCC.

passages.text: First-line treatments

Generally, surgery and radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy are initiated together as the first line of management for head and neck cancers. This approach remains the principal treatment for advanced disease because it achieves effective locoregional control while preserving organ function. Incorporating 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) into treatment planning has improved the accuracy of response assessment after chemoradiotherapy. Concurrent chemoradiotherapy is especially vital in unresectable cases, where it aims to control local disease and delay systemic progression.
Second-line treatments

Second-line therapy is commonly initiated after failure of first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. Available options include targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors. In LUX phase III Head & Neck 3 trial, afatinib an oral pan-ErbB inhibitor improved progression free survival and objective response versus methotrexate (Methotrexate) in EGFR therapy naive patients. Moreover, subsets of patients treated with nivolumab or pembrolizumab (PD-1/PD-L1) directed achieve durable remissions. Nevertheless, donor-cell therapies yield inconsistent benefit because DTP cells can blunt antitumor immunity and develop resistance.
Third-line treatments

The therapeutic landscape for third-line treatment is narrow, with a focus on rechallenge strategies and investigational approaches. One promising avenue involves targeting tumor-promoting and resistance-mediating microRNAs. For example, miR-21 is associated with chemoresistance and tumor proliferation, while miR-375 exhibits tumor-suppressive properties. Modulating these miRNAs holds potential for overcoming resistance in advanced HNSCC. Rechallenge with previously effective agents or the introduction of alternative regimens such as taxanes can also be considered based on patient-specific factors and prior responses.

infons.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Head and Neck

passages.text: Fourth-line treatments

Fourth-line therapy is highly individualized and often requires enrollment in clinical trials to access novel immunotherapies or combination regimes. At this stage, biomarker-guided decision-making and DTP-informed therapeutic design are critical. Agents that target stress-response pathways, mitochondrial function, or chromatin remodeling may help sensitize DTP cells. Personalized approaches are essential to manage the cumulative complexity of prior treatments, ongoing tumor evolution, and microenvironmental interactions. In summary, HNSCC management is a complex, dynamic continuum that demands layered interventions across multiple lines of therapy. Although advances in imaging, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy have improved disease control, treatment failure driven by DTP cells remains a formidable barrier. Integrating DTP-specific strategies into current protocols may yield more durable responses and improve survival outcomes in advanced HNSCC.

Drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells constitute a transient, slow-cycling subpopulation of cancer cells that survive lethal therapy through reversible, nonheritable adaptations. These adaptations include therapy-induced quiescence, activation of stress-response networks, and coordinated chromatin and metabolic reprogramming, thereby sustaining minimal residual disease and seeding relapse when selective pressure abates. The modern oncologic concept was formalized by Sharma et al. (2010), who operationally defined these cells as drug-surviving, reversibly adapted cancer subclones rather than mutation-fixed resistant variants. Table 1 summarizes foundational studies delineating DTP biology and its therapeutic implications.
DTP cells versus other cellular states

Drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells can be distinguished from other tumor cell states, including cancer stem cells (CSCs) and dormant cells by four features: slow proliferation, low drug permeability, a labile cellular phenotype, and a capacity for selective, irreversible genetic change under intense therapeutic pressure. Collectively, these properties support a self-renewing compartment that can withstand therapy and persist. Unlike CSCs, which are defined by stemness programs, DTP cells display a mobilizable phenotype and function as a reservoir for relapse and drug resistance. Clear differentiation of DTP cells from other cancer cell states is therefore essential for effective treatment design, underscoring the need to define their distinct characteristics.
Quiescence and reversibility of DTP cells

passages.text: Mechanism underlying DTP-cell development: Adapted from our August 2024 publication, "Targeting of FSP1 Regulates Iron Homeostasis in Drug Tolerant Persister Head and Neck Cancer Cells via Lipid-Metabolism-Driven Ferroptosis". Development of drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells under continuous treatment and re-sensitization after a drug holiday continuous drug exposure for 8 days induced a transient DTP state and withdrawal for 28 days restored drug sensitivity.
Fig 3

Drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells constitute a rare, stress-adapted fraction of tumor cells that enter a reversible slow-cycling/quiescent state under therapeutic pressure, thereby withstanding otherwise lethal exposures to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or targeted/immune agents. This tolerance is typically non-genetic and plastic: when treatment pressure is removed, DTPs can exit quiescence, re-enter the cell cycle, and reacquire pharmacologic susceptibility, distinguishing them from fixed, mutation-driven resistance. Multiple programs appear to underwrite this transient state, including epigenetic reprogramming (chromatin remodeling that dampens pro-apoptotic transcription), metabolic rewiring (shifts toward lipid and redox homeostasis), augmentation of DNA-damage repair, and activation of pro-survival signaling nodes (JAK/STAT, MAPK, PI3K) often reinforced by stromal cues in the tumor microenvironment. Because these cells are quiescent and frequently display stem-like features, they are well-positioned to seed minimal residual disease and drive relapses after therapy cessation. Accordingly, defining the determinants of DTP entry, maintenance, and exit is pivotal for designing eradication strategies that couple frontline therapy with rational co-targeting of the DTP state. (Fig. 3) adapted from our August 2024 publication, "Targeting of FSP1 Regulates Iron Homeostasis in Drug-Tolerant Persister Head and Neck Cancer Cells via Lipid-Metabolism-Driven Ferroptosis" summarizes this trajectory. In our model, a DTP phenotype emerges after 8 days of continuous drug exposure; following a 28-day drug holiday, cells resume proliferation with restored drug sensitivity, confirming reversibility of tolerance in washout assays. These observations motivate therapeutic concepts that either prevent DTP induction, force exit from quiescence into lethal cycling or exploit DTP-specific liabilities (ferroptotic vulnerability) to eliminate this reservoir before disease re-expansion.
DTP cells in cancer

Transformation of drug-sensitive cells into DTP cells under continuous therapy: Initial drug exposure generates a small, slow-cycling drug-tolerant persister (DTP) subpopulation within a heterogeneous tumor. With sustained dosing (doxycycline), DTP cells expand and become less affected by treatment. Prolonged pressure allows a fraction of DTPs to acquire fixed resistance via secondary mutations, gene copy-number gains, or pathway rewiring, enabling therapeutic escape. Clarifying this trajectory is key to designing schedules and agents that prevent persistence and delay resistance.

These differences likely reflect tumor-intrinsic and microenvironmental factors and can inform treatment scheduling and early-intervention windows.

infons.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Head and Neck

passages.text: Fig 5

Distribution of time to DTP persistence across cancers: The interval required for drug-tolerant persistence varies markedly by malignancy: HNSCC, breast cancer, and non-small-cell lung cancer typically exhibit persistence within ~2-4 weeks, whereas glioblastoma and bladder cancer require ~1-2 months. This heterogeneity likely reflects distinct adaptation programs including metabolic reprogramming, oxidative-stress responses, epigenetic plasticity, and genetic alterations that enable persister survival under therapeutic pressure. In more aggressive tumors, prolonged persistence may arise from complex regulatory networks that delay the transition to stable resistance. These differences highlight the need for tailored interventions that target the specific persistence mechanisms operating in each cancer type.

infons.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Head and Neck

passages.text: Fig 6

Drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells confer treatment resistance across multiple malignancies, including HNSCC. Unlike "self-determined" cancer cells that acquire fixed genetic alterations and enter classical dormancy, DTP cells display a reversible form of drug tolerance characterized by slow cycling and survival during conventional therapy without stable genetic change. DTP cells are therefore a primary source of persistent disease after initial therapy and a frequent driver of relapse and progression. Their capacity to endure therapeutic pressure arises from multiple adaptive programs. A central mechanism is metabolic reprogramming: rather than relying on glycolysis, DTP cells shift toward oxidative phosphorylation to satisfy minimal energetic needs during quiescence, thereby sustaining survival under treatment and enabling regenerative outgrowth once selective pressure is removed. In parallel, DTP cells engage stress-response signaling that dampens the effects of chemotherapy and targeted agents, and they augment DNA-damage management, promoting tolerance to platinum-based regimens. Epigenetic remodeling further tunes therapy-response genes, reinforcing drug tolerance. Mitochondrial quality control is also implicated: PINK1-driven mitophagy supports DTP formation, and genetic or pharmacologic disruption of PINK1/mitophagy can facilitate elimination of these cells and improve MAPK-directed therapy. Additional evidence indicates that PI3K-pathway deactivation reshapes phenotypic states: JARID1B(high) populations lose stem-like activity, while G0-like cells abandon priming; these shifts intersect with ferroptosis programs such that several agents induce ferroptotic death in HNSCC. Resistance frequently involves activation of the NRF2/ARE axis, and its inhibition can enhance chemotherapy efficacy. A cancer stem-cell phenotype can be engaged via the KDM5A/MPC1 axis in treatment-refractory HNSCC, increasing susceptibility to ferroptosis; likewise, PGRMC1 activation promotes ferroptosis in paclitaxel-resistant cells by elevating fatty-acid oxidation and sensitizing to system x_c^- (SLC7A11/xCT) inhibition. Moreover, epiregulin silencing augments cetuximab sensitivity by inducing ferroptosis, suggesting that epiregulin loss could support combinations of cetuximab with ferroptosis inducers. Differentiation into a DTP state is accompanied by reversal of pro-apoptotic programs and induction of stress-resistance genes. Understanding DTP biology in HNSCC is therefore essential, as these cells impede complete and durable responses (Fig. 4). Experimentally, DTP populations are generated by prolonged drug exposure of parental lines, yielding slow-cycling, drug-tolerant cells that are subsequently validated by reduced proliferation, characteristic transcriptional changes, and G0/G1 cell-cycle arrest; this in-vitro system enables controlled interrogation of DTP phenotypes and adaptations. Such knowledge informs the design of strategies that selectively target DTP cells, with the dual goals of enhancing efficacy and lowering relapse risk. Table 2 summarizes mechanisms underlying persistence and therapy resistance, including metabolic rewiring, genetic alterations, alternative survival pathways, chemotherapeutic evasion, and radio-resistance that permit survival, continued proliferation, and tumor re-initiation. The timeline for acquiring DTP phenotypes varies widely by malignancy, from weeks to months: in HNSCC, breast cancer, and NSCLC, DTP populations commonly emerge within 2-4 weeks of exposure, whereas glioblastoma and bladder cancer often require 1-2 months to establish persistence, reflecting distinct adaptive routes under selective pressure (Fig. 5, Fig. 6). Consistent with this heterogeneity, sarcomas also exhibit persister-like phenotypes that parallel the biology observed in epithelial malignancies. Recent findings in osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma models reveal the existence of slow-cycling subpopulations with enhanced oxidative phosphorylation, elevated antioxidant defenses, and resistance to conventional cytotoxic agents. These cells demonstrate a dependency on iron metabolism and reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis, rendering them highly susceptible to ferroptosis-inducing agents. The metabolic and redox adaptations observed in these mesenchymal tumors closely mirror the adaptive mechanisms of DTP cells identified in HNSCC and other carcinomas. Such convergence underscores a broader principle of therapy persistence that transcends tissue origin, highlighting the therapeutic potential of ferroptosis induction and metabolic rewiring strategies to overcome relapse and resistance across diverse types. Together, these observations underscore the need for tailored interventions that interrupt the specific persistence mechanisms operating within each cancer type. Although drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells have been primarily studied in malignant tumors such as HNSCC, emerging evidence suggests that similar persistence mechanisms may contribute to therapeutic resistance in aggressive benign neoplasms, including ameloblastoma and desmoid-type fibromatosis. These lesions exhibit locally invasive growth and high recurrence rates following conventional therapy, implying the presence of slow-cycling, therapy-tolerant cell subpopulations. Such DTP-like phenotypes have been linked to enhanced oxidative metabolism, DNA-repair activation, and transient stem-like states in non-malignant yet recurrent tumors. Therefore, the therapeutic strategies proposed in this review particularly those targeting metabolic reprogramming and DNA-repair vulnerabilities may also hold translational relevance for managing aggressive benign tumors that share persistence-associated biological traits.

passages.text: Metabolic adaptations in DTP cells

In head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cells undergo marked metabolic reprogramming to withstand therapeutic pressure. Rather than relying on glycolysis characteristic of rapidly proliferating tumor cells they transition to oxidative phosphorylation, adopting a low-energy, stress-tolerant state. This shift reduces vulnerability to agents that preferentially target fast-dividing populations, thereby facilitating persistence. By maintaining oxidative phosphorylation-driven dormancy, DTP cells evade both cytotoxic and targeted therapies. Consequently, disrupting these metabolic dependencies represents a rational strategy to re-sensitize tumors to standard treatments.

passages.text: DNA damage response and repair mechanisms

Cellular response to DNA damage and malignant transformation: Endogenous and exogenous insults trigger DNA-damage responses that preserve genomic integrity. When repair, apoptosis, or immune surveillance fails, damaged cells persist, promoting genomic instability and clonal evolution. Chronic injury also activates pro-inflammatory signaling and disrupts cell-cycle control, creating a tumor-promoting microenvironment and facilitating malignant transformation. Defining these pathways informs therapies that modulate DDR and prevent progression.
Fig 7

Prolonged survival and enhanced DNA-repair capacity are additional hallmarks of DTP cells in HNSCC, particularly under exposure to platinum-based chemotherapeutics that induce DNA damage. These cells display superior repair of DNA adducts and other therapy-induced lesions, thereby evading apoptosis and subsequent cell death. As illustrated in (Fig. 7), DNA-damage tolerance in DTP cells is linked to efficient homologous recombination and nonhomologous ending, the principal components of recombinational and non-recombinational repair pathways. Persistent activation of these mechanisms enables DTP cells to survive multiple chemotherapy cycles, facilitating the outgrowth of fully resistant populations. This augmented repair capacity underscores the limited long-term efficacy of DNA-damaging agents and highlights the importance of therapeutically targeting DNA-repair pathways to eradicate DTP cells.

passages.text: Epigenetic reprogramming and transcriptional plasticity

One characteristic feature of DTP cells in HNSCC is their capacity for epigenetic reprogramming, which enables them to modify gene-expression patterns in response to drug exposure. NRF2-driven metabolic reprogramming, particularly via oxidative phosphorylation, contributes to treatment failure in recurrent HPV-related HNSCC, making NRF2 a promising therapeutic target. DTP cells exhibit transcriptional plasticity, temporally altering gene expression to activate anti-apoptotic signals and suppress pro-apoptotic programs, thereby enhancing drug tolerance. This epigenetic plasticity enables DTP cells to switch between drug-resistant and proliferative phenotypes, supporting survival during therapy and re-entry into growth after drug withdrawal. The transcriptional adaptability of DTP cells poses a major treatment challenge because it allows rapid adjustment to therapeutic stress. Modulating epigenetic machinery may disrupt this plasticity and enhance the efficacy of standard therapies.

The TME is central to the survival and adaptation of DTP cells. Interactions among cancer-associated fibroblasts and immune cells within this milieu support DTP-cell persistence during treatment. Protective niches foster metabolic reprogramming, management of oxidative stress, and immune evasion. In addition, TME-driven redox signaling accelerates epigenetic change and promotes a slow-cycling DTP phenotype, reinforcing drug tolerance. Components of the TME therefore represent actionable therapeutic targets, as interrupting these cues can destabilize DTP maintenance and enable durable remission. The TME's role is integral to both the development and the maintenance of DTP states. DTP cells exhibit survival advantages metabolic remodeling, anti-apoptotic activity, and epigenetic adaptability that are not purely intrinsic but are acquired and sustained through TME interactions. Such interactions enable evasion of cytotoxic effects even under continuous drug exposure. Multiple TME-derived factors thus contribute to treatment failure and relapses through DTP-mediated resistance. The persistence of these cells, supported by the TME, underscores the need for strategies that disrupt adaptive programs and signal cascades sustaining DTP populations. Targeting TME-DTP crosstalk may reduce drug tolerance and relapse rates, yielding more durable therapeutic responses. A focus on the TME-DTP axis could ultimately shift treatment paradigms by embedding microenvironmental drivers of resistance into therapeutic planning. Table 3 summarizes mechanisms underlying the development of DTP cells in HNSCC.

passages.text: Pathways targeted in platinum-based chemotherapy for HNSCC: Cisplatin and carboplatin induce cytotoxicity by forming DNA adducts, triggering replication stress, checkpoint arrest, and apoptosis. Treatment response is shaped by drug transporters (uptake/efflux), DNA-repair pathways (e.g., NER, HR), apoptotic and pro-survival signaling, and mitochondrial programs governing metabolic adaptation and redox balance. Resistance typically arises via enhanced repair, altered transport, and apoptosis evasion, supporting combination strategies that co-target repair and survival nodes to improve efficacy.

passages.text: Fig 8

Development of a xenograft model harboring radiotherapy-tolerant persister (RTP) cells: Xenograft mice bearing human HNSCC xenografts received fractionated radiotherapy (>=48 Gy over 14 days). Although bulk tumor regressed, a residual slow-cycling RTP subpopulation remained within the tumor bed and retained tumor-repopulating capacity. Prior studies show RTP enrichment for stem-like markers (CD44^high/ALDH1^high) and activation of PI3K/AKT-MAPK signaling, consistent with intrinsic radio resistance and risk of local recurrence. RTP presence was inferred on day 14 post-treatment, indicating a barrier to complete tumor eradication.

infons.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Head and Neck

passages.text: Fig 9

Platinum-based chemotherapy remains foundational in HNSCC, with cisplatin or carboplatin the most used backbones in current practice (Fig. 8). Across comparative randomized data and subsequent analyses, substituting paclitaxel for 5-fluorouracil in cisplatin-containing regimens has not demonstrated an overall-survival advantage in HNSCC. Many tumors contain subpopulations of cycling DTP cells that acquire drug tolerance and precipitate relapses. In our laboratory testing, FSP1 levels were elevated in patients who relapsed after cisplatin therapy, accompanied by upregulation of lipid-metabolism gene programs, implicating FSP1 as a driver of drug resistance. Higher FSP1 expression may therefore serve as a predictor of impending relapse and a means to identify patients at greatest risk. Patients with HNSCC could benefit from improved delivery of FSP1 inhibitors. Accordingly, a functional link between FSP1 and acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) signaling and drug resistance may be established under cisplatin exposure in HNSCC DTP cells. Ivermectin has also been reported to sensitize cancer cells to cisplatin and other agents. Targeting the balance between FSP1 and ACSL4 may provide a strategy to overcome chemoresistance. For appropriately selected patients with locally advanced disease who are not surgical candidates, concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiation is guideline-recommended and improves outcomes relative to radiotherapy alone, although toxicity remains a concern. Both excision repair cross-complementation group 1 (ERCC1) and T-class biomarkers help predict responses to chemotherapy in HNSCC. Robust evidence indicates that ERCC1 may predict outcomes with 5-fluorouracil/cisplatin therapy. ALDH1A3 (Aldehyde dehydrogenase 1 family) functions as a marker of drug-resistant gastric cancer cells; therapies engaging crosstalk with the ALDH1A3/mTOR pathway can eliminate resistant clones in gastric cancer. Cyclin E2 has been identified as a target of miR-30a in oral cancer, nominating miR-30a as a biomarker and potential therapeutic target for resistance to 5-fluorouracil. Lower PTEN expression appears to indicate resistance to cetuximab in HNSCC, positioning PTEN as a candidate biomarker for personalized therapy in this setting. Previously, we examined KDM5D as a therapeutic target in HNSCC; KDM5D is overexpressed in tumors from patients with HNSCC, in CSCs, and in cisplatin-resistant cells. Elevated KDM5D expression correlates with poor responses to platinum and earlier relapses. One further study reported that PIK3CA and RAS mutations predicted cetuximab resistance in recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, whereas PTEN loss predicted resistance to cetuximab plus radiotherapy. Definitive radiotherapy cures most patients with non-metastatic HNSCC; nevertheless, 15-30 % experience locoregional failure, and over half of these relapses occur within the first six months after treatment completion, indicating persistence of radiation-tolerant clones that escape initial ablation. Experimental work in nude-mouse xenografts (FaDu and SCC25) showed that two weeks of clinically relevant fractionated irradiation ( 30 x 2-3 Gy; total >=48 Gy) eradicated bulk tumor mass but consistently left a slow-cycling, tumor-repopulating reservoir; tumor-control-dose analyses further demonstrated that squamous carcinomas required >50 Gy for 50 % control, underscoring intrinsic radio-tolerance. Derivative radio-resistant clones (FaDu-R) display an expanded cancer-stem-cell fraction (CD44^high/ALDH1^high), accelerated wound closure, heightened invasiveness, and hyperactivation of PI3K/Akt/MAPK programs long linked to post-irradiation survival. Multi-omics analyses of patient tumors have additionally shown that NFE2L2 (NRF2) gain of function or KEAP1 loss occurs in roughly one-quarter of HPV-negative HNSCCs and independently predicts radio-resistant disease, in part by rewiring intratumoral myeloid cells and strengthening redox defenses. Importantly, pharmacologic co-targeting of these adaptations is feasible: glutaminase inhibition with telaglenastat (CB-839) disrupts NRF2-driven metabolic buffering and resensitizes persister cells to ionizing radiation in both in-vitro and in-vivo HNSCC models. Collectively, current evidence supports the model illustrated here: a 14-day course of radiotherapy ablates the primary HNSCC lesion yet leaves a discrete reservoir of radiation-tolerant persister (RTP) cells that, unless specifically targeted, can repopulate the tumor and drive clinical relapse (Fig. 9). Another study associated high dickkopf-1 (DKK1) expression in HNSCC with an immunosuppressive TME and radio-resistance, identifying DKK1 as a potential target for enhancing radioimmunotherapy. NF-kappaB plays a central role in promoting radio resistance to cancer. In glioblastoma, the NF-kappaB-YY1-miR-103 axis drives resistance by enhancing DNA repair and stemness; in HNSCC, NF-kappaB promotes radio-resistance through senescence-associated cytokines, particularly via the CXCR2 ligand axis. In addition, MET (cellular mesenchymal-epithelial transition factor) increases radio-resistance in HNSCC by promoting cellular plasticity and stem-cell features; the MET inhibitor SU11274, when combined with radiotherapy, may mitigate resistance and improve outcomes. Studies have also highlighted miR-9 as a biomarker of response to radiotherapy and cetuximab; high miR-9 levels promote resistance by regulating the Sp1 pathway. Radio-resistance remains a major challenge in HNSCC and is driven by mechanisms such as STAT1 activation in HPV-negative disease and NFE2L2 (NRF2) mutations that promote tumor growth and immune evasion. Targeting these pathways particularly with agents such as CB-839 to counter NRF2-driven resistance may enhance radiosensitivity; biomarker-based strategies are therefore needed to improve outcomes. Periostin, acting through ERK/Akt, promotes EMT and radio-resistance in HNSCC and thus represents a biomarker and therapeutic candidate for overcoming radio-resistance. Cetuximab-resistant HNSCC commonly exhibits compensatory Ras/MAPK activation often with reduced DUSP5/DUSP6 and increased AURKB expression. Pharmacologic ERK1/2 or AURKB blockade can re-sensitize models to EGFR inhibition; resistance is further reinforced by Ras upregulation and heightened EGFR-ligand signaling, and co-targeting Ras prenylation/formylation or PI3K/Akt has restored treatment sensitivity. In oral cancer, activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome increases IL-1beta and enhances survival, contributing to 5-fluorouracil resistance; targeting this inflammasome may improve 5-fluorouracil efficacy. Initial exposure to cisplatin effectively induces DNA damage in HNSCC cells; however, DTP populations adapt cellular programs to evade drug-induced toxicity. DTP cells augment DNA-repair capacity and reduce reliance on chemotherapy-sensitive pathways, thereby surviving treatment. They also undergo metabolic reprogramming and activate stress-signaling pathways to avoid chemotherapy-induced apoptosis. Inhibiting IAP family proteins in HNSCC slows growth, promotes apoptosis, reduces invasiveness, and enhances chemosensitivity, nominating IAPs as promising therapeutic targets. Notch1 upregulation is associated with chemoresistance and poor survival in HNSCC, whereas Notch1 downregulation improves drug sensitivity, supporting Notch1 as a potential biomarker of treatment response. Multiple adaptive programs including enhanced DNA-damage repair, redox/metabolic rewiring, and phenotypic plasticity sustain DTP survival under platinum pressure and ultimately drive relapse. In platinum-experienced recurrent/metastatic HNSCC, afatinib has demonstrated improved progression-free survival versus methotrexate (Methotrexate) with acceptable safety, a finding corroborated in subsequent analyses. Together, these data underscore the limitations of current chemotherapy in eliminating DTP cells and highlight the need to develop synergistic therapeutic strategies that disrupt their survival mechanisms.

passages.text: Targeted therapy and DTP cells

EGFR-targeted therapy is effective for HNSCC tumors that harbor DTP cells. EGFR is frequently upregulated in these tumors and is therefore a principal molecular target for agents such as cetuximab. However, primary resistance to EGFR-directed therapy remains a major concern, because DTP cells often reroute signaling through alternative pathways to ensure survival. AZD4547, an inhibitor acting on the FGFR/AKT/SOX2 axis, effectively reduces cell viability, cell migration, and colony formation in HNSCC. Notably, AZD4547 enhances the effects of paclitaxel (Taxol). Macrophage-derived exosomes have been shown to diminish the chemosensitivity of oral cancer cells via the AKT pathway; this observation highlights exotics as potential targets to improve chemosensitivity. Upon cetuximab exposure, DTP cells frequently shift reliance to PI3K/AKT and ERK cascades, enabling survival despite EGFR blockade and sustaining adaptive resistance. This signaling plasticity allows DTP cells to persist without EGFR activation and to repopulate when treatment is paused. The persistence of these cells under EGFR-targeted therapy remains problematic because their presence can lead to long-term resistance. Secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) promotes HNSCC growth and confers cetuximab resistance by activating the KRAS/MEK pathway; thus, targeting SPP1 or using a MEK inhibitor may help overcome cetuximab resistance. In HPV-negative HNSCC, reduction or loss of SMAD4 is linked to cetuximab resistance and EMT; dual targeting of EGFR together with JNK/MAPK signaling has been proposed to restore responsiveness, and tumors with preserved SMAD4 expression appear more likely to benefit. To counter DTP-driven resistance, combinations that pair EGFR inhibition with agents against compensatory nodes such as PI3K/AKT or MEK have been proposed to limit adaptive signaling and improve efficacy. The aim of these strategies is to reduce the adaptive plasticity of DTP cells and thereby improve the effectiveness of EGFR-targeted therapy in HNSCC. Ongoing clinical trials are exploring new therapeutic regimens to overcome resistance to EGFR-directed therapy. Tyrosine 821 of the AXL receptor tyrosine kinase drives radio-resistance and cetuximab resistance in HNSCC by activating ABL1; targeting both EGFR and ABL1 may help overcome resistance and improve treatment response. Cetuximab resistance in HNSCC is also driven by SNAIL, lymphotoxin-beta, and protein arginine methyltransferase 1; this resistance can be mitigated by combining EGFR and NF-kappaB inhibitors. We demonstrated that FSP1 confers drug resistance by regulating iron homeostasis and lipid synthesis, which makes FSP1 a promising target for combating chemoresistance. FSP1 supports the survival of cancer cells under chemotherapy, particularly chemotherapy-tolerant DTP cells. DTP cells isolated from patients with HNSCC show elevated FSP1 levels and upregulation of lipid-metabolism associated genes such as ACSS2, CD36, and FABP4. Therefore, lipid metabolism is critical for drug tolerance. This finding highlights the importance of intracellular lipids in sustaining DTP cells. Deregulation of FSP1 has been observed in drug-resistant HNSCC, supporting the rationale for targeting FSP1 and developing FSP1 inhibitors. Targeting FSP1 may reduce rates of relapse and metastasis among patients with HNSCC.

passages.text: Immunotherapy and immune evasion in DTP cells

infons.name: Chemical and Drug Induced Liver Injury

passages.text: Currently, immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis are effective in the treatment of HNSCC. As first-line therapy for PD-L1-positive recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, pembrolizumab administered with or without chemotherapy is recommended. Compared with standard regimens, pembrolizumab improves overall survival and yields a more favorable severe-toxicity profile in recurrent or metastatic disease. Sideroflexin-3 expression is upregulated and correlates with poor prognosis, immune suppression, and paclitaxel resistance; accordingly, it may inform therapeutic decision-making. In HNSCC, lysosomal integral membrane protein 2 has been evaluated as a therapeutic target and associated with increased autophagy, cancer-stem-cell properties, and resistance to immunotherapy. Although immunotherapy offers meaningful benefit, DTP cells exhibit immune features that confer resistance to treatment. In HNSCC-associated progenitor cells, STAT1 promotes tumor progression and immunosuppression, whereas tripartite motif-containing 24 (TRIM24) a STAT1 repressor emerges as a potential therapeutic target. DTP cells can also inhibit antigen-presentation pathways, hindering immune recognition and clearance. These cells further downregulate immune checkpoints, creating conditions that favor immune evasion. This immune-evasive behavior is particularly prominent in recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, enabling DTP cells to withstand immune attack. Combining T-cell and natural killer (NK) based immunotherapies may improve outcomes by targeting resistant clones within an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Such combination approaches aim to address limitations of immunotherapy in resistant HNSCC.

passages.text: Therapeutic strategies targeting DTP cells in HNSCC

infons.name: Chemical and Drug Induced Liver Injury

passages.text: Targeting unique metabolic characteristics

DTP cells in HNSCC display altered metabolic profiles; accordingly, their unique metabolic features are now being explored as potential therapeutic targets. DTP cells shift from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation to survive therapeutic stress. This metabolic shift presents an opportunity to disrupt DTP-cell survival by using inhibitors that selectively target components of the oxidative phosphorylation pathway. Research indicates that combining metabolic inhibitors with standard therapies for ovarian cancer, such as platinum-based chemotherapy, enhances treatment efficacy because DTP cells cannot easily switch to an alternative energy-generation pathway. Clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate combination therapies aimed at eliminating DTP cells and reducing recurrence rates.
