The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12967-025-07328-y.
Background

Peripheral nerve injury (PNI) often causes motor and sensory dysfunction and remains a persistent clinical challenge. Although the peripheral nervous system possesses intrinsic regenerative capacity, this potential is limited by intrinsic regulatory mechanisms and the post-injury microenvironment, making effective nerve repair difficult. Advances have been made in surgical techniques such as nerve anastomosis and autologous nerve transplantation have improved outcomes but fail to activate the regenerative potential of nerves, leading to incomplete functional recovery. Therefore, elucidating the intrinsic mechanisms of nerve regeneration and developing novel therapeutic strategies to overcome bottlenecks in PNI repair remain essential.

Precise intercellular crosstalk is plays a central role in nerve regeneration, and interactions between macrophages and Schwann cells are critical for coordinating axonal regrowth after PNI. Traditionally, these interactions were attributed to rely on cytokines and extracellular vesicles (EVs). However, recent studies have identified migrasomes, large membrane vesicles (0.5-3 mum) released during cell migration, as a novel mode of intercellular communication. Migrasomes originate from retraction fibers at the trailing edge of migrating cells, where they accumulate cellular components before being released and internalized by neighboring cells, influencing multiple pathological processes. As highly migratory immune cells, Macrophages are major producers of migrasomes in vivo and in vitro. Emerging evidence suggests that macrophage-derived migrasomes can regulate the phenotype and function of recipient cell by transferring bioactive molecules. However, whether migrasomes mediate macrophage-Schwann cell communication during peripheral nerve regeneration remains unknown.

SJMHE1, a small peptide derived from Schistosoma japonicum heat shock protein 60 (HSP60), exhibits broad anti-inflammatory effects in animal models, including inhibition of collagen-induced arthritis, acute and chronic colitis, and allergic rhinitis. Excessive inflammation disrupts Schwann cell function and impairs peripheral nerve regeneration. Our previous study demonstrated that SJMHE1 promotes PNI repair by inducing anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages. Notably, SJMHE1 also accelerates Schwann cell maturation and myelin regeneration in vivo, but exerts no direct effect on Schwann cell proliferation or migration in vitro, suggesting the existence of indirect regulatory pathways in vivo. Whether SJMHE1 promotes nerve regeneration by modulating Schwann cell function through macrophage-derived migrasomes remains to be determined.

Here, we investigated the role of SJMHE1-induced macrophage-derived migrasomes (SM-M) in regulating Schwann cell function. We found that SJMHE1 induces macrophages to produce migrasomes that enhance Schwann cell proliferation and migration by delivering miR-26b-5p, which targets the PTEN/AKT signaling axis. These findings reveal a novel mechanism through which SJMHE1 promotes peripheral nerve regeneration and provide a foundation for its development as a therapeutic agent for PNI.
Materials and methods
SJMHE1 peptide synthesis

The SJMHE1 peptide derived from Schistosoma japonicum HSP60 (residues 437-460; sequence: VPGGGTALLRCIPVLDTLSTKNED), was synthesized and purified by SYNPEPTIDE CO., LTD Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China). The peptide, with a purity exceeding 99%, was used for all experiments.
Animals

Male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats weighing 180-200 g were purchased from Changzhou Cavens Laboratory Animal Co., Ltd. All animals received humane care, and experimental procedures followed the Guidelines for the Protection and Use of Experimental Animals and the Measures for the Administration of Animal Use of Jiangsu University. All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Experiment Ethics Committee of Jiangsu University (Approval No.:UJS-IACUC-AP-20190305056).
Sciatic nerve transection injury models

Rats were acclimated for one week and then randomly divided into two groups (n = 7 per group): Control group (PBS) and SJMHE1 treatment group. All animals were anesthetized with 4% isoflurane for induction and maintained with continuous inhalation of 2% isoflurane during surgery. The rat sciatic nerve transection injury model was established following our previous protocol. Briefly, the sciatic nerve was transected and bridged with a silicone tube to form a 5-mm gap. A 5 microL mixture of PBS or 5 microL of SJMHE1 (10 microg) and Matrigel (BD Biosciences, MA) in a 1:1 (v/v) ratio, and each mixture was injected into the nerve conduit using a pre-cooled microsyringe. On day 7 after conduit implantation, tissue samples from the proximal stump were collected for CD68 and S100 immunofluorescence staining to assess macrophage activity; Western blotting (WB) analysis was also performed to examine the expression of migrasome-related markers in the tissues.

For localization studies, FITC-labeled SJMHE1 was locally injected at the injury site. At the 24 h post-injury, the rats were euthanized, and the injured nerves were collected for frozen sectioning and immunofluorescence staining with CD68 and S100. Fluorescence colocalization analysis was used to identify the target cells of SJMHE1.
Adoptive transfer of macrophages

The adoptive transfer protocol was based on previous studies. Rat peritoneal macrophages were isolated using an established extraction method and transfected with TSPAN4 small interfering RNA (TSPAN4-siRNA; GenePharma, Shanghai, China). Cells were divided into two groups: negative control (NC-siRNA) and TSPAN4-siRNA. After treatment with 0.5 microg/mL SJMHE1 for 24 h, macrophages (2 x 105 cells/50 microL DMEM) were injected into the injury site of the rat sciatic nerve crush injury model. The experimental groups (n = 3 per group) included PBS, SJMHE1 + NC-siRNA, and SJMHE1 + TSPAN4-siRNA. Fourteen days after model establishment, rats were euthanized, and injured nerve tissues were collected for hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining to assess morphology, and for NF200 and S100 immunofluorescence to evaluate axonal regeneration and Schwann cell activation.
Cell culture

The mouse macrophage cell line RAW264.7, rat Schwann cell line RSC96 and rat pheochromocytoma cell line (PC12, a neuronal cell model) were purchased from the Cell Bank of the Typical Culture Preservation Committee, Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China). Cells were cultured in DMEM (Gibco, Grand Island, NY, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Beyotime, Nantong, China) at 37  C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2.
Formation of migrasomes

RAW264.7 cells were pretreated with 0.5 microg/mL SJMHE1 for 24 h, and untreated cells served as controls. Subsequently, 5 x 103 treated or untreated RAW264.7 cells were cocultured with 5 x 103 RSC96 cells (1:1 ratio) on glass coverslips for 24 h. Following standard preparation procedures for scanning electron microscopy (SEM), migrasome formation was observed using a SEM (JSM-7900 F, JEOL, Japan).

To further assess SJMHE1-induced migrasome formation, RAW264.7 cells treated or untreated with 0.5 microg/mL SJMHE1 for 24 h were fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde and examined by SEM for retraction fibers and attached migrasomes. As described previously, cells were also stained with 1 microg/mL Wheat Germ Agglutinin (WGA; Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA) and imaged under a confocal microscope to visualize migrasome structures around the cell periphery.

For ultrastructural analysis, RAW264.7 cells treated or untreated with 0.5 microg/mL SJMHE1 for 24 h were digested with 0.25% trypsin and collected for transmission electron microscopy (TEM). After standard TEM sample preparation, migrasome morphology was examined using a TEM (JEM-1200EX; JEOL Ltd., Tokyo, Japan).
Isolation and characterization of migrasomes

Macrophages treated or untreated with 0.5 microg/mL SJMHE1 were separately seeded into 100 mm culture dishes and maintained in conditioned medium containing serum-depleted EVs. When cell confluence reached 40-50%, cells were washed twice with PBS, digested with 0.25% trypsin, and collected into 50 mL centrifuge tubes. All subsequent steps were conducted at 4  C. Migrasomes were isolated following a previously described protocol. Briefly, the samples were centrifuged at 1000 x g for 10 min and then at 4000 x g for 20 min to remove cells and debris. The supernatant after centrifugation was filtered through a 0.45 mum membrane, which was subsequently inverted and flushed with PBS using a medical syringe containing PBS. The resulting filtrate was transferred to a 100 kDa ultrafiltration tube and centrifuged at 2000 x g for 5 min to collect the migrasomes. Migrasomes derived from SJMHE1-treated macrophages were designated as SM-M, and those derived from untreated macrophages were designated as M-M.

Migrasome morphology and ultrastructure were examined using TEM (JEM-1200EX; JEOL Ltd., Tokyo, Japan). Particle size distribution was determined by nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) using a NanoSight NS300 (Malvern Instruments Ltd., Worcestershire, UK). Protein concentration in the migrasome suspension was quantified with a BCA protein assay kit (Beyotime), and the expression of migrasome-specific markers was analyzed by WB.
Treatment with SM-M or M-M in vivo

The rat sciatic nerve crush injury model was established according to previous studies. Experimental groups (n = 3 per group) included control, M-M, and SM-M. Briefly, the exposed sciatic nerve was crushed three times with hemostatic forceps for 15 s each, producing complete transverse axonal rupture whereas preserving the epineurium. A total of 100 microL of PBS, M-M, or SM-M (containing 40 microg of M-M or SM-M suspended in 100 microL PBS) was injected into the crush site using a microinjector. Fourteen days after injury, the hindlimbs were photographed for macroscopic evaluation, and footprint analysis was conducted. Subsequently, rats were euthanized, and neural tissues were harvested for HE staining and immunofluorescence for NF200 and S100.
Footprint analysis

Sciatic nerve function was evaluated using the sciatic functional index (SFI) as previously described. The hind paws of rats were coated with red ink, and each rat was allowed to walk along a paper-lined runway. Clear footprints were selected for analysis, and SFI was calculated using the following equation: SFI = (-38.3 x (EPL-NPL)/NPL) + (109.5 x (ETS-NTS)/NTS) + (13.3 x (EIT-NIT)/NIT) - 8.8. where "E" denotes the experimental foot, and "N" the normal foot; EPL, ETS, and EIT represent footprint length, toe width, and intermediary toe spacing of the experimental foot, respectively, and NPL, NTS, and NIT represent the corresponding parameters of the normal foot. The SFI value ranges from - 100 to 0, where 0 indicates normal neural function and - 100 indicates complete loss of neural function.
Immunofluorescent staining
Immunofluorescence staining was performed following our previously described protocol.

For the transection injury model, neural tissues from the proximal stump collected on day 7 were sectioned longitudinally after paraffin embedding. Sections were incubated with rabbit anti-CD68 antibody (1:5000, GB11067, Servicebio, Wuhan, China) and rabbit anti-S100 antibody (1:5000, GB13359, Servicebio), followed by goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody conjugated to CY3-tyramine(1:500, G1223, Servicebio)/iF488-tyramine(1:500, G1231, Servicebio). Each washing step was performed with PBS for 5 min.

For the crush injury model, neural tissues were collected 14 days post-surgery, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA), and processed for paraffin embedding system. Sections were stained with rabbit anti-rat S100 (1:200, GB113884, Servicebio) and mouse anti-rat NF200 (1:100, GB12144, Servicebio), followed by Cy3 goat anti-rabbit antibody (1:300, GB21303, Servicebio) and Alexa Fluor 488 goat anti-mouse (1:400, GB25301, Servicebio) secondary antibodies. Each washing step was repeated three times in PBS for 5 min.

To assess migrasome uptake by Schwann cells, RSC96 cells were first labeled with the green fluorescent dye DIO and co-incubated for 2 h with migrasomes pre-labeled with the red dye CM-Dil. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. All reagents were obtained from Beyotime. Fluorescent images were captured using a CKX-53 fluorescence microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan).

To further simulate in vitro migrasome uptake, CM-Dil-labeled SM-M was co-cultured for 2 h with RSC96 and PC12 cells (1:1 seeding ratio). Red fluorescence in these cells was observed under a CKX-53 fluorescence microscope to evaluate SM-M internalization.
Cell proliferation assay

The proliferation of RSC96 cells was evaluated using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Biosharp, Hefei, China) assay and 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) kit (Beyotime). For the CCK-8 assay, RSC96 cells were seeded in a 96-well plates at a density of 5 x 103 cells/well and cultured overnight. The medium was then replaced with fresh medium containing SM-M at different concentrations and incubation for 24 h. CCK-8 reagent was added, and the plates were incubated for 1 h. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a Multiskan FC microplate reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). For the EdU assay, RSC96 cells (5 x 104) were plated in 24-well plates and treated with SM-M or M-M for 24 h, followed by staining according to the manufacturer's instructions. Images were captured using an Olympus CKX-53 fluorescence microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan). The EdU was calculated as: [EdU stained cells (red fluorescence) / DAPI stained cells (blue fluorescence)] x100%.
Cell migration assay

Cell migration was analyzed using Transwell chambers (8 mum pore size; Corning, Cambridge, MA, USA). For the transwell assay, RSC96 cells (1 x 105 in 200 microL serum-free medium) were seeded in the upper chamber of Transwell (8 mum pore size; Corning, Cambridge, MA, USA), whereas the lower chamber was filled with 600 microL of complete medium supplemented with 10% FBS. After 24 h incubation at 37  C, non-migrated cells on the upper surface were gently removed, and cells adhering to the lower surface of the Transwell membrane were then fixed with 4% polyformaldehyde (PFA) and stained with 0.1% crystal violet. Images were obtained using a Leica ICC50 HD microscope (Wetzlar, Germany).

For chemotaxis assays, the procedure was similar except that the lower chamber contained culture medium supplemented with 10% FBS and either M-M or SM-M, which served as chemoattractants. After 24 h, the cells on the lower surface were gently removed. cells adhering to the lower surface of the Transwell membrane were fixed and stained as described above, and images were recorded using the same microscope.
WB analysis

Proteins were extracted using RIPA buffer (Beyotime) and quantified with a BCA protein quantification kit (Beyotime). WB analysis was performed as previously described. The following primary antibodies were used: TSPAN4 (1:1000, A10253, Abclonal, Wuhan, China); PIGK (1:1000, ab201693, Abcam, Cambridge, MA, USA); EOGT (1:1000, ab190693, Abcam); NDST1 (1:1000, 26203-1-AP, Proteintech, Rocky Hill, NJ, USA); CPQ/PGCP (1:1000, 16601-1-AP, Proteintech); beta-actin (1:2000, 4970T, Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA); PTEN (1:1000, 9188T, Cell Signaling Technology), AKT (1:1000, 4691T, Cell Signaling Technology); phospho-AKT (1:1000, 4060T, Cell Signaling Technology); and GAPDH (1:2000, HY-P80137, MedChemExpress, Monmouth Junction, NJ, USA). Goat anti-rabbit IgG-HRP (1:2000, 7074P2, Cell Signaling Technology) was used as the secondary antibody.
MiRNA sequencing and analysis

To profile miRNA cargoes of SM-M and M-M, total RNA was extracted and subjected to miRNA sequencing. Library preparation, sequencing, and bioinformatic analyses were performed by LC-Bio Technology (LC-Bio Technology Co., Ltd., Hangzhou, China).
Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR)

Total RNA was extracted from cells using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and reverse-transcribed into cDNA using the GenePharma reverse transcription kit (GenePharma, Shanghai, China). Quantitative PCR was performed with SYBR Green Master Mix (GenePharma). Relative gene expression was analyzed using the 2-DeltaDeltaCt method and normalized to U6 for miRNAs and beta-actin for mRNAs.
Cell transfection

RSC96 cells at approximately 60% confluency were transfected with 30 nM miRNA/siRNA or 1 microg PTEN plasmid using GenePharma transfection reagent in Opti-MEM medium (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Synthetic miR-26b-5p mimic, miR-23a-3p mimic, mimic control, miR-26b-5p inhibitor, inhibitor control; siRNA targeting PTEN, and nonspecific siRNA control, PTEN overexpression plasmid and control vector plasmid were purchased from GenePharma.
Luciferase reporter assay

To validate the interaction between miR-26b-5p and the 3'-UTR of PTEN, HEK293T cells were co-transfected with 100 nM miRNA mimics and 1 microg of dual-luciferase reporter plasmid containing either the wild-type (WT) or mutant-type (MUT) PTEN 3'-UTR (GenePharma). At 48 h post-transfection, cells were lysed, and luciferase activity was measured using the Luc-Pair  Dual-Luciferase Assay Kit 2.0 (GenePharma). Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase for each sample.
Statistical analysis

All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (version 8.0; GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA). Data are presented as mean +- standard deviation (SD). Statistical significance between two groups was evaluated using the Student's t-test, whereas comparisons among multiple groups were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test. A P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
SJMHE1 mediates macrophage-Schwann cell communication via inducing macrophage-derived migrasomes

In our previous studies, we have demonstrated that: (1) SJMHE1 promotes peripheral nerve regeneration through a macrophage-dependent mechanism; (2) macrophages are capable of generating migrasomes; (3) migrasomes are membrane vesicle structures dependent on cell migration, which participate in multiple pathological processes. Based on these foundations, we hypothesized that SJMHE1 may modulate migrasome formation in macrophages, and these migrasomes contribute to nerve regeneration.

To verify this hypothesis, we established a rat sciatic nerve transection model with local SJMHE1 injection. At 7 days post-injection, compared with the control group, the SJMHE1 group exhibited a marked increase in macrophage numbers in proximal nerve tissues, accompanied by higher fluorescence intensity of S100, a Schwann cell marker (Fig. 1A). Numerous round vesicle-like structures were observed between Schwann cell-formed myelin fibers, most displaying a "tadpole-like" morphology (Fig. A1, A2, a1 and a2). These structures were CD68-positive, confirming their macrophage origin, and were internalized by Schwann cells (Fig. A3, a3). Given their larger size and characteristic morphology, distinct from conventional EVs, these structures closely resembled migrasomes as previously described. Thus, we inferred that SJMHE1 may induce macrophages to form migrasomes, which then participate in intercellular communication with Schwann cells.

To further validate, we simulated the in vivo microenvironment using an in vitro coculture system. SEM revealed that, compared with the control group, SJMHE1-treated macrophages formed denser retraction fiber networks at their tailing edges, with a markedly higher number of migrasomes attached to these retraction fibers. In contrast, Schwann cells, which exhibited a flattened morphology, rarely produced retraction fibers or migrasomes (Fig. 1B). Importantly, migrasomes at the tips of macrophage-derived retraction fibers were observed in direct contact with the borders of Schwann cell bodies, corroborating the in vivo findings. WB analysis further showed that SJMHE1 administration significantly upregulated the expression of migrasome-related markers, including TSPAN4, PIGK, EOGT, NDST1, and CPQ in proximal nerve tissues (Fig. 1C-D). Notably, as shown in Supplementary Figure S1, we constructed a rat sciatic nerve injury model and locally injected FITC-labeled SJMHE1 (green). Co-localization analysis revealed that SJMHE1 primarily overlapped with macrophages (labelled by CD68), while minimal co-localization was observed with other key cell types involved in peripheral nerve regeneration, such as Schwann cells (labelled by S100). This partly suggests that SJMHE1 may specifically regulate migrasome production in macrophage.

To further verify that macrophage-derived migrasomes mediate the pro-regenerative effect of SJMHE1 on peripheral nerves, we first knocked down TSPAN4 (via TSPAN4-siRNA) in macrophages (Supplementary Figure S2A). TSPAN4 is a key gene essential for migrasome biogenesis, and its silencing has been shown to significantly suppress migrasome formation. Subsequently, we performed adoptive transfer of two distinct macrophage cell populations to the sciatic nerve injury site in rat: SJMHE1-treated macrophages transfected with either TSPAN4-siRNA or negative control NC-siRNA (called SMTSPAN4-siRNA and SMNC-siRNA, respectively). SMNC-siRNA treatment effectively promoted the process of nerve regeneration (higher number of nerve fibers at the injury site, and the upregulated S100 and NF200 expression), yet this promotional effect was impaired when adoptively transferring SMTSPAN4-siRNA (Supplementary Figure S2B and S2C). This result at least partially confirms that migrasomes released by SJMHE1-treated macrophages in vivo are functionally involved in promoting nerve regeneration.

Collectively, these data strongly indicate that, beyond directly promoting peripheral nerve regeneration by inducing M2 macrophages, SJMHE1 may mediate macrophage-Schwann cell communication by regulating the formation of macrophage-derived migrasomes.
SJMHE1 promotes the formation of macrophage migrasomes in vitro

We previously reported that SJMHE1 enhances macrophage migration. As migrasome formation is closely associated with cell motility, we inferred that SJMHE1 treatment might increase migrasome production. As expected, we found that SJMHE1-treated macrophages formed longer retraction fiber networks in their tail regions and exhibited a significantly higher number of migrasomes (Fig. 2A-C). However, the particle size of migrasomes did not differ significantly between the SJMHE1 and control groups (Fig. 2D). To further confirm these results, we used WGA staining to visualize migrasomes. The results showed that SJMHE1-treated macrophages displayed numerous retraction fibers, with WGA-positive migrasomes localized at fiber branching points or termini. The particle size of these migrasomes was similar to that of the control group (Fig. 2E-H), consistent with SEM findings. Taken together, these data demonstrate that SJMHE1 promotes the formation of migrasomes in macrophages.
Isolation and characterization of SJMHE1-induced macrophage-derived migrasomes

To visualize migrasome formation at the ultrastructural level, SJMHE1-treated macrophages were digested, fixed, and sectioned for TEM. Results showed that migrasomes were observed as discrete structures within the intercellular spaces. Compared with the control group, SJMHE1-treated macrophages produced significantly more migrasomes containing variable numbers of smaller internal vesicles, a typical feature of migrasomes (Fig. 3A).

Next, using the previously established separation and purification method, we isolated macrophage migrasomes (M-M) and SJMHE1-induced macrophage migrasomes (SM-M) (Fig. 3B). TEM imaging showed that both purified M-M and SM-M presented as large elliptical vesicles with surface folds and attached retraction fibers with smaller migrasomes visible nearby (indicated by red arrows) (Fig. 3C). NTA revealed distinct peaks above 800 nm in both groups (Fig. 3D), consistent with previously reported migrasome size distributions. Furthermore, WB confirmed that both M-M and SM-M expressed characteristic migrasome-specific markers, including TSPAN4, PIGK, EOGT, NDST1, and CPQ. These results confirm that the large vesicles isolated from macrophages are indeed migrasomes.
SM-M promotes Schwann cell function after peripheral nerve injury

To assess whether SJMHE1 regulates Schwann cell function through macrophage-derived migrasomes, we established a rat sciatic nerve crush injury model and locally injected PBS, M-M, or SM-M at the crush site (Fig. 4A-B). Because nerve regeneration typically begins around 14 days after injury, we evaluated the macroscopic morphology of the ipsilateral hind paws and performed footprint analyses at this time point. Although partial spreading of the hind paw toes was observed in the SM-M group, no significant differences were detected compared with the PBS or M-M groups, as confirmed by footprint analysis (Fig. 4C, Supplementary Fig. S3). This likely reflects the early regenerative stage at day 14, when regenerating axons have not yet formed complete functional connections across the injury site, resulting in limited behavioral recovery.

Because EVs often regulate recipient cell function through internalization, and SM-M are membrane vesicles of similar nature, we hypothesized that SM-M might act via cellular uptake. To test this, SM-M were labeled with CM-Dil (red) and co-incubated with RSC96 cells pre-labeled with DiO (green). Following confirmation of SM-M uptake, we explored its effects on Schwann cell function. Both CCK-8 and EdU assays showed that SM-M significantly increased RSC96 cell proliferation (Fig. 5C-E). Transwell assays demonstrated enhanced RSC96 cell migration under SM-M treatment (Fig. 5F-G). Considering that migrasomes are known to exert localized signaling effects that guide directional cell movement, we further examined their role in Schwann cell chemotaxis. When SM-M were added to the lower chamber of a Transwell system, a markedly greater number of RSC96 cells migrated toward the lower chamber compared with controls (Fig. 5H-I). These results indicate that SM-M not only promote Schwann cell proliferation and migration but also direct their migration through signal localization, providing indirect evidence that SJMHE1 regulates Schwann cell function via communication mediated by macrophage-derived migrasomes.
miR-26b-5p functions as an effector of SM-M in promoting Schwann cell proliferation and migration

Our previous work showed that macrophage-derived migrasomes are enriched in miRNAs. To elucidate the mechanism by which SM-M promote Schwann cell proliferation and migration, we performed miRNA sequencing on SM-M and M-M. The analysis identified 178 upregulated and 161 downregulated miRNAs in SM-M compared with M-M (Fig. 6A). The most differentially expressed miRNAs were visualized in a heatmap (Fig. 6B). KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of target genes revealed significant involvement of the PI3K-AKT pathway, which regulates cell proliferation and migration (Fig. 6C). Additional pathways associated with axonal growth and regeneration, including Wnt, ErbB, and mTOR signaling, were also enriched. Given that miRNAs carried by EVs generally exert biological functions through upregulation, we focused on the five most highly upregulated candidates: miR-26b-5p, miR-17-5p, miR-20a-5p, miR-23a-3p, and miR-191-5p. Bioinformatics analysis using TargetScan and miRDB predicted that PTEN is a common target of all five miRNAs (Fig. 6D).

We then performed validation via qRT-PCR to identify core regulatory miRNAs in SM-M, and found that miR-26b-5p was the most significantly upregulated miRNA (Fig. 6E); thus, it was selected as the primary focus for subsequent analyses. Consistently, compared with the control group, SM-M treatment notably increased miR-26b-5p expression levels in RSC96 cells (Fig. 6F). To explore its function, RSC96 cells were transfected with miR-26b-5p mimics or inhibitors, and transfection efficiency was verified by qRT-PCR (Fig. 6G). Cell growth curves and EdU assays showed that miR-26b-5p mimics significantly enhanced RSC96 cell proliferation, whereas inhibition of miR-26b-5p reduced proliferation (Fig. 6H-J). Similarly, migration assays indicated that miR-26b-5p overexpression promoted, whereas inhibition of miR-26b-5p impaired RSC96 cell migration (Fig. 6K-L). We also explored the function of miR-23a-3p, another upregulated miRNA in SM-M. As shown in Supplementary Figure S4, miR-23a-3p mimics dramatically enhanced RSC96 cell proliferation and migration; however, compared with miR-23a-3p mimics, miR-26b-5p mimics exhibited a stronger ability to promote Schwann cell proliferation and migration. These findings indicate that miR-26b-5p is not only the most upregulated miRNA in SM-M, but also exerts the most prominent regulatory effect on Schwann cell functions.

Given that PTEN was a predicted target of miR-26b-5p, we next examined their expression relationship in Schwann cells. Both SM-M treatment and miR-26b-5p mimics reduced PTEN protein levels, whereas miR-26b-5p inhibition increased PTEN levels (Fig. 6M-N). Because PTEN negatively regulates the PI3K/AKT pathway, we further measured AKT phosphorylation. miR-26b-5p overexpression significantly elevated phosphorylated AKT (P-AKT) levels, consistent with the activation observed in SM-M-treated cells (Fig. 6O).
miR-26b-5p mediates SM-M-induced Schwann cell function by targeting the PTEN/AKT axis

Apart from TargetScan and miRDB, analyses using miRTarBase and miRmap also identified PTEN as a potential target of miR-26b-5p (Fig. 7A). The PTEN-encoding gene is highly conserved among humans, rats, and mice, and contains a seed sequence complementary to miR-26b-5p (Fig. 7B). To confirm whether the 3'-UTR of PTEN is a direct binding site for miR-26b-5p, we performed a dual-luciferase reporter assay. Overexpression of miR-26b-5p markedly reduced luciferase activity in constructs containing the wild-type (WT) PTEN 3'-UTR binding site, but had no effect on constructs carrying a mutant binding site (Fig. 7C). These findings confirm that PTEN is a direct target of miR-26b-5p.

We next assessed the functional role of PTEN in Schwann cells. To minimize off-target interference, four PTEN-targeting small interfering RNAs (siPTEN1-4, corresponding to siRNA-333, siRNA-653, siRNA-1069, and siRNA-282, respectively) and a negative control (si-NC) were designed and transfected into RSC96 cells. Knockdown efficiency was verified by real-time quantitative PCR and WB (Fig. 7D-E). Among these, si-PTEN1 (siRNA333) showed the strongest inhibition and was selected for further experiments. RSC96 cells were transfected with either si-PTEN1 or a PTEN overexpression plasmid (OE-PTEN) (Fig. 7F). Compared with controls, PTEN knockdown significantly enhanced RSC96 cell proliferation and migration, whereas PTEN overexpression suppressed both processes (Fig. 7G-I), indicating that PTEN acts as a negative regulator of Schwann cell proliferation and migration.

To clarify the regulatory relationship between miR-26b-5p and PTEN, a rescue experiment was conducted in which RSC96 cells were co-transfected with miR-26b-5p mimics and the OE-PTEN plasmid. PTEN overexpression alone significantly inhibited RSC96 cell proliferation and migration, whereas co-transfection with miR-26b-5p mimics reversed this inhibition (Fig. 7J-L). We further examined whether miR-26b-5p regulates the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in Schwann cells via PTEN targeting. As shown in Fig 7M, PTEN overexpression significantly reduced P-AKT levels, whereas PTEN knockdown upregulated P-AKT expression. Co-transfection of miR-26b-5p mimics with OE-PTEN restored P-AKT levels compared with OE-PTEN alone.

Combined with the above results, miR-26b-5p is likely a key effector of SM-M function, promoting Schwann cell proliferation and migration by activating the AKT signaling pathway through suppression of PTEN.
Discussion

PNI remains a major clinical challenge, as the intrinsic regenerative potential of the peripheral nervous system is often insufficient for full functional recovery. A critical obstacle is the excessive inflammatory response that occurs during the early post-injury phase, which disrupts the microenvironment homeostasis required for regeneration and directly impairs Schwann cell function. Thus, strategies that simultaneously modulate inflammation and preserve Schwann cell function are essential for effective PNI treatment. Our previous work demonstrated that SJMHE1, a peptide derived from Schistosoma japonicum, promotes PNI repair by inducing anti-inflammatory M2 macrophage polarization, thereby establishing a pro-regenerative microenvironment. In this study, we extend these findings by identifying a second complementary mechanism in which SJMHE1 enhances Schwann cell function via macrophage-derived migrasomes. This "dual-mode" of action, combining anti-inflammatory regulation with functional promotion of Schwann cells, distinguishes SJMHE1 from single-target interventions and highlights its potential as a multifaceted therapeutic candidate for PNI.

As a novel cell-to-cell communication vesicle, migrasomes have attracted considerable attention in recent years. Although several publications referred to migrasomes as EVs, migrasomes differ from traditional EVs (such as exosomes and microvesicles) considering the biogenesis, size, markers and functional roles: (1) Biogenesis: migrasomes are uniquely formed along the retraction fibers of migrating cells and released upon fiber breakage, whereas exosomes originate from endosomal sorting complexes required for transport and are released via multivesicular body fusion, and microvesicles bud directly from the plasma membrane; (2) Size: migrasomes typically range from 500 to 3000 nm, which is significantly larger than exosomes (30-150 nm) and microvesicles (100-1000 nm); (3) Markers: migrasomes are specifically labeled by TSPAN4, while exosomes are characterized by CD63/CD81/TSG101 and microvesicles by CD40/Annexin V; (4) Functional roles: unlike exosomes/microvesicles that mainly mediate cargo delivery in static cell microenvironments, migrasomes are tightly coupled to cell migration and excel at "spatiotemporally targeted communication" during dynamic processes (e.g., guiding cell migration via directional cargo release). The rationale for focusing on migrasomes in this study is twofold: first, our previous work confirmed that SJMHE1 exerts nerve repair effects through a macrophage-dependent mechanism, and macrophages, a kind of highly migratory cells, are proven to generate migrasomes; second, the "migration-dependent biogenesis" of migrasomes aligns with the dynamic cellular remodeling process of peripheral nerve regeneration (e.g., macrophage migration to injury sites, Schwann cell migration to form guidance tracks), making them more likely to participate in intercellular communication during nerve repair than statically released exosomes/microvesicles. Here, we observed that macrophages in the injured rat sciatic nerve release migrasomes at 7 days post-injury, and local SJMHE1 treatment significantly increased their number. Co-labeling for CD68 and S100 indicated that these migrasomes interacted with Schwann cells, suggesting a role in cell-to-cell communication. Although endogenous Schwann cell-derived migrasomes cannot be entirely excluded, our in vitro co-culture experiments confirmed that macrophages are the primary source of migrasomes, with minimal contribution from Schwann cells, consistent with our in vivo findings. Additionally, SJMHE1 also upregulated migrasome-specific markers (e.g., TSPAN4, a regulator of migrasome formation) in sciatic nerve tissue. Importantly, we further found that the effect of SJMHE1-treated macrophages in promoting nerve regeneration was attenuated following TSPAN4 gene knockdown, reinforcing migrasomes as key effectors of SJMHE1-mediated regeneration. It is well known that migrasome biogenesis is closely associated with both cell motility, thus, combined with our previous discoveries: (1) SJMHE1 treatment significantly enhances macrophage migration; (2) the biological functions of SJMHE1 rely on its binding to receptors on target cells, we reasonably speculate that SJMHE1 may regulate macrophage migrasome production through certain migration-related signaling pathways, which certainly requires further verification.

Directed collective migration of Schwann cells is fundamental to nerve repair and functional reconnection. Macrophages are known to guide Schwann cell migration via vascular polarization (e.g., through VEGF-A secretion), and migrasomes can act as signal effectors that regulate cell migration through spatial signal transmission. Here, our data reveal that SM-M exert potent signal-localizing effects, actively recruiting Schwann cells to migrate directionally. Moreover, SM-M are internalized by Schwann cells, promoting both proliferation and migration, which is consistent with the established role of Schwann cell dynamics as a critical target for PNI repair. Interestingly, M-M lacked these effects, contrasting with previous reports that macrophages-derived extracellular vesicles enhance Schwann cell function. This discrepancy likely reflects fundamental differences between migrasomes and traditional EVs in biogenesis. Notably, we found that CM-Dil-labelled SM-M can be dually internalised by RSC96 and PC12 cells (Supplementary Figure S5) in vitro, indicating that SM-M internalisation in the nerve microenvironment is non-selective. The potential direct combination of SM-M on PC12 cells suggests a possible "Schwann cell + neuronal cell" dual-target mechanism for SM-M-mediated nerve regeneration, which is a direction meriting future study.

Migrasomes are a type of membrane vesicle structure originating from the cell membrane, with phospholipid bilayers as their core component. This structure can fuse with the membrane of recipient cells, thereby delivering its carried contents into the recipient cells. As a fundamental biological process, membrane fusion is universally present in various organisms. Beyond membrane fusion, recipient cells can also take up migrasomes through multiple endocytic pathways, including clathrin-dependent endocytosis and clathrin-independent pathways (e.g., caveolin-mediated uptake, macropinocytosis, phagocytosis, and lipid raft-mediated internalization). Based on the aforementioned biological mechanisms, we hypothesize that Schwann cells may take up migrasomes through multiple modes. However, the specific uptake mechanism may depend on the proteins and glycoproteins of migrasomes and recipient cells, which requires further investigation in subsequent studies.

Our previous studies found that migrasomes are enriched in miRNAs. As a conserved non-coding RNA, miRNAs are known to participate in nerve injury repair. Therefore, in the present study, we focused on miRNAs in SM-M. Our miRNA sequencing analysis identified a distinct miRNA profile in SM-M, with miR-26b-5p as the most significantly upregulated candidate. Functional assays confirmed that SM-M deliver miR-26b-5p to Schwann cells, where it enhances proliferation and migration, establishing miR-26b-5p as a principal effector of SM-M function. This finding expands the known roles of miR-26b-5p, which has previously been linked to cartilage protection in osteoarthritis and neural recovery after spinal cord injury via extracellular vesicle-mediated delivery, but had not been implicated in PNI. Importantly, miR-26b-5p function is cell- and tissue-specific; while it promotes Schwann cell activity here, it can drive tumor progression in hematological and solid malignancies. This duality necessitates careful evaluation of SJMHE1 or miR-26b-5p-based therapies in PNI patients with concurrent malignancies to mitigate potential oncogenic risks.

To unravel the molecular mechanism underlying miR-26b-5p-mediated Schwann cell regulation, we combined bioinformatic predictions with dual-luciferase reporter assays to confirm PTEN as a direct target. PTEN, a classical tumor suppressor and negative regulator of the PI3K/AKT pathway, inhibits cell proliferation and migration by suppressing AKT phosphorylation. Downregulation of PTEN is known to enhance Schwann cell activity via PI3K/AKT activation, and PTEN has been termed a molecular "brake" on peripheral nerve regeneration. Our data align with these findings: SM-M-derived miR-26b-5p targets PTEN, reducing its expression and activating AKT to promote Schwann cell proliferation and migration. While the PTEN/AKT axis is a key mediator, miR-26b-5p may regulate additional targets in Schwann cells, warranting further investigation.

Despite these insights, our work has limitations. First, we only used a single dose of both SJMHE1 and SM-M in animal studies. Further research is therefore required to elucidate the dose-dependent responses, half-lives, optimal therapeutic frequencies, and administration routes of SJMHE1 and SM-M. This will facilitate the determination of the optimal dosage and administration schedule for SJMHE1 or SM-M when applied as clinical agents. Second, SM-M is a complex membrane-bound structure that may contain not only miR-26b-5p, but also potentially functional proteins and other non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), which may synergistically regulate Schwann cell function. Dissecting the contributions of these components and their interactions with miR-26b-5p is essential. Third, the dynamic processes of migrasomes in the injured neural microenvironment in vivo remain unclear, including the spatiotemporal patterns of their release from macrophages, the efficiency and specificity of their uptake by Schwann cells, and their ultimate clearance mechanisms. Characterizing these properties is a prerequisite for evaluating its clinical translation potential. Fourth, while SJMHE1 shows promise in crush injuries and short-gap defects, long-distance nerve defects (a major clinical challenge) may require combination strategies, such as integrating SJMHE1 with engineered scaffolds (e.g., hydrogels) to functionalize nerve guides, an approach needing further validation.
Conclusions

Our study uncovers a novel mechanism underlying SJMHE1-mediated peripheral nerve regeneration: SJMHE1 induces macrophages to secrete migrasomes, which serve as carriers to deliver miR-26b-5p to Schwann cells. This miR-26b-5p then targets and inhibits PTEN, thereby activating the AKT pathway to enhance Schwann cell proliferation and migration, the key processes for nerve repair (Fig. 8). Additionally, this work identifies "macrophage-derived migrasomes" as a previously unrecognized mediator of macrophage-Schwann cell crosstalk during peripheral nerve regeneration and highlights SJMHE1 as a promising therapeutic peptide for PNI.

Schematic diagram of the mechanism by which SJMHE1 mediates peripheral nerve regeneration through macrophage-derived migrasomes. Local injection of SJMHE1 can induce macrophages to polarize toward the M2 phenotype and promote them to generate migrasomes loaded with miR-26b-5p. After being taken up by Schwann cells, these migrasomes activate the AKT signaling pathway by targeting and inhibiting PTEN protein expression, thereby enhancing the proliferation and migration capacities of Schwann cells

passages.text: PPIF+ neutrophils promote mtROS driven NETosis mediated progression of colorectal cancer
Objective

To elucidate the mechanism through which tumor-associated neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) contribute to the progression of colorectal cancer (CRC), characterize cellular populations within the CRC tumor microenvironment (TME), and identify potential therapeutic targets.
Methods

We retrieved the single-cell RNA-seq datasets of CRC from GEO, and performed clustering analysis and subgroup analysis on the quality-controlled single-cell transcriptome data. Subsequently, we interrogated signaling pathways, biological functions, developmental trajectories, survival outcomes, gene regulatory networks, and cellular communication among distinct cell subgroups to delineate tumor heterogeneity during CRC progression.
Results

Our analyses reveal that the DACH1+ and NKD1+ CRC subgroups play vital roles in the initiation, progression, and metastasis of CRC. PPIF+ neutrophil subgroups promote NETs formation and CRC progression by facilitating mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) production. Meanwhile, the C1QC+ Mac, RACK1+ Tem, RACK1+ B, and RACK1+ Plasma subgroups exert certain immunosuppressive effects within CRC TME, thus promoting CRC progression. Moreover, RACK1 may serve as a key ecological niche gene in CRC. Furthermore, PPIF+ neutrophils modulate the TME via TNFSF14-TNFRSF14 and TNFSF14-LTBR checkpoint axes, thereby sustaining the CRC progression.
Conclusion

Our research findings have revealed the biological characteristics of CRC under the influence of NETs. Altogether, this study underlines the therapeutic potential value of targeting NETs-related mechanisms in the context of CRC.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12967-025-07267-8.
Introduction

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common malignant tumor and the second leading cause of cancer death, with an estimated 1.9 million new cases and 900,000 deaths globally in 2020. It is worth noting that the incidence of CRC is still rapidly increasing, and even worse, the prognosis for postoperative recurrence and metastasis in CRC patients remains poor, with a 5-year survival rate of only 10% for stage IV CRC patients. Therefore, researching the pathogenesis of CRC and urgently seeking new drug targets and treatment methods is crucial to improve the prognosis of CRC patients.

The tumor microenvironment (TME) is comprised of cancer cells and a diverse cohort of stromal cell populations, including infiltrating immune cells like lymphocytes and macrophages, neutrophils, fibroblasts, and adipocytes. It also incorporates the extracellular matrix (ECM) and an array of soluble factors and signaling molecules generated by these cells, forming an intricate cellular network. Various types of immune cells can impact the progression and metastasis of cancer cells, and Immunotherapy works by altering TME to inhibit tumor progression, but its efficacy may be influenced by TP53 status, as P53 not only regulates DNA repair but also modulates immune responses within the tumor microenvironment. In the realm of CRC immunotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors are a prevalent treatment modality. For instance, programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) plays a pivotal role in modulating T cell function and preserving immune system homeostasis, thus establishing itself as one of the most extensively researched regulatory agents. Additional immune checkpoints encompass cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4), T cell immunoglobulin 3 (Tim-3), and lymphocyte activation gene 3 (Lag3). These immunotherapy targets engender advantageous conditions for the immune-based management of CRC. Therefore, a deep understanding of stromal cells and immune cells can provide new insights for developing and utilizing novel therapeutic targets to control the progression of CRC.

It is worth noting that neutrophils account for 50-70% of circulating white blood cells in human peripheral blood. As short-lived cells, neutrophils play an indispensable role in both healthy and tumor tissues. During innate immune response, neutrophils can form sticky web-like structures known as NETs. NETs are network structures released by neutrophils and primarily composed of decondensed chromatin and granule proteins. However recent investigations have uncovered the widespread presence of NETs within the tumor microenvironment of CRC and shown that NETs play a pro-cancer role in CRC progression. They can promote tumor cell proliferation, invasion, and metastasis, providing tumor cells with a microenvironment conducive to growth and survival. Meanwhile, the activation of epithelial mesenchymal transition like processes in CRC cells by NETs may also contribute to the progression of CRC. Therefore, in-depth exploration of the specific mechanisms of action of NETs in CRC is of great significance for revealing the pathogenesis of CRC and identifying new therapeutic targets.

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is an innovative technology for profiling the transcriptome of individual cells. It empowers the examination of gene expression alterations at the single-cell level, providing novel insights into the interplay among diverse cell subgroups in tumor tissues. In this study, we obtained scRNA-seq data from public databases, re-identified and annotated cell populations, determined specific subgroups of malignant cells and immune cells involved in immune responses, constructed cell differentiation trajectories, and explored the complex mechanisms of cell-cell interactions. We focus on how tumor associated NETs play a role in the TME, which may become a potential therapeutic target for improving treatment strategies and clinical outcomes.
Materials and methods
Data collection

scRNA-Seq data related to CRC were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. This study included 5 datasets, namely GSE161277, GSE178318, GSE188711, GSE200997, and GSE201348. A total of 37 CRC samples, 32 adjacent cancer normal samples, and peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples from 4 CRC patients were included. The detailed clinical characteristics of the patients were obtained from the original text and are listed in Table S1. Additionally, transcriptome data related to CRC (TCGA-COAD) and corresponding clinical information were downloaded from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), encompassing 471 CRC samples and 41 adjacent noncancerous tissue samples for subsequent bulk analysis. Subsequently, data preprocessing was carried out and the Seurat package was used for data standardization. GEO and TCGA are both open-source databases, and the patients involved in the databases have obtained ethical approval.
Processing scRNA seq data

Integrate the downloaded and preprocessed sample data to generate a feature count and digital gene expression matrix for a single cell with default parameters, forming an expression profile for a single cell. Subsequently, the scRNA-Seq data were integrated and converted into Seurat objects. Further quality control processing was conducted for nFeature (total number of genes), nCount (total gene expression), and the proportion of mitochondrial genes. Cells with the highest and lowest 1% feature counts and mitochondrial gene proportions exceeding 10% were filtered out.
Dimensionality reduction, clustering, and differential expression analysis

Standardize the data using the SC Transform function, and then perform unsupervised clustering and differential gene expression analysis on the preprocessed data using the Seurat software package. And use the FindClusters function to obtain cell clusters. FindAllMarkers function results Subsequently, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) algorithm was utilized to visualize the single-cell landscape in low-dimensional space. Furthermore, the FindAllMarkers function in the Seurat package was employed to identify differentially expressed genes between specific cell clusters and other clusters, with FDR correction and a significance threshold of llog2FCl > 1. The results of the FindAllMarkers function are listed in Table S2. Based on the identified marker genes, as well as markers validated in previous single-cell studies and in the laboratory, different cell clusters were further categorized into known cell types.
Analysis of copy number variation in chromosomes

Copy number variation (CNVs) between individuals is a major source of genetic variation in cancer individuals. InferCNV is used to explore tumor single-cell RNA-Seq data (https://github.com/broadinstitute/infercnv) to determine whether somatic cells exhibit large-scale chromosomal CNVs. To verify whether epithelial cells and malignant cells are correctly distinguished, this study used the InferCNV method to estimate the chromosome copy number of epithelial cells and malignant cells and visualized the relative expression intensity of genes on each chromosome through a heatmap. This analysis selected hg19 as the reference genome.
Functional enrichment analysis

To explore the potential biological roles of identified cell subgroups in the CRC microenvironment, gene ontology biological process (GO BP) analysis and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis were performed using the clusterProfiler package in R language. Enrichment results with p < 0.05 were considered significant. Additionally, the AddModuleScore function in the Seurat package was used to calculate the scores of the interested pathways or gene sets in different cell subgroups, and the results were visualized as violin plots.
Gene set enrichment analysis

Using the clusterProfiler package, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed with the molecular signature database (MSigDB) c5.bp.v7.4.symbols.gmt and c2.cp.kegg.v7.4.symbols.gmt gene sets as the background set to explore the activation or inhibition of the interested gene sets.
Pseudotime analysis

To explore the differentiation trajectory of cell subgroups in CRC development, pseudotime analysis of the interested cell populations was performed using the Monocle3 method in this study. The developmental trajectories of cell subgroups were reconstructed, and the results were visualized using the UMAP algorithm.
Gene set variation analysis and survival analysis

Gene set variation analysis (GSVA) is a non-parametric unsupervised analysis method mainly used to evaluate gene set enrichment results from microarray and transcriptome data. In this study, the genes of interested cell subgroups were selected (LogFC > 1.5), and the GSVA scores of different cell subgroups in the TCGA-COAD clinical cohort were computed using the GSVA package. Divide the samples into high and low score groups based on the median score. Then, use the R software package to analyze the survival rate and surfminer, and conduct an analysis of overall survival rate (OS) and recurrence-free survival rate (RFS).
Gene regulatory network analysis

In this study, gene regulatory networks (GRN) were analyzed using the Python module tool pySCENIC. This workflow begins with a counting matrix that describes the abundance of all cell genes. Firstly, use the GRNBoost2 method to infer co expression modules. Subsequently, indirect targets were removed from these modules using cis regulatory motif discovery (cisTarget). Finally, enrichment scoring was performed on the target genes (AUCells) of regulatory factors to quantify their activity, and the regulatory factor specificity score (RSS) was calculated. The final result is visualized using the ComplexHeatmap software package.
Cell communication analysis

Receptor-ligand mediated cell-cell communication is crucial for coordinating various biological processes such as development, differentiation, and disease. In this study, cell communication analysis was conducted using the iTalk package (Doi: https://doi.org/10.1101/507871) to infer the interactions between different cell subgroups. iTalk treats cell populations as interacting objects, calculates the expression of receptors and ligands in each cell subgroup, and uses this as an indicator of interaction to study the cell communication relationships between subgroups.
Construction of protein-protein interaction (PPI) network

In order to elucidate the targets of PPIF+ neutrophils enriched in the tumor environment promoting CRC progression, the PPI network was used to obtain the protein interaction targets of the receptor-ligand gene list in cell-cell communication based on the STRING database (https://string-db.org/). Subsequently, Cytoscape was employed to visualize the PPI network.
Clinical sample

Fresh CRC and surrounding tissue specimens were obtained from patients who had undergone surgery for CRC at the Department of General Surgery at Zhujiang Hospital, Southern Medical University. Tumor samples were obtained from the central region of the tumor, while paired normal samples were collected from macroscopically normal tissue 8-10 cm away from the tumor margin. The Zhujiang Hospital's Protection of Human Subjects Committee approved the study, and all participants provided informed consent.
Cell lines

Human CRC cell lines, including SW480, LOVO,HCT-116 were purchased from Procell Company (Wuhan, China). The cell line tested negative for mycoplasma contamination. SW480,LOVO and HCT-116 cells were maintained in DMEM medium (C11995500BT, Gibco) supplemented with 1% penicillin-streptomycin (P/S, 15,140,122, Gibco), and 10% FBS (164210-50, Procell Company Wuhan, China) in the incubator with 5% CO2 at 37  C.
Western blotting

Cells and tissue were lysed in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (P1049, Beyotime). Protein concentration was measured using the BCA protein assay kit (P0010, Beyotime). Equal amounts of protein (10-20 mug) were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes (IPVH00010, Merck millipore). Membranes were blocked with 5% skimmed milk for 1 h and incubated overnight at 4  C with primary antibodies against DACH1, NKD1, APC, s-Mus, Wnt-1, Catenin-betaand CyclinD1 (1:2,000). After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP- conjugated secondary antibody (1:10,000, SA00001-1, Proteintech) for 1 h at room temperature. Bands were visualized using an ECL reagent (BL520B, Biosharp) and quantified with ImageJ software. Primary antibodies used for Western blotting were listed in Table S3.
Real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis

Total RNA was extracted using the FastPure Cell/Tissue Total RNA Isolation Kit V2 (Vazyme, RC112) following the manufacturer's instructions. cDNA was synthesized using the HiScript III RT SuperMix for qPCR (+gDNA wiper) (R323, Vazyme). qPCR was performed using the ChamQ Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Q711) on a QuantStudio6 Real-Time PCR system (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA). Each sample was run in three technical replicates. The mRNA expression levels of target genes were normalized to GAPDH and calculated using the DeltaDeltaCt method. The qPCR primers used are listed in Table S4.
Flow cytometry

Collecting blood samples from colorectal cancer patients to extract PBMC (Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells) and neutrophils. Fluorescently labeled antibodies specific for macrophages (CD68), Neutrophils(CD66B) were used to stain the cells. After washing and resuspending, Cells were then stained using fluorescently labeled S100A8,Cit-H3 and MPO antibodies. After washing and resuspending again,immune cell subsets were analyzed for their proportions and surface marker expression profiles using flow cytometry. The results were analyzed using a CytoFlow cell analyzer (Beckman). Primary antibodies used for Flow cytometry were listed in Table S3.
Immunofluorescence staining

Clinical samples were fixed for 24 hours, then dehydrated and embedded in paraffin. Sections were cut into 4 mum slices and baked at 60  C for 1 hour to ensure adhesion. Staining was performed using the Treble-Fluorescence Immunohistochemical Mouse/Rabbit Kit (pH 9.0) (Immunoway Biotechnology, Plano, TX, USA). Following the manufacturer's protocol, slides were dewaxed, subjected to antigen retrieval, and blocked. The primary antibody (diluted) was applied and incubated overnight at 4  C in a humidified chamber. After incubation, slides were warmed at 37  C for 30 minutes, followed by incubation with polymer and fluorescent secondary antibodies. For sequential staining, sections were fully immersed in antibody stripping buffer and microwaved for 15 minutes. After three PBS washes, a second primary antibody was applied, and the staining steps were repeated until all targets were labeled. Primary antibodies used for Immunofluorescence staining were listed in Table S3.
Neutrophil isolation

Neutrophils were isolated using Solarbio Peripheral Blood Neutrophil Separation Kit (P9040). Fresh anticoagulated whole blood (within 2 h of collection) was layered onto a pre-established density gradient (4 mL Reagent A + 2 mL Reagent C) and centrifuged at 1000 g for 30 minutes at room temperature. The granulocyte layer and approximately 1 mL of supernatant separation solution were aspirated, washed with 10 mL cell wash buffer (250 g, 10 min), and treated with red blood cell lysis buffer if erythrocyte contamination occurred. After repeating the wash step (250 g, 10 min), cells were resuspended for further use.
Co-immunoprecipitation (co-lP)

To analyze the endogenous binding of DACH1 and NKD1, HCT-116 cells cultured in 100 x 100 mm dishes were processed according to the rProtein A/G Magnetic IP/Co-IP Kit protocol (ACE Biotechnology, BK0004-01). Cells were lysed with 1000 muL ice-cold 1x Lysis/Wash Buffer (Enhanced) supplemented with protease inhibitor cocktail. Lysates were centrifuged at 13,000 x g for 10 min to collect the supernatant; 20 muL rProtein A/G MagPoly Beads were magnetically washed twice with 180 muL 1x Lysis/Wash Buffer (Enhanced) and then incubated with 5 mug of either anti-DACH1, anti-NKD1, or anti-IgG antibodies in 500 muL buffer at room temperature for 30 min. Subsequently, 500 muL of the HCT-116 cell lysate supernatant was added to the bead-antibody complexes and incubated for another 30 min at room temperature. After incubation, the complexes were washed twice with 500 muL buffer using a magnetic stand. The bound complexes were then eluted and denatured in 50 muL 1x SDS loading buffer by boiling at 100  C for 10 min. Finally, the eluates were analyzed by Western blot. Primary antibodies used for Co-Immunoprecipitation and Western blotting were listed in Table S3.
Data statistics and analysis

All the bioinformatics analyses and research endeavors encompassed in this study are conducted on a specialized bioinformatics cloud platform (http://www.bioinforcloud.com). All single-cell data analysis was performed using Seurat v4.0. When the p value is less than 0.05, it is deemed to possess remarkable statistical significance. All experiments were performed in triplicate and repeated at least three times independently. For comparisons across multiple groups, statistical significance was assessed using ordinary one-way ANOVA. Two-group comparisons were analyzed by two-tailed Student's t-test. Data are presented as mean +- SD, with significance denoted as follows: *p < 0.05, **p < 0.005, ***p < 0.0005, ns (not significant) All analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 9.0 (GraphPad Software, USA).

This study included the analysis of 37 CRC samples, 32 adjacent cancer normal samples and 4 PBMC samples from CRC patients, as shown in (Fig. 1A). After rigorous quality control processing, a total of 268,931 high-quality transcripts were obtained, clustered into 89 cell clusters. Based on known cell lineage marker genes, these cell clusters were further annotated into different cell types (Fig. 1B-C), including epithelial cells (EPCAM), endothelial cells (VWF), fibroblasts (COL1A2), macrophages (CD68), neutrophils (FCGR3B), T cells (CD3D, CD3E), B cells (CD79A), and plasma cells (XBP1) (Fig. 1D). Chromosomal heatmaps confirmed the presence of copy number alterations in the identified malignant CRC cells (Fig. 1E). Subsequently, to describe the differences between TME and normal control samples, we compared the cellular ecosystem composition in the three types of samples. Subsequently, to describe the differences between TME and normal control samples, we compared the composition of the cellular ecosystem. Compared with the control group, neutrophils were significantly enriched in CRC samples, and the infiltration of T cells, macrophages, and plasma cells was significantly increased in CRC samples, with the most significant increase in T cell infiltration. T cells dominated the cellular ecosystem in PBMC samples (Fig. 1F).

Neutrophil subgroup gene set score significantly correlated with CRC prognosis

The neutrophil population in TME exhibits heterogeneous phenotypes and functional diversity, playing a dual role in promoting or suppressing tumors. Through clustering analysis of 1,799 neutrophils, this study identified 5 neutrophil subgroups (Fig. 2A), with distinct expression of different markers (Fig. 2B). Compared to controls, the PPIF+ Neutrophil subgroup was specifically enriched in CRC, the same conclusion was supported by multiplex immunofluorescence results, while the RPS15A+ Neutrophil subgroup was specifically enriched in PBMC (Figs. 2C-D, S1A). To explore the biological roles of each neutrophil subgroup in the microenvironment, enrichment analysis of marker genes revealed that AKAP9+ neutrophil, DCAH1+ neutrophil, and NR3C2+ neutrophil subgroups exhibited similar expression patterns and enriched signaling pathways related to cell proliferation and angiogenesis (p < 0.05) (Figs. 2E-F). Additionally, PPIF+ Neutrophil and RPS15A+ Neutrophil subgroups also showed similar expression patterns, significantly enriching immune-related biological processes and chemotaxis-related KEGG pathways (p < 0.05) (Figs. 2E-F).

Due to the important role of NETs in promoting tumor progression and metastasis, and their involvement in causing autoimmune inflammation and bystander tissue damage, this study also investigated the expression of NETs scores in each subgroup. Remarkably, we found that the PPIF+ Neutrophil subgroup not only had the highest NETs score but also significantly activated the NETs gene set (Figs. 2G-H). Further research revealed that the specific marker of the PPIF+ Neutrophil subgroup, PPIF, encodes a major component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), and its overexpression may lead to inducing mPTP opening, resulting in increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS). The generation of mtROS and the opening of the mPTP both promote the induction of neutrophil extracellular traps formation (NETosis). Therefore, the high expression of PPIF in the PPIF+ Neutrophil subgroup may promote NETosis by inducing mtROS. Multiplex immunofluorescence analysis revealed significantly elevated expression of neutrophil extracellular trap (NET)-associated biomarkers, including citrullinated histone H3 (Cit-H3) and myeloperoxidase (MPO), in tumor tissues compared to normal controls (Fig. 2I). Meanwhile, we treated peripheral blood neutrophils from tumor patients with the PPIF inhibitor Cyclosporin A and subsequently assessed the proportion of Cit-H3+ and MPO+ neutrophils using flow cytometry. Results showed that PPIF inhibition significantly reduced NETs expression (Fig. 2J). Pseudotime analysis further reconstructed the differentiation trajectory of neutrophils, revealing the continuity of similar expression patterns among subgroups (Fig. 2K). In addition, GRN analysis identified the essential regulators and most specific regulators within each subgroup (Fig. 2L), with the PPIF+ Neutrophil subgroup primarily regulated by IRF9 (Fig. S1B). Survival analysis indicated that a higher gene set score of the PPIF+ Neutrophil subgroup was associated with poor prognosis in CRC (Fig. 2M), suggesting that this subgroup may promote tumor progression and deterioration.

In conclusion, by identifying neutrophil subgroups in the CRC microenvironment, we discovered a subgroup, PPIF+ Neutrophil subgroup with the potential to promote tumorigenesis. The high expression of PPIF in this subgroup may promote NETosis through mtROS, thereby facilitating tumor progression and metastasis. In addition, NETs may trigger pro-inflammatory effects through various pathways such as releasing inflammatory mediators and forming immune complexes, leading to autoimmune inflammation and bystander tissue damage, thereby promoting the progression of CRC.

In order to determine the subgroups of malignant cells in CRC, clustering was performed on the corresponding 27,948 cells in the dataset and 9 major CRC subgroups were identified (Fig. 3A). These CRC subgroups expressed specific markers (Fig. 3B), among which, CRC subgroups for SLC26A3+, DACH1+ NKD1+, and CXCL8+ occupied the main components of the CRC cell ecology (Fig. 3C). Subsequently, this study further analyzed the BP and pathways enriched in the CRC subgroups to reveal the expression patterns of specific genes among different subgroups. According to BP, CRC subgroups can be divided into two major categories, one significantly activating functions related to energy metabolism and substance transport, and the other significantly activating functions related to epithelial differentiation and histone modification (p < 0.05), suggesting that these subgroups may have a stronger invasive potential (Fig. 3D). In addition, we noted that the DACH1+ NKD1+ CRC subgroups significantly activated tumor proliferation and metastasis-related signaling pathways such as MAPK, ErbB, and Wnt (p < 0.05) (Fig. 3E), indicating that this subgroup may be more prone to metastasis. By calculating the tumor stemness score (Fig. 3F), the SYME2+ CRC subgroup had the highest tumor stemness score. Therefore, we determined it as the starting point for subgroup differentiation and reconstructed the differentiation trajectory of the CRC subgroup (Fig. 3G).

As key markers of the DACH1+ NKD1+ CRC subgroups, NKD1 was found to be a novel CRC-related gene and its binding to the Wnt signaling body and beta-catenin was found to be crucial. In addition, DACH1, as a transcription factor, has been confirmed to promote the growth and self-renewal characteristics of CRC cells. These previous findings underscore the possible close relationship between the expression of DACH1 and NKD1, which was also confirmed in this study. In the DACH1+ NKD1+ CRC subgroups, DACH1 and NKD1 were co-expressed and significantly positively correlated (Fig. 3H-I), and the gene set scores from this subgroup also demonstrated a correlation with poor survival in CRC, suggesting that DACH1 may promote the activation of the Wnt signaling pathway by regulating the expression of NKD1, thereby mediating the malignant progression of CRC (Fig. 3J). Multicolor immunofluorescence assays further confirmed the specific expression of DACH1 and NKD1 in tumor tissues (Fig. 3K). Next, the interaction of endogenous DACH1 and NKD1 in HCT-116 colorectal cancer cell lines was confirmed by Co-IP assay (Fig. 3L). To further investigate the relationship among DACH1, NKD1 and the Wnt signaling pathway, we performed Western blot and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analyses on clinical specimens. The experimental results were consistent with our bioinformatics predictions (Figs. 3M,3P, S2A). To investigate DACH1 and NKD1-mediated Wnt signaling pathway activation, we conducted gene perturbation experiments in SW480 and LOVO colorectal cancer cell lines. Following the knockdown and overexpression of DACH1 and NKD1 the expression of Wnt pathway-related molecules (APC, s-Mus, Wnt-1, Catenin-beta, CyclinD1) was evaluated. The results of qPCR and Western blotting analyses demonstrated a significant correlation between DACH1and NKD1 expression and the activation of the Wnt signaling pathway (Figs. 3N-O, 3Q-R, S2B-C). In addition, the CRC subgroups for IGKC+ and CXCL8+ were also associated with poorer OS in CRC (Figure S2D). Subsequently, we reconstructed the GRN of the CRC subgroups, clustering cell type-specific regulators into 3 major modules and predicting the essential regulators in each CRC subgroup (Figure S2E). By ranking the RSS, we further identified the most specific regulators for each subgroup (Figure S2F).

In conclusion, we identified CRC subgroups, identified the subgroups with higher malignancy, and provided specific regulators for regulating different CRC subgroups, which will provide new insights into strategies for inhibiting tumor metastasis and proliferation.

High density tumor associated macrophages play an important role in malignant progression. Through cluster analysis of macrophages, 9 different subgroups were identified, each expressing different specific markers (Figs. 4A-B). Compared with the control group, the CIQC+ Mac subgroup and AQP9+ Mac subgroup were specifically enriched in CRC, while the S100A8+ Mac subgroup was specifically enriched in PBMC (Fig. 4C). Notably, the C1QC+ Mac subgroup and the AQP9+ Mac subgroup are specifically enriched in CRC. Multiplex immunofluorescence results were consistent with the cellular ecological analysis (Fig. 4D-F). Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated a significant increase in the proportion of S100A8+ macrophages in the CRC patients compared to the normal controls (Fig. 4G). To explore the potential role of macrophage heterogeneity in regulating the tumor immune microenvironment, enrichment analysis of subgroup marker genes was performed. The enrichment analysis shows that the C1QC+ Mac subgroup is enriched in negative regulation of immune effector processes, cell chemotaxis, and biological functions of the ECM tissue, as well as chemokine signaling pathways, cell adhesion molecules, and NOD-like receptor signaling pathway (p < 0.05) (Fig. 4H-I). This study also explored the expression of M1 and M2 scores in each subgroup. Importantly, we found that the C1QC+ Mac subgroup had stronger M2 signal expression compared to M1 signal, and the angiogenic signal was also stronger (Fig. 4J), suggesting that this subgroup may be in a polarized state between M1 and M2, potentially promoting the growth and invasion of the tumor. Proposed pseudotime analysis indicates that the developmental trajectory of Mac evolves from the NOP53+ Mac subgroup as a starting point to other subgroups (Fig. 4K). Survival analysis confirms that lower abundance of the NOP53+ Mac subgroup and the RACK1+ Mac subgroup, and higher abundance of the IFI27+ CRC subgroup, are associated with worse OS and RFS in the TCGA clinical cohort of CRC patients (Fig. 4L). Furthermore, we also constructed a GRN for Mac and analyzed and identified the necessary and most specific regulators in each subgroup, including transcription factors (TFs), such as TCF7 and NR2F1 (Figure S3A).

In summary, we identified that the C1QC+ Mac subgroup is enriched in negative regulation of immune effector processes, cell chemotaxis, and biological functions of the ECM tissue, as well as chemokine signaling pathways, cell adhesion molecules, and NOD-like receptor signaling pathway (p < 0.05), which may weaken the host immune response, affect the migration and invasion capabilities of tumor cells. It is worth noting that it exhibits M2 polarization, and through M2 polarization of the C1QC+ Mac subgroup, it may secrete multiple growth factors and cytokines to promote the growth of tumor cells, thereby promoting the progression of CRC.

In order to identify the functional states of different T cell subgroups, we conducted a deep analysis of T cells using unsupervised clustering based on UMAP, which identified 10 T cell subgroups (Fig. 5A). To assess the functional states of different T cell subtypes, specific markers were identified for 6 subgroups: CD8+ T cells, natural killer T cells (NKT), central memory T cells (Tcm), effector memory T cells (Tem), T helper 17 cells (Th17), regulatory T cells (Treg), and naive T cells (Fig. 5B), each with distinct expression of specific markers (Fig. 5C). Notably, the RACK1+ Tem RACK1+ Tcm and JUND+ Treg subgroups showed a significantly higher specific enrichment in CRC compared to other subgroups (Fig. 5D). Multiplex immunofluorescence staining of clinical samples from colorectal cancer patients also confirmed the RACK1+ Tem cells were significant enrichment in tumor tissues (Figs. 5E-F). This subgroup may be closely related to the occurrence, development, or prognosis of CRC. Enrichment analysis showed that the RACK1+ Tem and Tcm subgroups not only enriched biological functions such as protein targeting, cell trend, and T cell activation, but also enriched oxidative phosphorylation signaling pathways (p < 0.05) (Figs. 5G-H), suggesting that the RACK1+ Tem and Tcm subgroups may interact with immune cells and exert immune efficacy, but their participation in oxidative phosphorylation, thereby affecting the metabolism and function of subgroups themselves, leading to weakened immune killing function. To better understand the dynamic transformation of T cells in the biological timeline, a pseudotime analysis was performed to reconstruct the differentiation trajectory of T cell subgroups, revealing that the ZBTB20+ Naive subgroup serves as the starting point for the differentiation of other subgroups (Fig. 5I). In addition, GRN analysis showed that these cell subgroups are divided into four modules regulated by transcription factors such as NKX3-1, MTA3, and IRF9 (Figs. 5J-K).

These results indicate that the infiltration of RACK1+ Tem and Tcm subgroups in CRC is increased, and both significantly activate the oxidative phosphorylation pathway (p < 0.05), indicating that this subgroup undergoes impaired metabolism and function, and immune function is suppressed, leading to immune escape.

For a long time, B cells that secrete antibodies have been considered to be the core element of intestinal homeostasis, and plasma cells and B lymphocyte differentiation maintain antibody production. However, tumor-associated B cells in CRC have not been well characterized. Therefore, we conducted a joint study on B cells and plasma cells, identifying 10 B subgroups and 7 plasma subgroups, respectively. Specifically expressing MS4A1, CD22, and CD19 were identified as B cells, while those specifically expressing TNFRSF17, CD38, JCHAIN, and SDC1 were identified as plasma cells (Figs. 6A-B). Each subgroup specifically expressed different biomarkers. Among them, CELF2+ positive and IGHG2+ positive were highly expressed in the B cell subgroup and plasma cell subgroup, respectively (Figs. 6C-D).

It is worth noting that the RACK1+ B subgroup and RACK1+ Plasma subgroup are specifically enriched in CRC (Fig. 6E). Multiplex immunofluorescence results showed higher RACK1 expression in B cells and plasma cells within tumor tissues compared to the normal controls (Figs. 6F-G, S4A-B). Enrichment analysis showed that the RACK1+ B subgroup was enriched in pathways such as protein processing and focal adhesion in the endoplasmic reticulum (p < 0.05) (Fig. 6H). The RACK1+ Plasma subgroup is rich in the RIG-I-like receptor signaling pathway (p < 0.05) (Fig. 6I). The pseudotime analysis shows that the developmental trajectory of B cells evolves from the CELF2+ B subgroup as a starting point to other subgroups, and the plasma's trajectory evolves from the ARID1B+ Plasma subgroup as a starting point to other subgroups (Figs. 6J-K). We reconstructed the gene regulatory network of B cell and plasma cell subgroups, these cell subgroups are divided into two modules, regulated by transcription factors such as TGIF1 and FOXO1, and specific scores of the regulatory elements corresponding to the subgroups were calculated and ranked (Figures S4C-D).

In summary, we identified the B subgroup and Plasma subgroup, finding that they both exhibit specific high expression of RACK1+ in the subgroup and may promote the progression and metastasis of tumors by affecting signaling pathways and immune response processes.
