passages.text: Several genes expressed by DPSCs were found to be involved in the metabolism and response to acetylcholine (supplementary Fig. 2A). To further interrogate whether DPSCs express cholinergic components, targeted qPCR was employed. DPSCs were found to express, gene transcripts for the CHRNA4 (alpha4), CHRNA7 (alpha7), CHRNA9 (alpha9), CHRNB1 (beta1), CHRNB2 (beta2), and CHRNE (epsilon) nicotinic receptor subunits, gene transcripts for CHRM2 (m2AChR), CHRM3 (m3AChR), and CHRM5 (m5AChR) and gene transcripts for acetylcholinesterase (ACHE) (supplementary Fig. 2B - 2D).

To confirm whether expression of gene transcripts for the m2AChR, m3AChR and m5AChR translated to expression of the relevant proteins, immunocytochemistry was performed. Positive immunostaining for the m2AChR, m3AChR and m5AChR was detected in DPSCs (Fig. 1B).

Dental pulp stem cells express a functional muscarinic type 2 receptor and activation induces a reversible inhibition of cell proliferation

To determine if DPSCs expressed a functional m2AChR, proliferation was assessed following treatment with pharmacological agonists and antagonists. DPSCs proliferation was inhibited in the presence of the m2AChR agonists, McN-A 343 (McN), significantly at 50 and 100 microM (Fig. 2A), and Arecaidine propargyl ester hydrobromide (APE), significantly at 100 microM (Fig. 2B; dose-response and recovery data shown in Supplementary Fig. 3B).

To confirm that the effect on DPSCs proliferation was subtype specific, and since McN is reported to have off-target effects on the m1AChR in humans, experiments with McN and APE were repeated in the presence and absence of Pirenzepine (PZ; a selective m1AChR antagonist) and/or Methoctramine (MC, a selective m2AChR antagonist). Neither PZ or MC alone had any effect on DPSC proliferation (supplementary Fig. 3A). Interestingly, MC, but not PZ, abolished the McN (Fig. 2C) and APE (Fig. 2D) induced inhibition of proliferation.

To determine whether activation of the m2AChR led to irreversible changes in DPSCs proliferation capacity, recovery experiments were performed. DPSCs treated with 100 microM APE exhibited significantly inhibited proliferation after 72 h of treatment (P < 0.001). However, withdrawal of APE after 72 h of treatment resulted in a resumption of proliferation over the next 72 h suggesting that the inhibitory effect of APE was reversible (Fig. 2E). To confirm that, in line with the reported literature, 100 microM APE was the optimal concentration, dose-response inhibition and recovery experiments were performed using concentrations ranging from 0 to 500 microM. The data suggested that concentrations of APE >= 250 microM caused irreversible changes in cell proliferation suggestive of cellular toxicity (supplementary Fig. 3B) and therefore 100 microM APE was used throughout the remainder of this study, in line with previous studies. Furthermore, CCK-8 analysis, which measures dehydrogenase levels inside viable cells, showed that DPSCs incubated in 100 microM APE are still viable over the experimental time course, compared to cells deprived of serum. However, there were significantly less cells compared to the control (P < 0.0001) indicative of inhibited proliferation (Fig. 2F). Furthermore, an LDH assay and Annexin V/PI staining also confirmed that APE had no cytotoxic effects on DPSCs, including the initiation of apoptosis (supplementary Fig. 4).

Activation of the dental pulp stem cell muscarinic type 2 receptor arrests cell cycle progression but has no impact on their stemness

The evidence suggests that activation of the m2AChR causes reversible inhibition of proliferation without affecting DPSCs viability. This suggested that the m2AChR may modulate cell cycle progression. Cell cycle analysis was performed by BrdU and PI staining. Figure 3A shows a significant reduction of cells in both the G1 ( P < 0.0001) and S (P < 0.01) phase, and accumulation of cells in the G2/M phase (P < 0.0001), after incubation with 100 microM APE. Furthermore, Fig. 3B shows that activation of the m2AChR with 100 microM APE caused a significant downregulation in expression of transcripts encoding cyclin-A2 (CCNA2, P < 0.0001), cyclin-B1 (CCNB1, P < 0.01) and cyclin-B2 (CCNB2, P < 0.01). In contrast, m2AChR activation caused upregulation of cyclin-D1 (CCND1, < 0.001), cyclin-D2 (CCND2, P < 0.0001), cyclin-E2 (CCNE2,  P < 0.0001), cell division cycle 14 A (CDC14A, P < 0.0001), cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 1 A (P21) (CDKN1A, P < 0.0001) and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA, P < 0.0001). However, no difference in expression of cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2 A (P16) (CDKN2A, ns) was observed.

DPSCs are positive for mesenchymal stem cell stemness markers including CD90, CD105, and CD73. However they do not express CD45 along with several other hematopoietic stem cell markers. Furthermore, DPSCs also express markers of pluripotency such as Sox2, Nanog, and Oct4. To confirm that activation of the m2AChR did not induce spontaneous differentiation, or affect stemness, expression of these key genes was investigated after 72 h exposure to 100 microM APE. The results demonstrate that APE had no effect on DPSCs expression of CD90 (THY1), CD105 (ENG), CD73 (NT5E), Sox2, Nanog and Oct4 and confirmed that they do not express CD45 (PTPRC) (supplementary Fig. 5i - vii). These data suggest that activation of the m2AChR with a selective agonist modulates cell cycle progression and places DPSCs in a quiescent state without affecting their stemness or pluripotency.

Activation of the dental pulp stem cell muscarinic type 2 receptor inhibits their migration and osteogenic differentiation capabilities

To evaluate the effect of m2AChR activation on DPSCs migration, a wound healing assay was performed. Figure 4A shows that activation of the DPSC m2AChR with 100 microM APE significantly inhibits cell migration (P < 0.0001), and this inhibition of migration could be attenuated by pretreatment with the selective m2AChR 0.1 microM of the antagonist MC.

To evaluate the effect of m2AChR activation on DPSCs osteogenic differentiation, DPSCs were incubated for 4 weeks in osteo-inductive medium (OS) with and without 100 microM APE added at various stages during the osteogenic differentiation process. Figure 4B shows that in the presence of OS alone after 4 weeks the cells formed mineralised nodules as confirmed by Alizarin Red and Von Kossa staining. In contrast the formation of mineralised nodules was clearly inhibited in the presence of 100 microM APE. In addition, Alizarin Red stain quantification revealed that addition of 100 microM APE at the start of differentiation and after 7, 14 and 21 days significantly inhibited mineralisation. Furthermore, analysis of expression of key genes involved in the osteogenic differentiation process showed that addition of 100 microM APE inhibited the OS media induced expression of alkaline phosphatase (ALP, P < 0.0001), bone morphogenic protein 2 (BMP2, P < 0.001), alpha-1 type I collagen (COL1A1, P < 0.0001) and secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1, P < 0.05). In contrast, although there was a small decrease in expression of RUNX2, this was not statistically significant (supplementary Fig. 5, viii - xii).

Activation of the dental pulp stem cell muscarinic type 2 receptor results in differentially expressed genes

Whole transcriptomic sequencing was performed to holistically investigate the effect of activation of the DPSCs m2AChR. All sequenced samples passed the quality control criteria and exhibited > 96% mapping to the reference genome (Human Genome) (data not shown). Multivariate analysis using principal component analysis (PCA) showed that the duration of stimulation caused the highest variance in clustering by 52% (x-axis), followed by 11% due to the nature of the stimulation (supplementary Fig. 6A).

Analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) revealed that after 4 h 117 genes were significantly upregulated and 329 significantly downregulated (Fig. 5A). After 24 h stimulation, 205 genes were significantly upregulated and 474 significantly were downregulated (Fig. 5B). Heatmap analysis of normalised log2 fold change in gene expression was utilised to determine the top 50 DEGs (ranked by padj value) at 4 h (Fig. 5C) and 24 h (Fig. 5D). APE treatment resulted predominantly in downregulated gene expression at 4 h, whereas 24 h treatment showed a shift toward upregulation.

KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of DEGs revealed that after 4 h incubation with 100 microM APE there was only 1 significantly upregulated KEGG pathway, a metabolic pathway involved in the production and degradation of alanine, aspartate, and glutamate. After 24 h incubation with 100 microM APE there were 6 significantly downregulated KEGG pathways involved in cell metabolism, adhesion, and migration. Moreover, after 24 h incubation with 100 microM APE there were 3 significantly upregulated KEGG pathways involved in cellular metabolism and hormone production (Fig. 6A and supplementary Fig. 6B).

Protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis was performed based on the STRING database (v11.5), and a PPI network visualization was created with Cytoscape (v3.10.0). The PPI network of significant DEGs consists of 27 proteins after 4 h m2AChR activation and 184 proteins after 24 h. The proteins at 4 h activation produced 16 pairs of PPIs, while the proteins at 24 h activation produced 269 pairs of PPIs (Fig. 6B).

The PPIs at 4 h activation did not produce enough interactions to generate a meaningful network (data not shown). The main network of PPIs generated from the 24 h m2AChR activation data revealed most interactions were between genes involved in the cell cycle, DNA replication, cell migration and MAPK signalling cascades (Fig. 6C).

Muscarinic type 2 receptor signalling in dental pulp stem cells engages the MAPK/ERK pathway

The RNAseq data indicated activation of the m2AChR led to upregulation of genes associated with the MAPK/ERK pathway (Fig. 6C). Therefore, subsequent experiments were conducted to determine whether m2AChR activation in DPSCs initiates the MAPK/ERK signalling cascade.

Targeted qPCR confirmed that expression of key genes involved in MAPK/ERK signalling, including ERK1 (MAPK3), ERK2 (MAPK1) and Proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), were significantly upregulated (P < 0.01, P < 0.05 and P < 0.0001, respectively) in DPSCs in response to m2AChR activation. Furthermore, an in-cell ELISA confirmed that m2AChR activation caused a transient significant increase in intracellular levels of Phosphorylated ERK1/2 up to 30 min after activation with peak levels being observed after 15 min (P < 0.0001, compared to 0 min). Collectively, the data suggests that m2AChR signalling in DPSCs is mediated by the MAPK/ERK pathway Fig. 7.

Discussion

This study provides the first comprehensive characterisation of the cholinoceptive properties of human DPSCs and supports a model in which m2AChR activation is associated with a reversible quiescent-like state without compromising viability or pluripotency. While DPSCs have been extensively studied for their regenerative and neurogenic potential, their cholinergic signalling pathways have remained unexplored. Here, the expression of muscarinic receptors (mAChRs) and multiple nicotinic receptor (nAChR) subunits was confirmed, and for the first time, the presence of a functional muscarinic type 2 receptor (m2AChR) was demonstrated in DPSCs. Pharmacological activation of this receptor induced a reversible cell cycle arrest, accompanied by suppression of cell migration and osteogenic differentiation, without affecting stemness or viability. These findings suggest that cholinergic pathways, specifically m2AChR signalling, may play a regulatory role in modulating DPSC behaviour and maintaining quiescence.

Previous studies in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), with which DPSCs share phenotypic and functional similarities, have suggested the presence of cholinergic signalling components, including AChRs, and implicated cholinergic signalling in the regulation of proliferation and differentiation. In this study, DPSCs were found to express cholinoceptive genes but no transcripts of genes involved in acetylcholine biosynthesis or transport (e.g., ChAT, CrAT, VAChT), indicating that they are not intrinsically cholinergic. However, expression of multiple nAChR subunits, including those that may form functional alpha7 and alpha4beta2 receptors, were detected, consistent with findings in other MSC populations. In addition, expression of the m2, m3, and m5 muscarinic receptors were confirmed at both transcript and protein levels, implicating DPSCs as non-neuronal responders to cholinergic stimuli.

Pharmacological interrogation revealed that m2AChR activation using Arecaidine propargyl ester hydrobromide (APE) significantly inhibited DPSC proliferation. This effect was reversible and not associated with cytotoxicity, apoptosis, or loss of mesenchymal or pluripotency markers, suggesting that the cells were placed into a reversible, non-senescent quiescent state. These observations are consistent with prior studies reporting similar m2AChR-mediated inhibitory effects in other stem cell populations, including rat adipose-derived MSCs and human glioblastoma stem cells. However, this is the first report to show that phenotypically defined DPSCs express a functional m2AChR and that activation of this receptor is associated with a reversible quiescent-like state.

passages.text: Flow cytometric analysis and gene expression profiling confirmed arrest at the G2/M phase. This was associated with downregulation of mitotic cyclin genes (CCNA2, CCNB1 and CCNB2) and upregulation of G1-associated cyclin genes (CCND1, CCND2 and CCNE2), PCNA, and the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A (P21), without a change in CDKN2A (P16). The upregulation of P21, a canonical marker of quiescence, alongside unchanged P16 levels, supports the interpretation that the arrest is reversible and not associated with permanent senescence. Increased PCNA expression further supports the presence of a transient cell cycle block, rather than loss of replicative potential. Together, these findings suggest that m2AChR activation initiates a P21-driven checkpoint response, placing DPSCs into a reversible quiescent state.

Quiescence, defined as a reversible, non-proliferative state, is conserved across hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), neural stem cells (NSCs), and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), where it serves to protect stem cells from exhaustion and genotoxic damage. Beyond p21/p27 and canonical p53/Notch/TGF-beta/FOXO axes, recent work in human DPSCs has also shown that circadian clock genes (REV-ERBalpha) can regulate autophagy and inflammation, adding another mechanism by which the function of DPSCs is regulated.

In DPSCs, quiescence regulation is less well-characterized. However, our data provide functional evidence suggesting that M2 receptor activation induces a transient and reversible proliferation arrest that is consistent with a quiescent state. Specifically, we observed significant upregulation of CDKN1A (p21), with no change in CDKN2A (p16), which supports a quiescent rather than senescent phenotype. This is consistent with mechanisms reported in MSCs and NSCs, where transient activation of the p53-p21 axis mediates quiescence in response to stress or external signals without triggering permanent arrest Furthermore, the recovery of proliferation following M2 agonist withdrawal, as demonstrated by MTT and CCK8-assays, aligns with the established characteristics of quiescent stem cells re-entering the cell cycle. This mirrors observations in HSC and NSC models, where removal of inhibitory signals leads to renewed proliferation.

Quiescence is an important mechanism for preserving stem cell integrity, especially under transient stress or in preparation for differentiation or mobilisation. In this context, the ability to modulate DPSC quiescence via external receptor activation is highly relevant. Importantly, this state was achieved without downregulation of key stemness markers (CD90, CD73 and CD105) or pluripotency-associated transcription factors (Oct4, Nanog and Sox2), confirming that m2AChR signalling did not induce spontaneous differentiation but maintained the undifferentiated phenotype (Supplementary Fig. 5, i-vii).

Functionally, activation of the m2AChR impaired both DPSC migration and their ability to undergo osteogenic differentiation. Inhibition of mineralised nodule formation was observed at all induction stages, suggesting that m2AChR activation not only prevents differentiation onset but may also interfere with cells already committed to the osteoblast lineage. Suppression of key osteogenic markers (ALP, BMP2, COL1A1 and SPP1) further supports this interpretation. The observed impairment in DPSC migration is in line with previous findings in mesenchymal stem cells, where cholinergic signalling modulated cell motility. However, the present data also demonstrate that m2AChR activation directly modulates osteogenic differentiation, as evidenced by phenotypic changes and downregulation of key osteogenic genes. In a broader tissue context, DPSC-endothelial interactions have been demonstrated to be mediated by FN1-ITGA5 and activation of PI3K/AKT signalling promotes endothelial proliferation, migration and tube formation, thereby supporting angiogenesis during pulp development. This process is further reinforced by PDGFRbeta+ DPSC subpopulations with strong pro-angiogenic activity through PI3K/AKT signalling. These microenvironmental programmes highlight the intrinsic capacity of DPSCs to contribute to vascularisation, providing a benchmark for in vivo behaviour against which receptor-level quiescence may be tuned.

To explore the underlying signalling mechanisms, transcriptomic analysis was performed at 4 and 24 h post-m2AChR activation. Early downregulation of genes involved in metabolism and proliferation was observed, followed by upregulation of stress response and survival pathways. KEGG pathway analysis revealed downregulation of adhesion- and migration-related pathways, many of which were driven by genes encoding cell adhesion molecules (e.g., CDH15, CNTN3, PCDHB10, and ROBO4). In contrast, upregulated pathways at 24 h included ferroptosis resistance and steroid biosynthesis, indicating a shift toward metabolic adaptation and survival.

Protein-protein interaction analysis revealed that many affected genes clustered around the cell cycle and MAPK signalling. Based on this, and previous reports implicating m2AChR-mediated activation of ERK1/2 in MSCs, the role of the MAPK/ERK pathway was investigated. Targeted qPCR and in-cell ELISA confirmed an early, transient upregulation and phosphorylation of ERK1/2 upon APE stimulation, peaking at 15 min and declining by 40 min. While ERK1/2 signalling is classically linked to proliferation, it can also mediate checkpoint restraint depending on activation strength and duration. Studies have shown that sustained ERK1/2 activity can upregulate CDK inhibitors, enforce G2/M arrest, or reactivate APC/C to promote exit into a G0-like state. In the present study, the combination of ERK1/2 phosphorylation, enrichment of MAPK-associated genes, and accumulation of DPSCs in G2/M is consistent with checkpoint-mediated quiescence downstream of m2AChR activation. However, further detailed investigations are required to fully delineate the role of the MAPK/ERK pathway in m2AChR signalling using specific pathway inhibitors to fully rule out the role of other signalling cascades such as PI3K/AKT, CXCR7/4, or NRG1/ErbB which may also contribute. In addition, the precise upstream mechanisms linking m2AChR activation to ERK1/2 phosphorylation need to be directly investigated. Previous reports indicate that m2AChRs can signal through Gi/o-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, through Gbetagamma subunit release, or via transactivation of receptor tyrosine kinases. In addition, cholinergic control in dental pulp extends beyond muscarinic receptors as evidenced by the fact that the alpha7nAChR has been shown to regulate autophagy and IL-1beta production in deciduous DPSCs, underscoring the need to investigate further the receptor-specific crosstalk between cholinergic pathways and stress-response programs.

A further limitation of this study is the absence of direct genetic validation of m2AChR function, such as siRNA knockdown or CRISPR-mediated knockout of CHRM2. While our conclusions are supported by selective pharmacological inhibition and downstream functional assays, future studies incorporating gene-specific loss-of-function models will be important to fully confirm the causal role of m2AChR signalling in DPSC quiescence and differentiation. Moreover, as all data were derived from in vitro 2D cultures, it remains uncertain how these findings translate to the native pulp tissue architecture or to complex in vivo microenvironments. Future studies employing 3D pulp-like models or animal systems will be essential to determine the physiological relevance of m2AChR-mediated quiescence and its therapeutic potential in regenerative endodontics.

Taken together, this study indicates that DPSCs possess a functional cholinoceptive system, and that m2AChR activation is associated with engagement of the MAPK/ERK pathway and a reversible quiescent-like state (Supplementary Fig. 7). While the primary findings contribute to fundamental DPSC biology, there are also translational implications worth noting. The ability to pharmacologically induce a reversible, non-toxic quiescent state may be valuable in settings such as in vitro cell banking, storage, or shipment, where maintaining stemness and viability is essential. Recent studies have further demonstrated that PDGFRbeta+ DPSC subsets remodel extracellular matrix and drive angiogenesis through integrin-mediated pathways, and that FN1-ITGA5-PI3K/AKT signalling facilitates DPSC-endothelial communication during pulp development. Placing reversible m2AChR-mediated quiescence within this broader framework of ECM-integrin regulation highlights how receptor-level control could complement microenvironmental programmes that preserve stemness while supporting vascularisation. Although the clinical application in regenerative endodontics remains speculative and limited by cost, complexity, and current standard-of-care options such as apexification or revascularisation, understanding how to modulate DPSC activity ex vivo could guide future scaffold design or therapeutic preparation protocols. Therefore, further investigation is warranted to assess how such regulatory strategies could integrate with evolving stem cell-based therapies.

passages.text: Deciphering context-specific Axitinib escape pathways via multi-omics and explainable machine learning
Background

Resistance remains a major barrier to targeted cancer therapies. Axitinib, a VEGF receptor inhibitor with anti-angiogenic activity, is effective in several cancers but shows heterogeneous patient responses, reflecting context-specific molecular adaptations. A comprehensive multi-omics approach is needed to define these mechanisms and uncover compensatory survival pathways limiting Axitinib efficacy.
Methodology

We conducted a high-throughput analysis of ~ 1000 pan-cancer cell lines treated with 44 FDA-approved targeted drugs. Basal transcriptomic (~ 36,000 transcripts) and proteomic (~ 9000 proteins) profiles were integrated to predict cell-line-specific drug response using a multi-classifier machine learning framework. Multiple models, including ensemble, linear, and kernel-based classifiers, were trained per drug and evaluated via fivefold cross-validation. Axitinib, the best-predictive drug, was further analyzed using explainable AI (LIME) to identify resistance-driving features for each cell line. Resistant cell lines were clustered using agglomerative hierarchical clustering based on LIME-identified features and highly correlated partners. Optimal clusters were determined via silhouette scoring. Enrichment analysis, pathway annotation, and literature mining were used to uncover cluster-specific resistance mechanisms.
Results

Axitinib achieved the highest predictive accuracy across all 44 drugs. The machine learning pipeline reliably classified cell lines as resistant or sensitive from basal transcriptomic and proteomic data. LIME identified key resistance-driving features at the individual cell line level. Clustering based on these features revealed two resistance subtypes shaped by tissue origin and survival constraints. In blood-derived cancers, resistance involves purine metabolism rewiring and alternative growth factor signaling to sustain proliferation. In solid tumors, resistance reflected adaptation to hypoxia, including ECM remodeling, mechanosensing, EMT, immune evasion, and senescence-induced paracrine signaling.
Conclusion

Axitinib resistance emerges through tissue- and context-specific adaptations. Multi-omics profiling with explainable machine learning reveals distinct survival strategies, underscoring the need for precision re-sensitization approaches tailored to tumor context.

Highlights

A new blueprint for understanding therapeutic failure. This study provides a scalable, multi-omics framework that decodes how different cancer types evolve unique solutions to the same drug, offering a new approach to anticipating and overcoming therapeutic resistance.

Resistance is driven by pre-existing expression, not target mutation. We found that resistance to Axitinib is primarily governed by pre-existing gene and protein expression patterns, rather than by mutations in the drug's direct targets (VEGF receptors).

Explainable AI reveals two divergent resistance strategies. Our machine learning model derived features uncovered that resistant cancers employ two distinct, lineage-specific strategies: solid tumors adapt by remodeling their microenvironment and evading immune attack, while blood cancers rewire their metabolism and use alternative growth factors to survive.

Background

Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide, posing a persistent challenge to global health. According to the World Health Organization (2024), around 20% of individuals are expected to develop cancer during their lifetime, with 1 in 9 men and 1 in 12 women dying from the disease. Although therapeutic modalities have progressed from conventional interventions such as surgery and chemotherapy to sophisticated approaches including immunotherapy and targeted therapies, sustained disease remission remains a significant challenge in numerous cases. Among these approaches, targeted therapies have brought a paradigm shift by aiming at specific molecular abnormalities that drive tumor growth and survival. These therapies, including monoclonal antibodies and small-molecule inhibitors, are designed to interfere with critical cellular processes such as proliferation, angiogenesis, metastasis, and immune evasion. Over the years, the repertoire of targeted therapies has expanded beyond kinase inhibitors and immunomodulators to include proteasome inhibitors, metabolic modulators, apoptosis inducers, and epigenetic modifiers. While these treatments have shown promise, their clinical success is frequently challenged by the emergence of resistance .Notably, resistance is not solely acquired over time; many tumors exhibit inherent or pre-existing resistance mechanisms that render therapies ineffective from the outset.

Intrinsic resistance, arising from the baseline molecular features of tumor cells, represents a significant barrier to the efficacy of targeted therapies. These mechanisms can involve pathway redundancy, mutations near the drug's target site, activation of compensatory signaling pathways, and alterations in cellular trafficking or metabolism. Tumor heterogeneity further adds to this complexity by enabling parallel resistance strategies within subpopulations of tumor cells. Some of these subclones may carry genetic alterations that inherently confer resistance, while others may promote genomic instability, leading to the emergence of mutations that support survival and proliferation despite treatment. Thus, a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms that confer resistance, especially those present prior to treatment, is essential for designing more durable and personalized therapeutic interventions.

Receptor Tyrosine Kinases (RTKs) are a well-established class of therapeutic targets in cancer, given their central roles in regulating cell proliferation, angiogenesis, differentiation, and migration. Dysregulation of RTK signaling is a hallmark of many cancers, driving malignant transformation and tumor progression. The RTK family comprises 58 members across 20 subfamilies, many of which are active during development and become aberrantly activated in tumors. Their pathological relevance has led to the development and FDA approval of multiple RTK inhibitors aimed at disrupting tumor-promoting signals. Axitinib is a highly potent RTK inhibitor that selectively targets VEGFR1, VEGFR2, and VEGFR3, with minimal off-target activity against other kinases such as KIT and PDGFR. Axitinib stands out as a potent VEGFR inhibitor with half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50) for VEGF family receptors that are ten times lower than those of other TKIs. It has also been shown to bind to the BCR-ABL fusion protein (albeit in a different conformation from VEGF binding), thereby selectively inhibiting the drug-resistant T315I mutant isoform. Despite these promising attributes and clinical benefits observed in select patient populations, resistance to Axitinib remains a significant challenge. Therefore, a deeper understanding of these mechanisms is essential for improving the efficacy of Axitinib and similar RTK-targeted therapies.

In this study, we have employed explainable AI algorithms in tandem with supervised machine learning classifiers on transcriptomic and proteomic data from cancer cell lines with known sensitivity or resistance to Axitinib. By identifying key molecular signatures and signaling pathways associated with resistance, our work uncovered various diverse and often pre-existing strategies that tumor cells deploy to evade targeted inhibition.
Methodology
Data sourcing and dataset preparation

Drug response data The drug response data comprising cell lines, the administered drugs, and the corresponding IC50 values, were obtained from the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) database. As of January 2023, the GDSC hosted IC50 values for 580 drugs across 1000 human cancer cell lines. The database consists of two versions, GDSC1 and GDSC2, with GDSC2 being the more recently ingested. We used all available drug response data from GDSC2. For drugs absent in GDSC2, we supplemented the data with corresponding entries from GDSC1. In cases where duplicate datasets for the same drug existed within GDSC2, we selected the version with the larger number of profiled cell lines to maximize statistical power and minimize sampling bias.

Each drug was subsequently categorized into two response classes: Sensitive and Resistant. For a given drug, cell lines with IC50 values exceeding the maximum concentration or dose administered were classified as Resistant, while those with IC50 values below the maximum dosage were classified as Sensitive. To enhance clinical relevance, the dataset was further filtered to retain only FDA-approved targeted therapies. Additionally, drugs with highly imbalanced class labels (i.e., where either the Sensitive or Resistant class accounted for less than 5% of total samples) were excluded as a quality control measure to ensure balanced representation and robust downstream modeling.

Omics datasets The pan-cancer cell lines were described using molecular features: transcriptomic and proteomic data, available in the Cell Model Passport. Proteomic profiles were obtained as protein intensity values from mass spectrometry and log2-transformed to minimize skewness. Similarly, RNA-seq data expressed as transcripts per million (TPM) were extracted and log2-transformed to normalize distributions across cell lines, improving feature comparability. Further, the mutation data of the pan-cancer cell lines were also taken from Cell Model Passports.
Automated feature engineering and model training

An automated feature engineering and machine learning pipeline was developed to identify the targeted drugs whose response profiles (resistance or sensitivity) could be accurately predicted using supervised classifiers, as described below:

Feature reduction  The biological datasets, comprising transcriptomic and proteomic features, were inherently high-dimensional. Dimensionality reduction was therefore a crucial step to reduce noise while retaining interpretability. We applied Boruta, a wrapper-based technique built on the random forest classifier. Boruta demonstrated strong performance in identifying features most relevant in distinguishing resistant and sensitive cell lines, thereby achieving substantial dimensionality reduction while maintaining high predictive accuracy and contributing in optimizing model performance.

Model training  Following dimensionality reduction, several supervised machine learning classifiers, including Logistic Regression, Linear Support Vector Classifier, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors, XG Boost, Gaussian Naive Bayes, and Multi-layer Perceptron, were applied to each drug-specific transcriptomics and proteomics dataset. To ensure balanced label representation and mitigate overfitting, stratified fivefold cross-validation was employed. Model performance was evaluated using multiple metrics: Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC), precision, recall, accuracy, and F1 score. The average performance across these metrics was used to identify drugs for which resistance could be most reliably predicted.
Explainability of machine learning predictions

To interpret the model predictions and identify the key molecular drivers of resistance, the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) algorithm was implemented. LIME provides instance-specific explanations by estimating the influence of each feature on a model's prediction, indicating whether a feature supports resistance or sensitivity in a binary classification context. As an instance-based explainer, LIME generates perturbed samples around each data point and fits a sparse linear model to the corresponding predicted responses. This enables interpretation of model decisions by approximating local decision boundaries using interpretable, linear surrogates. LIME explanations were applied to the best-performing classifier for both the transcriptomic and proteomic datasets, where the classifier was trained and evaluated using five-fold stratified cross-validation to ensure robustness and generalizability. For each of the five folds, the LimeTabularExplainer was initialized independently and applied to all instances (i.e., cell lines) using the training data for a specific drug. For each instance, LIME identified the top ten features, transcripts and proteins that most significantly contributed to the classification decision (sensitive or resistant) in transcriptome and proteome dataset respectively. To ensure a comprehensive view of feature relevance, LIME explanations were generated for both the training and test datasets.

To focus the interpretation specifically on resistance-associated features, only the genes identified in resistant cell lines were pooled across all folds and used for subsequent analysis. This step was essential to ensure that the LIME results reflect molecular signatures driving resistance, thereby providing biologically meaningful insights into the resistant phenotype.
Correlation-based feature augmentation to capture biologically relevant signals

Feature selection, applied prior to model training, eliminates covarying features to improve model performance and interpretability. However, transcripts or proteins involved in the same biological process or pathway often exhibit coordinated changes in expression to propagate signals to downstream effectors. In light of this, and to enhance biological interpretation, the LIME-derived gene sets were expanded by including transcripts and proteins from the original datasets that showed strong expression correlation (absolute Pearson correlation coefficient >l0.8l) with the LIME-identified features.

To ensure the biological relevance of these correlated features in determining resistance, a Levene's test was applied to compare expression variance between Sensitive and Resistant cell lines. Only those correlated features that demonstrated a statistically significant difference (p value < 0.05) between the two groups were retained. These selected correlated transcripts or proteins, together with the original LIME-derived features, constituted the final feature set used for downstream analyses.
Feature-driven stratification of resistant cell lines

LIME-based interpretability analyses resulted in a heterogeneous set of contributing features from different cell types for classification into the resistant phenotype. This observation hints at the existence of multiple strategies to deploy resistance against Axitinib. Therefore, clustering was performed to stratify the cell lines based on the derived resistant features. Agglomerative hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance and average linkage was applied to all resistant cell lines, utilizing the final set of resistance-contributing features. The optimal number of resistant clusters in both transcriptome and proteome datasets was determined using the silhouette index.
Elucidating the different mechanisms of resistance

Following clustering of the resistant cell lines based on the final contributing feature sets of transcripts and proteins, two distinct groups were obtained. Downstream analyses focused on resistant cell lines common to the clusters derived from both the transcriptomics and proteomics datasets. To identify features (transcripts and proteins) with consistent expression within each cluster, a non-parametric Levene's test was performed to detect features with minimal variability in expression, despite differences in tissue origin, suggesting their critical role in promoting resistance. Simultaneously, a non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test was conducted to assess differences in mean expression levels, identifying features that were significantly upregulated in specific clusters and thus likely contributing to resistance within that group. Transcripts and proteins that showed both low variance and high mean expression within a cluster were prioritized.

Resistance-associated features demonstrating both stability (low variance) and elevated expression (high mean) were subsequently submitted to KEGG Mapper for pathway enrichment analysis. In addition, features that did not exhibit significant differences in mean or variance between clusters were also analyzed using KEGG, as they may contribute equally to both clusters. Pathways uniquely enriched within individual clusters were identified, along with those that were commonly enriched across both clusters.

To determine whether resistance to Axitinib arises from impaired drug binding to VEGF receptors or from ineffective VEGF ligand-receptor interactions that could disrupt angiogenesis, the mutation profiles of key VEGF ligands (VEGFA, VEGFB, VEGFC, VEGFD) and receptors (FLT1, KDR, FLT4) were retrieved from Cell Model Passports and further systematically evaluated. The variants were categorized based on their predicted functional consequences: essential splice site, frameshift, nonsense, and splice-region variants were considered likely loss-of-function; intronic, upstream, and downstream variants were classified as likely neutral, though regulatory potential was considered. Missense and in-frame insertion/deletion mutations were categorized as of uncertain functional impact. Special emphasis was placed on KDR missense mutations, which were mapped to amino acid positions and annotated with reference to UniProt functional domains to assess potential effects on Axitinib binding and resistance. Comparative mutation frequencies were calculated for resistant versus sensitive cell lines to determine whether specific mutations were enriched in resistance.

Results
Overview of the dataset

ML Performance Across 44 FDA Drugs Identifies Axitinib as Best Predicted by Multi-Omics A Number of Resistant and Sensitive cell lines for all the 44 FDA-approved. B Number of classifiers per drug with an average ML metric score >0.7 in transcriptomic and proteomic datasets. Circle size represents the number of classifiers meeting this threshold. C Chemical Structure of Axitinib - the drug that performed the best on both the transcriptomics and proteomics datasets. D Performance metrices of all the ten classifiers for Axitinib on the transcriptomics and proteomics data. E ROC curves for the best classifier in transcriptomic - Gradient Boosting evaluated via five-fold cross-validation, and ROC curves for the best classifier in proteomic - XG Boost evaluated via five-fold cross-validation.

After filtering the GDSC database to include only FDA-approved drugs, a total of 44 drugs were retained, 11 from GDSC1 and the remaining from GDSC2. The number of associated cell lines varied by drug, ranging from 225 for Tretinoin to 968 for Palbociclib (Fig. 2A).

For each drug, the transcriptomic dataset comprised cell lines as instances, with 36,000 genes represented as features based on their expression levels. All cell lines were labeled as either resistant or sensitive. Similarly, the corresponding proteomics dataset included 8498 proteins, with protein intensity values serving as features for each resistant and sensitive cell line.

To ensure balanced representation for downstream analyses, nine drugs with highly imbalanced sample distributions (i.e., with resistant or sensitive labels representing less than 5% of total samples) were excluded. These drugs include Fulvestrant, Vismodegib, Rucaparib, Tretinoin, Ruxolitinib, Tivozanib, Imatinib, Gefitinib, and Alectinib. Specific details corresponding to each drug comprising the dataset is provided in Supplementary Sheet 1.
Feature engineering and model implementation automation

Boruta is known to be well-suited for high-dimensional omics data, where correlated variables and noise can otherwise inflate importance scores, and hence became the method of choice. As expected, it demonstrated superior performance by significantly reducing data dimensionality while preserving both predictive accuracy and feature interpretability. For instance, in the Axitinib transcriptomics dataset, 954 cell lines with ~ 36,000 transcripts were analyzed, resulting in a 99.62% reduction in feature dimensionality using the Boruta algorithm. Of these, 625 cell lines were classified as resistant and 329 as sensitive. A similar trend was observed in the Axitinib proteomics dataset, which included 937 cell lines described by ~ 9000 proteins and underwent a 98.68% reduction in features. Here, 617 cell lines exhibited resistance, while 320 were sensitive. The prevalence of resistant samples in both datasets is a notable pattern that influences classification performance metrics.

A total of ten machine learning classifiers were implemented on the omics datasets: Logistic Regression, Linear Support Vector Classifier, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors, XGBoost, Gaussian Naive Bayes, and Multi-layer Perceptron Classifier. Among these, XGBoost and Gradient Boosting consistently outperformed others across multiple evaluation metrics. Detailed results for all 35 drugs, evaluated using these classifiers on the transcriptomic and proteomic datasets, are provided in the Supplementary Sheet 2 and 3, respectively.

The average metric score, computed across Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), AUC-ROC, precision (resistance and sensitivity), recall (resistance and sensitivity), accuracy, and F1 score, was used to assess classifier performance. In the transcriptomic dataset, 23 drugs had at least one classifier with an average metric score above 0.7. Notably, Axitinib, Bosutinib, Crizotinib, Niraparib, Sorafenib, and Venetoclax surpassed this threshold with 9 out of 10 classifiers (Fig. 2B). In the proteomic dataset, 17 drugs achieved this benchmark. Specifically, Axitinib, Crizotinib, Sorafenib, and Venetoclax again stood out, each achieving high scores with 9 out of 10 classifiers (Fig. 2B). Notably, when only 2-3 classifiers show strong performance for a given feature set, it may indicate overfitting and raise concerns about generalizability. In contrast, in our analysis, the consistent high performance across 9 classifiers suggests the robustness and generalizability of the selected features and feature engineering approach.

We chose Axitinib (Fig. 2C) to demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework in elucidating the resistance mechanisms that make cell lines unresponsive to Axitinib. All ML metric scores across five fold cross-validation for Axitinib on transcriptome and proteome datasets are shown in Fig. 2D.

The inherent label imbalance in both transcriptomic and proteomic datasets was reflected in the precision scores. For the transcriptomic dataset, Precision (Resistance) reached 0.85 and Precision (Sensitive) 0.79 with Gradient Boosting. In the proteomic dataset, XGBoost yielded Precision (Resistance) of 0.84 and Precision (Sensitive) of 0.80. Recall values were also high: 0.90 (Resistance) and 0.69 (Sensitive) for transcriptomics, and 0.91 (Resistance) and 0.67 (Sensitive) for proteomics. Although the class imbalance can lower the balanced MCC, the strong precision and recall scores confirm the models' effectiveness in identifying resistant cases.

Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves for the top-performing models:Gradient Boosting for transcriptomic and XGBoost for proteomics are presented in Fig. 2E. Both models were evaluated via fivefold cross-validation. The AUC scores for the transcriptomic dataset ranged from 0.77 to 0.81, with specific fold results: 0.80 (cv1), 0.80 (cv2), 0.81 (cv3), 0.77 (cv4), and 0.78 (cv5). The proteomic dataset showed similar performance with AUCs of 0.78 (cv1), 0.80 (cv2), 0.77 (cv3), 0.81 (cv4), and 0.79 (cv5). Despite slight variations across folds, both classifiers demonstrated consistent discriminatory power, indicating a strong ability to predict resistance patterns from transcriptomic and proteomic profiles.
Explainable AI (xAI) algorithm providing resistant mediators in Axitinib treated cells

The LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) algorithm was employed to identify key features contributing to the classification of each individual cell line as resistant or sensitive to Axitinib.

LIME-Identified resistance features and their correlated transcripts and proteins across omics layers A Transcriptome LIME features and average cell Count B Proteome LIME features and average cell count C Heatmap depicting correlations between LIME-identified transcriptomic features and other statistically significant correlated transcripts D Heatmap depicting correlations between LIME-identified proteomic features and other statistically significant correlated proteins.

In this study, 125 transcripts (Supplementary Sheet 4) and 112 proteins (Supplementary Sheet 5) were consistently identified by LIME as one among the top 10 contributors to resistance predictions across resistant cell lines, evaluated over five cross-validation folds. The frequency with which each LIME-identified transcript (Fig. 3A) and protein (Fig. 3B) appeared in the top 10 across all folds is reported, highlighting robust, recurrent resistance-associated features. Further, we quantified recurrence across folds: ~ 71% of transcriptomic features appeared in >= 3 folds (34% in all 5), while proteomic features showed even stronger consistency (~ 85% in >= 3 folds, 42% in all 5). These results indicate that a substantial proportion of features are robust across cross-validation runs (Supplementary Sheet 6).

This explainable AI-driven analysis provided a biologically grounded interpretation of model predictions and helped uncover key molecular mediators driving resistance across multiple Axitinib-treated cell lines.
Augmenting LIME-derived features with correlated transcripts and proteins

To deepen the biological insight into resistance mechanisms in Axitinib-treated cell lines, additional features highly correlated with the LIME-identified transcripts and proteins were incorporated. Specifically, transcripts and proteins exhibiting Pearson correlation coefficients greater than l0.8l with LIME-derived features were selected. To further refine this expanded set, a Levene test was applied to identify features with significantly different expression variances between resistant and sensitive groups.

Only the correlated features that also showed statistically significant expression differences (p value < 0.05) between the two groups were retained (Fig. 3C and D). These features, together with the original LIME-identified resistance mediators, were designated as the final feature set for downstream biological analyses (Supplementary Sheet 7).
Resistance Stratification via Transcriptomic and Proteomic Clustering

Hierarchical agglomerative clustering was performed independently on transcriptomic and proteomic datasets using the LIME-identified features combined with their highly correlated counterparts. The optimal number of clusters was determined to be two, based on silhouette index values of 0.50 for transcriptomics and 0.37 for proteomics (Fig. 4A and B). The resulting clusters were labeled as T_c1 (86 cell lines) and T_c2 (539 cell lines) for transcriptomics, and P_c1 (85 cell lines) and P_c2 (532 cell lines) for proteomics. t-SNE visualizations (Fig. 4A and B) illustrated the cluster separations, with Cluster 1 shown in purple and Cluster 2 in red. A cross-comparison of clusters between the transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed a high degree of overlap: 75 cell lines were common to T_c1 and P_c1, while 520 cell lines overlapped between T_c2 and P_c2 (Fig. 4C and D, Supplementary Sheet 8). This concordance supports the consistency of the clustering approach and validates the feature selection pipeline, including LIME and correlated feature enrichment.

Heatmaps of gene and protein expression (Fig. 4E and F) further highlight differences between clusters. Notably, Cluster 1 comprised all blood-derived cell lines, while Cluster 2 primarily comprised solid tumor-derived lines, largely of epithelial origin. This pointed towards a distinct, tissue-specific resistance mechanism in hematopoietic malignancies.

IC50 distribution analyses (Fig. 5A-C) provide additional biological context: blood-derived cell lines (Cluster 1) displayed lower IC50 values, indicating lower levels of resistance. The narrower and left-skewed IC50 distribution in Cluster 1 contrasts with the broader and right-shifted distribution in Cluster 2, which reflects higher and more variable resistance across diverse tissue types. These findings suggest that Cluster 1 may rely on more immediate and uniform resistance mechanisms, while Cluster 2 employs diverse and potentially more complex strategies.
Reinforced evidence for cluster-specific resistance features via statistical analyses

To identify transcripts and proteins contributing to resistance within each cluster, two non-parametric statistical tests were applied: the Levene test to assess intra-cluster variance and the Mann-Whitney U test to evaluate differences in mean expression levels between clusters.

This analysis identified 140 cluster-specific features associated with resistance in Cluster 1 and 207 in Cluster 2, with an additional 68 features shared across both clusters (Fig. 5D and E, Supplementary Sheet 9). The larger number of discriminative features in Cluster 2 supports the hypothesis of greater molecular heterogeneity and diverse resistance mechanisms, consistent with the broader tissue origins of these cell lines. In contrast, the relatively smaller and more cohesive Cluster 1 highlights a tissue-specific and potentially more uniform resistance profile, particularly in blood-derived malignancies.
Discussion

This study presents a robust and interpretable machine learning framework to identify key molecular drivers of drug resistance in cancer cell lines, with a particular focus on Axitinib. Given the comparable mutational landscapes across the resistant and sensitive cell lines, including similar mutation types and burdens, resistance could not be attributed to genomic alterations alone and instead appears to be driven by differential gene and protein expression. By leveraging transcriptomic and proteomic datasets curated from the Cell Model Passports in tandem to the drug response data derived from GDSC and employing the Boruta algorithm for feature selection, we achieved substantial dimensionality reduction without compromising predictive performance. Consistently high classifier scores across multiple evaluation metrics, particularly from XGBoost and Gradient Boosting classifiers, affirmed the robustness of the selected features. The use of LIME explainable AI enabled instance-level interpretation, revealing transcripts and proteins most predictive of resistance. These were further enriched by incorporating highly correlated features that also exhibited significant expression differences between resistant and sensitive lines. Clustering analyses based on these refined features stratified resistant cell lines into two distinct groups across both omics layers, reinforcing the coherence of the feature selection pipeline. Notably, these clusters revealed tissue-specific resistance patterns, with blood-derived lines forming a uniform group distinct from the more heterogeneous solid tumors. As detailed below, this integrative approach highlighted biologically meaningful mediators of resistance, which were used to elucidate possible resistance mechanisms driven by these features, offering both reassurance of methodological rigor and a foundation for future experimental validation and therapeutic exploration.
Examining the role of VEGFR mutations and expression in Axitinib resistance

The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling axis is central to angiogenesis, involving a family of ligands: VEGF-A, VEGF-B, VEGF-C and VEGF-D with three primary receptor tyrosine kinases: VEGFR-1 (FLT-1), VEGFR-2 (KDR/FLK-1), and VEGFR-3 (FLT-4). These receptors are predominantly expressed on endothelial cells and share a conserved structure comprising seven extracellular immunoglobulin-like domains, a single transmembrane domain, and an intracellular split tyrosine kinase domain. VEGF-A binds both FLT-1 and KDR, with KDR mediating most of the angiogenic responses, including endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and survival. VEGFR-1, despite its higher affinity for VEGF-A, exhibits weaker kinase activity and often functions as a decoy receptor, modulating KDR signaling. VEGF-B exclusively binds FLT-1, influencing monocyte migration and other processes. VEGF-C and VEGF-D primarily interact with FLT-4, promoting lymphangiogenesis, but can also activate VEGFR-2 under certain conditions, implying KDR to be the critical VEGFR receptor for mediating angiogenesis. Axitinib is a selective inhibitor of FLT-1, KDR, and FLT-4, with half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50) of 0.1 nM, 0.2 nM, and 0.2 nM, respectively.

To better understand potential mechanisms behind Axitinib resistance, we examined mutation profiles of VEGF ligands and receptors in resistant and sensitive cell lines to identify any significant alteration that could affect Axitinib binding and its inhibitory effects. We also assessed the baseline expression levels of the receptors and their natural ligands in the resistant and sensitive cell lines to determine whether there is an inherent consistent difference in the expression level that contributes to the resistance towards Axitinib.

VEGF receptor-ligand mutations and expression differences in Axitinib-resistant and sensitive cell lines. Comparative analysis of VEGF signaling components in Axitinib-resistant and sensitive cell lines. The bar plots depict the proportion of mutations observed in resistant versus sensitive cell lines for VEGF receptor genes (KDR, FLT1, FLT4) and VEGF ligand genes (VEGFA, VEGFB, VEGFC, VEGFD). Additionally, differential transcript expression levels of these genes were evaluated and compared between the resistant and sensitive groups to assess potential regulatory shifts associated with drug response

All observed mutations in VEGF ligands and receptors across the analyzed cell lines were systematically categorized based on their predicted functional consequences. Essential splice site, frameshift, nonsense, and splice-region mutations were classified as likely loss-of-function variants due to their potential to truncate the encoded protein or disrupt critical RNA processing mechanisms. In contrast, mutations located in downstream, upstream, and intronic regions were predominantly considered neutral, as they are less likely to directly affect protein-coding sequences. However, potential regulatory impacts of these non-coding mutations on gene expression or splicing efficiency cannot be entirely excluded. Variants within the 3' and 5' untranslated regions (UTRs) were categorized as having either neutral or loss-of-function effects, given their roles in modulating mRNA stability, localization, and translational efficiency. In-frame insertions/deletions and missense mutations were categorized as having uncertain consequences, as their impact depends on the specific amino acid changes and the structural and functional context within the affected protein domains. Comparative analysis of the mutational profiles of VEGF receptors and ligands, as summarized in Fig. 6, revealed no consistent pattern or recurrent mutations that could clearly explain the differences in resistance or sensitivity among the cell lines. Notably, the majority of receptor mutations (~ 40%) were intronic and predicted to have no direct functional consequence. Less than 2% of mutations affected splice sites in VEGF receptors across both resistant and sensitive cell lines. Approximately 10% of Axitinib-resistant cell lines exhibited missense mutations in VEGF receptors. For further analysis, particular focus was placed on KDR, given that its downstream signaling pathways are central to angiogenesis. Missense mutations identified in FLT-1 and KDR were mapped to their respective amino acid positions and annotated using UniProt listings of functional domains and motifs. This mapping aimed to determine whether these mutations impacted key structural regions of the receptors.

Structural studies have elucidated the binding interactions of Axitinib with the receptors. In KDR, Axitinib binds within the ATP-binding cleft of the kinase domain, stabilizing the receptor in an inactive conformation, thus highlighting the importance of the kinase domain in Axitinib's mechanism of action. Notably, several mutations observed in the kinase domain of KDR, such as p.I915V, p.I915T, p.S925F, p.K939R, p.G942E, p.R944Q, p.R946H, p.D958Y, p.E979G, p.P992S, p.H1004N, p.R1032Q, p.S1037L, p.V1041L, p.A1065T, p.R1066C, p.R1118Q, p.R1126S, p.G1145R, and p.L1156F, are located in close proximity to or within the ATP-binding pocket and activation loop regions critical for Axitinib binding. Mutations in these areas could potentially alter the conformation of the kinase domain, affecting Axitinib's binding affinity and leading to reduced drug efficacy or resistance in the ~ 10% of the resistant cell lines.

Interestingly, transcript expression analyses of VEGF ligands and receptors revealed statistically significant differences (p value < 0.05) in multiple transcripts between resistant and sensitive cell lines. Elevated expression of KDR was observed in Axitinib-resistant lines, while the expression of certain ligands, such as VEGFA and VEGFC, also demonstrated significant upregulation. This suggests that alterations in the direct target of Axitinib or its ligands are unlikely to be the primary contributors to resistance, and therefore, resistance may be driven by other mechanisms beyond simple alterations in these key genes.
Dissecting diverse mechanisms of resistance in Axitinib-resistant cell lines

Resistance-associated features identified through the machine learning framework were further examined for their distribution across the two transcriptomic-proteomic clusters. Some features showed consistent expression across both clusters, suggesting a shared role in mediating resistance, while others exhibited low variance and high mean expression in only one cluster, indicating cluster-specific relevance.

Functional enrichment of these features using KEGG pathway mapping revealed their involvement across diverse biological categories, including metabolism, cellular maintenance, signal transduction, cancer pathways, systemic diseases, viral and microbial infections, physiology, hormone-regulated functions, and addiction-related pathways. This broad distribution underscores the multifaceted nature of resistance mechanisms.

Resistance frequently arises through perturbations in intracellular signaling cascades, which in turn modulate transcription factor activity. These transcriptional changes lead to altered expression of downstream effector proteins, reprogramming cellular metabolism and maintenance to enhance survival under drug pressure. Intriguingly, some viral proteins share sequence homology with endogenous growth factors; their aberrant expression during infection can mimic growth factor signaling, potentially enhancing tumorigenic signaling and contributing to resistance.

Together, these findings illuminate the complex, context-dependent interplay of signaling disruption, metabolic adaptation, and potentially viral mimicry that underlies diverse resistance strategies in Axitinib-resistant cancer cell lines.

A total of 68 genes (including transcripts and proteins) were identified as mediators of drug resistance common to both Cluster 1 and Cluster 2. When mapped to KEGG pathways, these genes revealed several shared biological processes, albeit with cluster-specific patterns of gene usage and functional divergence. The most prominent shared pathways are shown in Table 1.

These pathways are intricately interconnected and collectively contribute to epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and extracellular matrix (ECM) modifications, which play crucial roles in mediating resistance mechanisms as discussed below:
Mechanosensing and ECM stiffness

The tumor microenvironment (TME) exerts a significant influence on drug resistance through mechanical stress and ECM remodeling. During tumor progression, mechanical alterations in the TME activate mechano-transduction programs that drive tumor proliferation and therapeutic resistance.

Cells sense these mechanical cues, such as stiffness, strain, and topography, through specialized proteins, including proteoglycans, glycoproteins, and adhesion molecules. Our analysis identified several key mechanosensors and ECM components significantly upregulated in both clusters, particularly in Cluster 2. These include - (i) Collagens: COL6A2, COL6A3, (ii) Laminins, Fibrinogen, Fibronectin, Vitronectin: LAMB3, F5, FNDC3B, VTN (iii) Adhesion Molecules: CAV1, CAV2, SDC4, NECTIN4, (iv) Integrins and GPCRs: ITGA3, ITGB1, ITGB5, ITGAV, GPRC5A, GNG12, LIF, TGFBI, (v) Mechano-transduction regulators: YAP, TAZ.

These mechanosensors regulate the activity of growth factor receptors (like EGFR, TGFbeta and MET) that activate downstream signaling pathways such as PI3K-AKT, RAS-MAPK, FAK/Src/beta-catenin, JAK-STAT, Wnt, FoxO, TNF, ErbB, and Hippo. All of which were present in KEGG analysis. These cascades are further supported by KEGG pathway enrichment involving actin cytoskeleton reorganization, motor proteins, focal adhesion, and intercellular junctions. Activation of these signaling routes leads to enhanced cytoskeletal dynamics via ROCK/Rho and Myosin II (upregulated), promoting nuclear translocation of key transcription factors. These events drive stemness, EMT, and survival in hypoxic environments, ultimately leading to resistance through four main mechanisms: (i) Enhanced drug efflux, (ii) Increased DNA repair and mutation tolerance, (iii) Sustained cell cycle progression, (iv) Evasion of apoptosis.

Mechanosensors have been directly implicated in resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g., Axitinib) and other cancer therapeutics. For instance, Glioblastoma cells grown in HA-based stiff hydrogels were resistant to EGFR inhibitor erlotinib; Lung cancer cells exposed to collagen-mediated integrin signaling showed resistance to multiple EGFR inhibitors; Colorectal liver metastases exhibited reduced response to bevacizumab under increased ECM stiffness; Breast cancer cells developed resistance to sorafenib and lapatinib via beta1-integrin/JNK and YAP/TAZ signaling; Melanoma cells showed BRAF inhibitor resistance via ECM-induced YAP/TAZ activation. Specifically, for Axitinib, one study highlighted that inhibition of YAP1/TAZ in cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), when combined with VEGF blockade, synergistically suppressed tumor angiogenesis, suggesting YAP1 as a major VEGF-independent pro-angiogenic regulator.
Apoptosis evasion

Apoptosis is tightly regulated by the balance between proapoptotic and antiapoptotic proteins, with a higher ratio of the former favoring cell death. Key signaling pathways such as PI3K/Akt govern the expression of these apoptotic regulators. Notably, increased expression of AKT (identified in our gene set) has been linked to resistance against chemotherapeutic agents including paclitaxel and cisplatin in ovarian cancer, and doxorubicin in gastric cancer, underscoring its role in suppressing chemotherapy-induced apoptosis. Furthermore, elevated levels of the antiapoptotic protein BCL2L1 (also present in our dataset) have been associated with poorer survival outcomes in ovarian cancer patients, reinforcing its contribution to therapy resistance through apoptosis evasion.
Unique resistance mechanisms in Cluster 1

Cluster 1 cell lines exhibited a distinct resistance profile with 140 identified resistance-mediating transcripts/proteins. Theseresistance mediators got mapped to 118 KEGG pathways, of which 22 pathways were exclusive to Cluster 1, pointing to unique molecular adaptations. These pathways suggest specialized resistance strategies, particularly in blood-derived cell lines. The complete list of these pathways and enriched resistance mediators can be found in Supplementary Sheet 11.
Metabolic manipulation to maintain cellular reductive agents and production of energy currency, ATP and GTP, independent of oxygen

Cancer cell adaptation to axitinib via metabolic rewiring and stress responses. Axitinib's anti-angiogenic effects induce hypoxia and nutrient deprivation, forcing cells to reprogram energy metabolism by upregulating glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) and Purine synthesis, ensuring continued ATP and nucleotide synthesis independent of oxygen. These adaptations lead to an accumulation of NADH and H+ , resulting in reductive stress and elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. The ROS induce protein denaturation and DNA damage; in response, cells enhance the expression of chaperones for protein refolding and upregulate DNA repair proteins to counteract genomic instability

Cluster 1 cell lines adapt to VEGF pathway inhibition by rewiring their metabolism. They boost de novo purine biosynthesis, which produces the essential nucleotides ATP and GTP, the energy currency of the cells. This shift allows the cells to maintain energy production without relying on the oxygen-dependent mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC), helping them survive under hypoxic and oxidative stress conditions. This is evidenced by the observed over expression of PAICS (phosphoribosylaminoimidazole carboxylase and phosphoribosylaminoimidazolesuccinocarboxamide synthase) in cluster 1 cell lines, which catalyzes critical steps (steps 6 and 7) in purine biosynthesis, supporting this compensatory mechanism. Further, it has been previously demonstrated that Purine biosynthesis is upregulated when ETC members are inhibited. However, this reliance on purine biosynthesis introduces redox stress due to an imbalance between nucleotide synthesis and salvage pathways, potentially increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and leading to DNA damage. In response, cluster 1 cell lines show increased expression of genes involved in critical genome maintenance processes, as evidenced by enrichment in KEGG pathways such as DNA replication, homologous recombination, Fanconi anemia pathway, ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling, Polycomb repressive complex, nucleotide excision repair, mismatch repair, and nonhomologous end-joining [Supplementary Sheet 11]. These pathways collectively contribute to maintaining genomic stability under stress conditions. Concurrently, redox stress-induced protein misfolding necessitates an upregulation of ribosomal proteins and chaperones such as ANP32E, which are upregulated significantly in cluster 1 cell lines, which support proteostasis and mitigate misfolded protein accumulation respectively as shown in Fig. 7.
Bypassing VEGF dependency via alternative growth receptor signaling
We also observed the upregulation of alternative growth-promoting receptors in Cluster 1, suggesting a potential bypass of VEGF dependency through lineage-specific signaling mechanisms.

Several genes highly expressed in these blood-derived cell lines are known to support immune cell development and proliferation: (i) TRAF3IP3, promotes the growth of B-cell and T-cell, (ii) SPN (Sialophorin, also known as CD43), facilitates B-cell proliferation; also implicated in angiogenesis in lung cancer, (iii) CD53, enhances B-cell growth through IL-7 signaling. The elevated expression of these receptors indicates that Cluster 1 cells may compensate for VEGF pathway inhibition by engaging alternate growth signaling routes, ensuring continued proliferation via hematopoietic lineage-specific pathways.
Resistance mechanisms unique to Cluster 2

Analysis revealed 207 genes contributing to resistance in Cluster 2 cell lines. These resistance-associated genes were mapped to 218 KEGG pathways, of which 122 pathways were exclusive to Cluster 2 [Supplementary Sheet 12], reflecting the cluster's broad tissue diversity.
Fatty acid and lipid signaling in proliferation, immune evasion, and inflammation

Features from Cluster 2 cell lines were enriched in several phospholipid and fatty acid metabolism pathways: including glycerophospholipid metabolism, fatty acid degradation, ether lipid metabolism, and arachidonic, linoleic, and alpha-linolenic acid metabolism.

A key gene across these pathways is PLAAT3 (phospholipase A and acyltransferase 3), identified as a critical resistance mediator in Cluster 2. This multifunctional enzyme exhibits phospholipase A1/A2, O-acyltransferase, and N-acyltransferase activities, contributing to membrane lipid remodeling. It plays a pivotal role in the N-acylphosphatidylethanolamine (NAPE) metabolic process, catalyzing the calcium-independent hydrolysis of fatty acids from glycerophospholipids and facilitating the formation of NAPE, a precursor of bioactive N-acylethanolamines (NAEs). These enzymatic activities promote the breakdown of membrane lipids and release fatty acids such as linoleic, alpha-linolenic, and arachidonic acid, which act as signaling molecules involved in immune modulation and inflammation.

Linoleic acid, for instance, suppresses anti-tumor T-cell responses by inhibiting TNF-alpha production and promoting apoptosis. Naive T cells express E-FABP (epidermal fatty acid-binding protein), which mediates mitochondrial uptake of linoleic acid, triggering lipid peroxidation in peroxisomes and generating ROS, a process associated with chemical carcinogenesis. These ROS can induce DNA damage and apoptosis in T cells, thus impairing immune surveillance. Arachidonic acid, another hydrolyzed product, fuels inflammation by serving as a substrate for COX-2, leading to the production of PGE2 (prostaglandin E2). PGE2 not only promotes tumor-associated inflammation and progression but also acts as a ligand for TRP channels, particularly TRPV1, which modulates calcium signaling. Dysregulated calcium signaling is a hallmark of tumor growth and survival. This pathway is further amplified by the overexpression of ITPR3 (inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor type 3), which facilitates calcium release into the endoplasmic reticulum and activates the phosphatidylinositol signaling pathway. This signaling cascade produces lipid messengers like phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate, which in turn activates the PI3K-Akt pathway, central to cell survival and proliferation.

PLAAT3 Activity Links Lipid Hydrolysis to Immune Suppression, ROS Stress, and PI3K-Akt Activation. PLAAT3 catalyzes the hydrolysis of membrane phospholipids, releasing fatty acids such as linoleic acid, alpha-linolenic acid, and arachidonic acid. These fatty acids serve as signaling molecules involved in immune modulation and inflammation. Linoleic acid, in particular, is transported into T cells via epidermal fatty acid-binding protein (E-FABP), promoting lipid peroxidation within mitochondria and peroxisomes, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) that induce DNA damage and apoptosis of naive T cells. Arachidonic acid contributes to pro-inflammatory signaling through its conversion to prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) modulating calcium signaling. This pathway stimulates phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate production and activates the PI3K-Akt signaling axis, promoting cell survival and proliferation, while contributing to tumor-associated angiogenesis

Metabolic and Signaling Changes Promoting EMT (Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition)

Inhibition of the VEGF-driven angiogenic pathway by Axitinib leads to oxygen deficiency, triggering a shift from O-linked to N-linked glycosylation in post-translational modifications. This metabolic adaptation not only reduces oxygen demand but also serves as a cellular signal for hypoxia, promoting physiological changes to survive under low-oxygen stress. A key target of this altered glycosylation is E-cadherin, an epithelial marker crucial for maintaining cell-cell and cell-ECM adhesion. In tumor cells, N-glycosylation of E-cadherin leads to the formation of complex branched glycans that promote its internalization into the cytoplasm, disrupting extracellular adhesion and weakening epithelial integrity. This detachment from the ECM further amplifies hypoxia-induced signaling pathways, such as Hippo, HIF-1, and Hedgehog, thereby facilitating EMT and enhancing tumor invasiveness.
Cancer-associated cellular aging via hypoxia-linked glucose dysregulation

Several pathways upregulated in Cluster 2, including Glucagon signaling, Carbohydrate digestion and absorption, Insulin secretion, AMPK signaling, Longevity regulation (human and multispecies), and AGE-RAGE signaling in diabetic complications, suggest a hypoxia-driven metabolic shift resembling diabetic conditions. Hypoxia disrupts glucose homeostasis by stimulating gluconeogenesis via glucagon signaling and impairing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, which increases the AMP/ATP ratio and activates the AMPK pathway through LKB1. AMPK activation promotes insulin secretion, but prolonged activation can lead to insulin resistance. Chronic hyperglycemia contributes to cellular aging and senescence across multiple tissues, as supported by the enrichment of longevity and AGE-RAGE-related pathways. Senescent cells, a known hallmark of cancer, actively remodel the tumor microenvironment by secreting pro-growth factors and cytokines that stimulate neighboring cells to re-enter the cell cycle. This is further supported by the activation of Apelin, cAMP, and Thyroid hormone signaling pathways observed in Cluster 2.

This section highlights the multifaceted and cluster-specific mechanisms underlying Axitinib resistance in cancer cell lines. Shared resistance features converged on EMT, ECM remodeling, and mechano-transduction pathways, reinforcing their central role in therapy evasion. Cluster 1 displayed adaptations favoring redox balance, DNA repair, and hematopoietic lineage signaling, whereas Cluster 2 uniquely exploited lipid signaling and calcium-mediated immune modulation. Together, these findings underscore the heterogeneity of resistance strategies and lay the groundwork for context-specific therapeutic interventions.
Conclusion

Our multi-omics machine learning framework reveals that resistance to Axitinib, an anti-angiogenic drug, is not a uniform response but an adaptive, lineage-specific strategy. Surprisingly, blood-derived cancers, expected to be less reliant on angiogenesis, show the greatest sensitivity, driven by VEGF's role as a growth factor rather than an oxygen supplier. In contrast, solid tumors resist via EMT, matrix stiffening, immune evasion, and senescence. This difference in the constraint perception by the pan-cancer cell lines was demonstrated by the Unsupervised clustering, the divergent strategies brought about by the resistant mediators, uncovered through explainable AI and classifier accuracy. The multi-omics ML-informed pipeline highlights how cancer cells evolve under distinct constraint pressures. By exposing resistance pathways like purine metabolism in hematologic malignancies and integrin-YAP signaling in solid tumors, our study not only decodes Axitinib resistance but also offers a scalable blueprint for understanding therapeutic failure across cancers.

While these findings provide a robust framework, they should be interpreted in the context of certain boundaries. Cell lines, though diverse and standardized, intrinsically cannot fully capture the complexity of patient tumors or the cross-talk with stromal and immune components. However, the use of a diverse pan-cancer cell line dataset (~ 1000 pan-cancer lines) helps mitigate this limitation by spanning multiple tissues and lineages, allowing us to observe secreted factors, immune-modulatory signals, and senescence-associated programs that echo microenvironmental pressures. Moreover, our analyses are computational; that converges with clinically established resistance mechanisms. However, further experimental validation, through perturbations, co-culture models, or patient-derived systems, will help us better understand and translate these insights into actionable therapeutic strategies.
