The successful development of radioligand therapies for prostate cancer, such as lutetium vipivotide tetraxetan (177Lu-PSMA-617), as well as advances in the understanding of histological features and expression of prostate cancer antigens reinvigorated the landscape of ADC development in prostate cancer. Table 2 shows completed and ongoing ADC clinical trials for prostate cancer, grouped by their molecular targets.
Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)

PSMA is a transmembrane protein found predominantly in prostate cells, and its expression increases as prostate malignancy progresses. In particular, PSMA expression increases following ADT:the cornerstone of prostate cancer treatment:making PSMA a prominent target for the treatment of CRPC. PSMA also has an internalization signal via its MXXXL cytoplasmic tail motif: upon binding, antibody-PSMA complexes undergo internalization from the cell surface into endosomal compartments via clathrin-coated pits, where the unique microenvironment facilitates the release of ADC payloads.

PSMA-targeting ADCs have been in clinical development over the past two decades. MLN2704, an ADC targeting the extracellular domain of PSMA with the antimicrotubule agent DM1 as the payload, was the first PSMA-based ADC to complete a phase I clinical trial in 23 patients with mCRPC. At a 4-week dosing schedule, MLN2704 was found to have dose-dependent pharmacokinetics and no measurable immunogenicity. The only dose-limiting toxicity observed was a grade 3 febrile neutropenia in 1 patient; other mild to moderate adverse events (AEs) included fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, neuropathy, leukopenia, lymphopenia, and reversible elevations of transaminases. MLN2704 demonstrated antitumor activity: of the 9 patients treated at the highest two doses, 2 (22%) had a > 50% decrease in prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and 1 (11%) had measurable regression in tumor size (NCT00052000). This was then followed by a phase I/II trial in which only 5 out of 62 patients with mCRPC (8%) had a decrease in PSA and PSA stabilization lasting >=90 days following treatment, suggesting limited efficacy of MLN2704. Moreover, this trial found that disulfide linker lability and rapid deconjugation in MLN2704 led to significant neurotoxicity, with 44 (71%) patients experiencing dose-limiting peripheral neuropathy halting clinical development. Thus, MLN2704 was ultimately discontinued.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: PSMA ADC, an ADC conjugating the antimicrotubule agent MMAE to a human IgG1 antibody targeting PSMA via a dipeptide linker, was the next PSMA-based ADC to enter clinical development. A phase I trial including 52 patients with mCRPC demonstrated a favorable toxicity profile and preliminary antitumor activity. Two dose-limiting toxicities (neutropenia and reversible elevations of transaminases) occurred, and 16 (31%) patients reported peripheral neuropathy. Durable reductions in PSA or circulating tumor cells (CTCs) were documented in 50% of patients. The following phase II trial enrolled 119 patients with mCRPC (83 taxane-experienced and 36 chemotherapy-naive; all patients had disease progression after abiraterone/enzalutamide) and showed that 19/113 (14%) patients had PSA declines >=50%; 60/78 (78%) patients with measurable CTCs had CTC declines >=50%. Of the 31 patients with RECIST-measurable disease, 4 (13%) had partial response, 19 (61%) stable disease, and 8 (26%) progressive disease. Despite the encouraging antitumor activity, the development of PSMA ADC was discontinued due to off-target toxicity from premature deconjugation, leading to significant rates of >= grade 3 neurotoxicity (24%), neutropenia (8%) and three patients died of sepsis-related death (2.6%).

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Another PSMA-based ADC investigated for the treatment of mCRPC, MEDI3726, also had similar issues with delivering its pyrrolobenzodiazepine (tesirine, SG3249) payload to the tumor without off-target effects due to heavy-light chain dissociation in the antibody. A phase I clinical trial investigated MEDI3726 among 33 patients with mCRPC after disease progression on abiraterone/enzalutamide and taxane therapy. While MEDI3726 showed some antitumor efficacy at high doses, clinical responses were not durable, and AEs led to treatment discontinuation in 11 (33%) patients. AEs such as skin toxicity and effusions occurred in 30 (91%) patients. MEDI3726 clinical development was thus halted.

The first-in-human phase I trial APEX-01 is investigating ARX517, a PSMA-targeting antibody conjugated to the auristatin amberstatin 269 (AS269) that inhibits microtubule polymerization. ARX517 uses oxime conjugation to attach the non-cleavable PEG linker carrying AS269 to site-specific synthetic amino acids in the antibody. The oxime chemistry is stable at physiological pH but labile in acidic environments such as the lysosome after ADC internalization, reducing premature payload release. A total of 24 patients with mCRPC were enrolled in the dose-escalation phase. Mild to moderate AEs included xerostomia (41.7%), fatigue (33.3%), diarrhea (20.8%), and thrombocytopenia (20.8%). At the highest dose tested (2.8 mg/kg), no dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) or treatment-related serious adverse events (SAEs >= grade 4) were reported, and >=50% PSA and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) decline were observed. RECIST responses were seen in 2/7 patients with measurable soft tissue disease. Enrollment in the expansion cohort is ongoing (NCT04662580).

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: While many PSMA-targeted ADCs have entered the clinical pipeline:including SHR-4394, which carries an undisclosed payload and is currently recruiting patients for its first phase I clinical trial (NCT06783829):many have failed to advance beyond phase I/II clinical trials due to modest PSA response rates, inadequate survival benefit, and significant toxicity. However, PSMA remains an important target, especially with the successful development of PSMA positron emission tomography (PET) and the PSMA-targeting radioligand therapy lutetium-177 vipivotide tetraxetan (177Lu-PSMA-617). PSMA-PET, which has high sensitivity and specificity for detecting PSMA-expressing metastatic lesions in prostate cancer, is the standard for selecting patients for PSMA-targeted therapies such as 177Lu-PSMA-617. 177Lu-PSMA-617 gained FDA approval in 2023 for patients with PSMA-positive mCRPC after progression on ARi and taxane-based chemotherapy, following the phase III VISION trial demonstrating that the combination of 177Lu-PSMA-617 with best standard-of-care (BSoC) therapy improved median overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival compared to BSoC alone (NCT03511664). While 177Lu-PSMA-617 currently demonstrates superior efficacy and a more favorable toxicity profile compared to PSMA-targeting ADCs, further development and refinement of PSMA-targeting ADCs could lead to improved efficacy and establish them as an important component of the PSMA-targeted therapeutic landscape.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: B7H3

Another promising target for ADCs in prostate cancer is B7H3, a costimulatory molecule commonly found on the surface of prostate cells that is overexpressed in prostate tumor cells. B7H3 has been shown to promote tumor metastasis and invasion via suppression of both CD8+ and CD4 + T cell proliferation and activity. As a result, overexpression of B7H3 is associated with disease spread, including increased extracapsular extension and seminal vesicle invasion, as well as worse outcomes, including higher risk of metastatic recurrence or subsequent development of CRPC. B7H3-based ADCs for the treatment of CRPC and other malignancies have been in clinical development.

Vobramitamab duocarmazine (MGC018) is an ADC composed of a duocarmycin payload conjugated to an anti-B7H3 antibody via a cleavable linker. Phase I dose escalation in 29 patients with advanced solid tumors showed two-dose limiting toxicities: grade 4 neutropenia and grade 3 fatigue. Results from the expansion cohort in mCRPC (n = 40) demonstrated that 4/7 patients had reductions in target lesions and 11/22 evaluable patients had >=50% PSA reduction. This study was terminated due to high rates of dose modifications and early treatment discontinuation (NCT03729596). A phase II study investigated MGC018 at a lower dose (2.0 and 2.7 mg/kg) and enrolled 182 patients with mCRPC (NCT05551117). Adverse effects included asthenia (40.7%), nausea (27.7%), fatigue (20.3%), decreased appetite (19.2%), anemia (17.5%), constipation (16.4%), and diarrhea (14.7%). The study was ultimately discontinued after five patients experienced fatal adverse events, including acute myocardial infarction, cardiac arrest, pneumonitis, and pleural effusion. Another phase I, dose-escalation, cohort-expansion study investigated MGC018 in combination with lorigerlimab (MGD019), an anti-PD-1 x CTLA-4 checkpoint inhibitor, in patients with advanced solid tumors including mCRPC, although it has since been paused (NCT05293496).

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Ifinatamab deruxtecan (I-DXd, DS-7300) is another ADC with an anti-B7H3 antibody linked to the TOPI inhibitor DXd. Findings from a Phase I/II dose-escalation and -expansion study in patients with advanced solid tumors demonstrated manageable safety profile and encouraging antitumor activity. Data from 73 heavily pre-treated mCRPC patients showed that 15/59 evaluable patients had a partial or complete response per RECIST, and the average duration of overall response (DOR) and progression-free survival (PFS) were 6.4 months and 4.8 months, respectively. The most common side effects reported were nausea, fatigue, vomiting, and chills, and grade >=3 treatment-related SAEs included anemia, neutropenia, dehydration, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. I-DXd illustrates the potential of TOPI inhibitor payloads in the treatment of CRPC, in contrast to the limited activity of irinotecan, topotecan, and other camptothecins as chemotherapy agents in CRPC. Enrollment in the trial for I-DXd in mCRPC is ongoing (NCT04145622).

YL201 contains a highly hydrophilic protease-cleavable linker-TOPI inhibitor payload (TMALIN ) with increased stability in the circulation and payload release in both the extracellular tumor environment and intracellular lysosomal compartment. Preliminary data from a phase I trial evaluating YL201 in 312 patients with advanced solid tumors, including 2 with prostate cancer, demonstrated overall promising antitumor activity: across all the tumor types, YL201 had a 40.8% objective response rate and 83.6% disease control rate. However, 97.1% of patients experienced TRAEs, most commonly hematological toxicities such as leukopenia (66.3%), anemia (64.7%), and neutropenia (61.5%); 36.2% of patients also experienced treatment interruptions while 5.4% discontinued treatment due to TRAEs (NCT05434234). Despite the frequency, TRAEs for YL201 were similar to those of other B7H3 ADCs, and YL201 had a manageable safety profile. A phase I/II trial evaluating YL201 in patients with advanced solid tumors including mCRPC (NCT06057922), as well as a phase II trial in patients with mCRPC (NCT06241846), are both currently recruiting subjects.

DB-1311/BNT324 is a B7H3-targeting ADC carrying a proprietary TOPI inhibitor payload that was granted fast-track designation by the FDA for mCRPC patients who have progressed on or after standard systemic regimens in 2024. Preliminary data from a phase I/II study including 73 patients with pre-treated CRPC showed encouraging efficacy and a manageable safety profile. Of the 52 patients with RECIST evaluable tumors, partial response was seen in 22 patients (objective response rate 42.3%) and stable disease was seen in 25 patients (disease control rate 90.4%), with a 6-month radiographic progression free survival rate of 67.7%. Common TRAEs included gastrointestinal and hematologic toxicities; 31 patients (42.5%) experienced >=grade 3 adverse events, and only 7 patients (9.6%) discontinued treatment due to toxicity. Enrollment of post-177Lu-PSMA-617 CRPC and taxane-naive CRPC patients is currently ongoing (NCT05914116).

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Other B7H3-targeting ADCs are also in clinical development. HS-20093, a TOPI inhibitor (HS-9265)-carrying ADC, was shown to have an acceptable safety profile and promising antitumor activity in a phase I study in patients with advanced solid tumors (NCT05276609), and is currently undergoing a phase II trial in mCRPC patients (NCT06001255). MHB088C carries a TOPI inhibitor payload, SuperTopoi , with 5 to 10 times greater potency than DXd; a phase I/II trial in 36 patients with heavily-pretreated mCRPC demonstrated a 14.3% objective response rate, a 95.2% disease control rate, and improvements in PSA levels, as well as a manageable safety profile with cytopenias as the most common >= grade 3 TRAE (CTR20231298). MGC026, which carries the TOPI inhibitor/exatecan payload SYNtecan E , was shown to have potent antitumor activity in B7H3+ patient-derived xenograft models of prostate cancer, and is currently undergoing a phase I clinical trial in patients with advanced solid tumors, including CRPC (NCT06242470).
STEAP1

STEAP1 (six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of the prostate 1) is another promising target for ADCs in prostate cancer. STEAP1 is a member of the STEAP1-4 family of metalloreductases, which are highly expressed in PCa tumors; STEAP1 overexpression has been detected in 90% of prostate cancers. Higher STEAP1 expression is associated with increased tumor proliferation, progression, invasiveness, risk of relapse, and Gleason score. One possible mechanism for this oncogenic overexpression is STEAP1's function as an intercellular communication channel for small molecules that promote stromal cell recruitment and proliferation, enhancing tumor survival and growth. STEAP1 upregulation has been seen in both PCa primary tumor cells and stroma cells in the tumor microenvironment. Notably, STEAP1 expression is sustained in even PSMA-negative prostate tumors and metastatic sites, providing an opportune target for patients with mCRPC.

annotations.text: six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of the prostate 1

passages.text: STEAP1 forms homotrimers and STEAP1/2 heterotrimers on the plasma membrane surface of prostate cancer cells. STEAP2 has previously been established as a therapeutic target antigen abundantly expressed in all stages of prostate cancer and directly correlated with the Gleason score. AZD0754, a STEAP2 CAR-T cell therapeutic agent, has demonstrated potent and specific cytotoxicity against STEAP2-expressing prostate cancer cells, validating STEAP2 as a therapeutic target in mCRPC. Recent studies of AMG 509, a STEAP1-directed T cell engager molecule under development for the treatment of prostate cancer, have also shown that targeting STEAP1 homodimers and STEAP1/2 heterotrimers leads to T cell-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Vandortuzumab vedotin (DSTP3086S, MSTP2109A, RG7450) is a humanized anti-STEAP1 IgG1 linked to MMAE that was evaluated in a phase I trial with 77 mCRPC patients. Dose-limiting toxicities included grade 3 transaminitis in 2 patients and grade 3 hyperglycemia and grade 4 hypophosphatemia in one patient, and common AEs, including fatigue, peripheral neuropathy, nausea, constipation, anorexia, diarrhea, and vomiting, occurred in >20% of participants. Early clinical efficacy was also observed: 11/62 (18%) patients who received doses >2 mg/kg had a >= 50% decline in PSA, and 2/36 (6%) of evaluable patients achieved radiographic partial responses. 16/27 (59%) of patients with unfavorable CTCs (>=5, a predictor of adverse prognosis) also saw conversion to favorable CTCs (<5, a predictor of favorable prognosis), suggesting prolonged disease stability. While DSTP3086S displayed evidence of antitumor activity with an acceptable safety profile, further optimization of DSTP3086S is necessary before any further clinical study. However, despite its discontinuation, DSTP3086S did highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting STEAP1 with ADC to treat mCRPC.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Three other STEAP1-targeting ADCs are under clinical investigation: ADRX-0405, ABBV-969, and DXC-008. Preclinical studies of ADRX-0405, which carries a TOPI inhibitor payload, have demonstrated good tolerability, potent bystander activity, and robust antitumor efficacy in prostate tumors with both high and low levels of target expression, and a phase I clinical trial investigating ADRX-0405 in patients with mCRPC and other advanced solid tumors is ongoing (NCT06710379). ABBV-969 and DXC-008 are dual-targeting PSMAxSTEAP1 ADCs carrying a TOPI inhibitor or tubulysin B analog payload, respectively; both are also currently undergoing phase I clinical trials in patients with prostate cancer (NCT06318273 and NCT06926283, respectively).
TROP2

Trop2 (trophoblast antigen 2), a membrane-bound glycoprotein, has also been investigated as a therapeutic target for ADCs in prostate cancer. Trop2 promotes prostate cancer growth, metastasis, and treatment resistance, and its expression is associated with inferior outcomes. Trop2 may also play a role in the neuroendocrine differentiation phenotype, a well-characterized mechanism for ADT-resistance in prostate tumors.

Sacituzumab govitecan (SG, IMMU-132) is an ADC linking a humanized anti-Trop-2 antibody (hRS7) to an SN-38 payload approved for the treatment of triple-negative breast cancer. Building upon preliminary activity from the phase I trial in CRPC, a phase II study is investigating SG in mCRPC (NCT03725761). Preliminary results from 20 participants showed no PSA50 responses. Another phase I trial investigated the combination of SG and an ATR (ataxia telangiectasia and Rad-3 related) inhibitor berzosertib in 12 patients with DNA damage response (DDR) gene-mutated or high-replication stress solid tumors; no dose-limiting toxicities were observed, and 2 patients with neuroendocrine prostate cancer showed partial responses to the drug combination.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: ESG401 is another ADC composed of an anti-TROP2 antibody conjugated to the TOPI inhibitor SN-38. Preliminary results from a phase I clinical trial in patients with pre-treated solid tumors (including prostate cancer) demonstrated a favorable safety profile and promising antitumor activity. ESG401 was found to have improved systemic stability and a prolonged half-life compared to SG, resulting in better tolerability: ESG401 had 11% less rates of grade >=3 neutropenia than SG, with most cases of neutropenia unperceivable and easily manageable. ESG401 also had an overall response rate of 34.2%, a disease control rate of 65.8%, and a clinical benefit rate of 50%. Enrollment in the trial is still ongoing (NCT04892342).

Datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd) is another anti-Trop-2 ADC consisting of the payload DXd, a highly potent TOPI inhibitor. Selective delivery of Dato-DXd is enhanced by the plasma-stable linker cleaved by tumor cell-enriched lysosomal enzymes. In the TROPION-PanTumor01 and TROPION-PanTumor02 phase I clinical trials, Dato-DXd demonstrated meaningful clinical activity and a manageable safety profile in advanced/metastatic HR + /HER2- and triple-negative breast cancers, urothelial carcinoma, and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) (NCT03401385, NCR05460273). While common AEs included nausea and stomatitis, Dato-DXd had an improved benefit-risk profile compared to SG, with lower incidences of neutropenia and diarrhea. Results from the Phase III TROPION-Breast01 and TROPION-Lung01trials demonstrated greater progression-free survival on Dato-DXd compared to standard-of-care therapy, leading to the FDA approval of Dato-DXd in metastatic HR + /HER2- breast cancer and EGFR + NSCLC. The ongoing TROPION-PanTumor03 Phase II clinical trial is assessing the safety, tolerability, and antitumor activity of Dato-DXd in patients with various advanced/metastatic solid tumors, including mCRPC. No results have been published yet (NCT05489211).

MHB036C is a TROP2-targeted ADC with an undisclosed TOPI inhibitor payload currently being investigated in a phase I/II trial of patients with advanced solid tumors, including mCRPC (NCT06373406). This builds upon preclinical data demonstrating superior potency of MHB036C in comparison to other anti-TROP2 ADCs such as DS-1062a currently being explored for NSCLC, as well as preliminary data from a first-in-human phase I/II trial in 26 patients with locally advanced or metastatic solid tumors showing a 33% partial response rate and manageable safety profile (CTR20231246).
CD46

CD46 is a cell-surface antigen highly expressed in advanced prostate cancer. FOR46 is an ADC composed of an anti-CD46 antibody conjugated to an MMAE payload. A recently completed phase I study demonstrated that FOR46 has an acceptable safety profile at clinically active doses in patients with mCRPC. Among the 33 patients enrolled in the dose-escalation phase, 9 patients achieved PSA50 decline, 1 out of 8 patients with measurable disease had a partial response, and 6 patients had stable disease lasting up to 39 weeks. The dose-limiting toxicity was grade 4 neutropenia. Ten patients were subsequently enrolled in the dose-expansion at RP2D (2.7 mg/kg) with improved safety profile: neutropenia (77%, Gr 3/4), infusion reactions (37%, all < Gr 2), fatigue (31%, all < Gr 2) and peripheral neuropathy (24%, all < Gr 2). The summary of both cohorts showed that 14 out of 31 (45%) patients with evaluable PSA achieved a PSA50 response with a median duration of >16 weeks; and of the 18 patients with measurable tumor lesions, 8 (44%) had tumor regression, with a median duration of >14 weeks.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Preclinical models have shown that enzalutamide-induced androgen receptor blockade increases CD46 expression and has an additive effect in combination with FOR46, supporting the ongoing trial evaluating FOR46 in combination with enzalutamide. Dose-limiting toxicities include Gr 4 neutropenia and hyponatremia and Gr 3 elevated transaminases, and the most common AEs are fatigue (64.7%), peripheral sensory neuropathy (47.1%), elevated transaminases (17.6%), alopecia (23.5%), decreased appetite (41.2%), neutropenia (17.6%), and weight loss (17.6%). Decline in PSA levels was observed in 13/16 evaluable patients, and stable disease for >=6 months was seen in 41.2% of patients. Moreover, 89Zr-DFO-YS5-PET imaging demonstrated tumor-specific uptake of FOR46. Enrollment for this study is ongoing (NCT05011188).

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Tissue factor (TF)

Tissue factor (TF) is a transmembrane protein aberrantly expressed in tumor cells and the tumor vasculature in many solid tumors, including cervical, bladder, and prostate cancer. Acting as the main initiator of the extrinsic coagulation pathway, TF forms a complex with activated factor VII (FVIIa) to induce clot formation, contributing to tumor-associated thrombosis. Additionally, TF triggers intracellular signaling cascades via protease-activated receptor 2 (PAR-2), promoting the production of proangiogenic factors, cytokines, and adhesion molecules, thereby fueling tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Experimental models have demonstrated that interference with TF expression or activity reduces tumor outgrowth and metastatic potential, while clinically, overexpression of TF has been found to be associated with disease progression and poor prognosis in solid tumors. Enrichment of TF in prostate cancer has supported the development of ADCs in CRPC.

JEWEL-101 is a first-in-human phase I study investigating XB002, a TF-targeting ADC carrying an auristatin-based payload with a protease-cleavable linker, in patients with advanced solid tumors. The auristatin-based payload, zovodotin, has lower off-target payload deconjugation and improved tolerability compared to other auristatins such as MMAE. Preliminary results from the dose-escalation stage have demonstrated that XB002 is well-tolerated, with only low-grade ocular toxicity and no bleeding events or treatment-related peripheral neuropathy. No efficacy results have been published, and cohort expansion was planned to continue in patients with mCRPC (NCT04925284). However, XB002 was discontinued due to the inability to compete against the existing TF-targeting ADC tisotumab vedotin.

Tisotumab vedotin, which carries an MMAE payload, is FDA-approved as a second-line treatment for recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, with potential indication in prostate cancer as well. A phase I/II and phase II trial of tisotumab vedotin in patients with solid tumors, including CRPC has been completed, but no CRPC-specific data have been reported (NCT03245736 and NCT02001623). However, across all tumor types, 15.6% of patients achieved an objective response, and the safety profile was manageable with the most common TRAEs being epistaxis (69%), fatigue (56%), nausea (52%), alopecia (44%), and conjunctivitis (43%).
Delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3)

The expression of delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3), a notch inhibitory ligand expressed on neuroendocrine carcinomas (NEC), correlates with aggressive clinical features and poor prognosis. DLL3 has limited expression in benign prostate tissue and localized prostate cancer but is expressed in CRPC with neuroendocrine features and de novo neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC).

Rovalpituzumab tesirine (Rova-T), a DLL3-targeting ADC linked to PBD payload, demonstrated antitumor activity in NECs including NEPC. A phase I/II study enrolled 101 patients with NECs, of which 21 were NEPC patients. Of the 69 NEC patients ultimately treated with the phase II dose, 9 had partial responses with a duration of response of 3.1 months; however, specific data for NEPC was not available. Serious adverse events at a dose of 0.3 mg/kg included pleural and pericardial effusions, photosensitivity reaction, dyspnea, tumor lysis syndrome, rhabdomyolysis, and kidney injury (NCT02709889). Following two phase III trials in small cell lung cancer (SCLC) patients, MERU and TAHOE, development of Rova-T was ultimately discontinued due to toxicity, limited efficacy and lack of survival benefit compared to standard-of-care therapies.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Despite issues with safety and efficacy halting development of Rova-T, DLL3 still remains a relevant anticancer target in prostate cancer. A recent phase Ib study of tarlatamab, a bispecific T-cell engager targeting DLL3 and CD3, in 40 NEPC patients demonstrated a manageable safety profile with promising antitumor activity, including partial responses in 22.2% of DLL3 + NEPC patients. This highlights the validity of DLL3 as a therapeutic target in NEPC (NCT04702737). DLL3-targeted ADCs currently under investigation for other indications may also have potential in prostate cancer, including ZL-1310, which has shown a favorable safety profile with significant antitumor activity and high response rate in patients with extensive stage SCLC (NCT06179069).
SLC44A4 (CTL4)

SLC44A4 (soluble carrier family 4 member 4 or CTL4) is a bicarbonate transporter involved in regulating the acidic tumor microenvironment, with increased expression in epithelial cancers and low expression in normal tissue. It is upregulated in 75% of primary prostate tumors, and higher SLC44A4 expression correlates with higher Gleason score. SLC44A4 was also identified as a driver of ADT resistance in CRPC.

ASG-5ME is an ADC consisting of an anti-SLC44A4 antibody conjugated to MMAE via a protease-cleavable valine-citrulline linker. A phase I trial investigated ASG-5ME in 46 patients with mCRPC. Of the 40 patients with measurable PSA, 11(25%) had a PSA decline >50%. Among 16 patients with RECIST evaluable tumors, 2 (12%) had a partial response, 7 (41%) had stable disease, and 7 (41%) had progressive disease. Ten patients (22%) terminated the study early due to AEs. Common AEs included fatigue (46%), diarrhea (24%), cardiotoxicity, ophthalmic toxicity, neurotoxicity, renal toxicity, and metabolic dysregulation. Two treatment-related deaths occurred: one due to ileus, severe hypotension, and renal failure, and the other due to sepsis post-hospitalization for hyperglycemia. Due to the significant toxicity and limited antitumor activity ASG-5ME development was discontinued.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: HER2

Overexpression of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), a transmembrane protein, is an oncogenic driver in many tumors, such as breast cancer. Moreover, HER2 is enriched in quiescent prostate cancer cells, which contribute to tumor progression, metastasis, and relapse. While no prostate cancer-specific clinical data are available for HER2-targeting ADCs, HER2-targeting ADCs have been extensively studied in breast cancer. Trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) was approved first as standard second-line therapy for HER2+ metastatic breast cancer, followed by the approval of trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) for both HER2+ and HER2-low breast cancers with significantly improved progression-free survival and overall response rates compared to T-DM1 or standard chemotherapy. T-DXd has a high drug-to-antibody ratio and membrane-permeable payload, allowing a bystander effect even in tumors with heterogenous or low HER2 expression. This is especially relevant in prostate cancer, where low level HER2 overexpression has been associated with rapid tumor cell proliferation and poor prognosis. A case report of a patient with HER2-expressing NEPC with rapid progression on seven different lines of therapy demonstrated substantial response on off-label treatment with T-DXd, including a 57% overall reduction in tumor volume across sites of metastases and improved performance status.

A166 is another HER2-based ADC, containing the antimicrotubule Duostatin-5 payload conjugated via a stable protease-cleavable valine citrulline linker. A recently completed, first-in-human phase I/II study of A166 in 49 patients with relapsed/refractory cancers expressing HER2 antigen or amplified HER2 gene, including mCRPC, indicated safety and clinical efficacy. Preliminary data from 35 patients in the dose-escalation phase demonstrated manageable toxicity, with common AEs being corneal epitheliopathy, keratitis, decreased appetite, dry eye, and blurry vision but no dose-limiting toxicities or drug-related deaths. Moreover, of the 27 evaluable patients, 9 had stable disease while 7 achieved partial response, resulting in a 59% disease control rate. However, no specific data for the mCRPC cohort has been published (NCT03602079).

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: HER3

Human epidermal growth factor receptor 3 (HER3) is a membrane-bound protein that activates downstream PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling to promote tumor growth, survival, and therapeutic resistance after dimerization with other ERBB family members (e.g., HER2). Preclinical studies have demonstrated that HER3 is frequently overexpressed in lethal prostate cancer, where it is associated with more aggressive disease, reduced time to castration resistance, and poor prognosis. In the tumor microenvironment, secretion of NRG1 by stromal myelomonocytic cells can also activate HER3 and induce ADT resistance, further supporting the role of HER3 in disease progression. Patritumab deruxtecan (HER3-DXd; U3-1402) and DB-1310 are two TOPI inhibitor-based anti-HER3 ADCs currently undergoing development for solid tumors, although data in prostate cancer patients is currently lacking. Following demonstration of potent and sustained antitumor activity against a HER3-expressing CRPC patient-derived xenograft model, a phase II trial for HER3-DXd in relapsed/refractory locally advanced/metastatic solid tumors is currently enrolling prostate cancer patients (NCT06172478). An ongoing phase I/II trial of DB-1310 in advanced/metastatic solid tumors is also enrolling patients with prostate cancer (NCT05785741), after DB-1310 was found to exhibit significant cytotoxicity and tumor growth inhibition, synergy with the EGFR inhibitor osimertinib, and the ability to overcome osimertinib in prostate cancer patient-derived xenograft models.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Nectin-4

Nectin-4 is a transmembrane cell adhesion molecule that is minimally expressed in normal adult tissues but is overexpressed in several malignancies, including subsets of prostate cancer such as prostate ductal adenocarcinoma. However, while canine models of metastatic prostate cancer highly express Nectin-4, Nectin-4 expression in human mCRPC is generally low and heterogenous, with only a minority of metastatic lesions (notably in lung and peritoneum) showing moderate membranous expression.

Enfortumab vedotin (EV) is an Nectin-4-targeting ADC carrying a MMAE payload that has been approved in combination with pembrolizumab in patients with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma, and is now undergoing investigation in prostate cancer. Preliminary data from a phase II study of EV in 11 heavily-treated refractory mCRPC patients demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and promising efficacy with a 64% overall response rate: no grade 5 TRAEs were reported, 5/11 patients achieved PSA decline >= 50%, 3/4 patients had an objective response, 4/7 had declines in CTCs, and 2/11 had stable disease for >=6 months. Enrollment in the trial is ongoing (NCT04754191).

LY4101174 and LY4052031 are two next-generation Nectin-4-targeting ADCs that have demonstrated robust antitumor activity across a range of Nectin-4 expression levels and in a Nectin-4-MMAE ADC-resistant tumor model in the preclinical setting. LY4101174, which carries an exatecan payload, is currently undergoing a phase I trial in patients with advanced/metastatic solid tumors, including prostate cancer (NCT06238479). A phase I study investigating LY4052031, which carries the camptothecin payload LSN3889710, in patients with advanced/metastatic solid tumors expressing Nectin-4 also recruited patients with prostate cancer, but was suspended before any data had been published (NCT 06465069).

Trophoblast glycoprotein (TPBG; 5T4) is a cell surface oncofetal antigen that is highly expressed in prostate cancer but rarely found in normal adult tissues. 5T4 expression is associated with increased prostate tumor progression, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and invasion and metastasis via potentiation of CXCL12/CXCR4 chemotaxis and favoring of the non-canonical Wnt pathway. Moreover, 5T4 is very efficiently endocytosed, making it an ideal target for ADCs. TUB-030 is a 5T4-targeting ADC carrying an exatecan payload that has demonstrated sub-nanomolar affinity to 5T4, efficient bystander activity against target-negative cells, high stability in plasma, and long-lasting antitumor activity in preclinical cancer models; TUB-030 is currently undergoing a phase I/II clinical trial in patients with advanced solid tumors, including prostate cancer (NCT06657222).
KAAG1

Kidney associated antigen 1 (KAAG1) is a cell surface antigen highly and selectively expressed in prostate cancer. KAAG1 is also rapidly internalized and trafficked by lysosomes upon antibody binding, making it an attractive target for ADCs. ADCT-901 is an anti-KAAG1 ADC carrying a PBD dimer payload, SG3199, that completed a phase I trial in patients with advanced solid tumors, including prostate cancer; however, no definitive clinical data is available yet (NCT04972981).
ASCT2

Expression of alanine-serine-cysteine transporter-2 (ASCT2; SLC1A5) is increased in primary and recurrent prostate cancer compared to normal tissue. Inhibition of ASCT2-mediated glutamine uptake and metabolism in prostate tumor cells has also been implicated in the reduction of cell cycle progression, cell proliferation, and metastasis, highlighting ASCT2 as a potential therapeutic target in prostate cancer. MEDI7247 is an anti-ASCT2 ADC carrying a PBD payload that has completed a phase I trial in patients with various solid tumors, including mCRPC; however, no definitive clinical data are available yet (NCT03811652).
LYPD3

LYPD3 (C4.4a) is a cell surface protein with limited expression on normal tissue but high expression in tumor cells, including in prostate cancer. LYPD3 overexpression is correlated with a more malignant phenotype and poor prognosis, and has been implicated in tumor invasion and metastasis. Moreover, LYPD3 is rapidly internalized, making it an attractive target for ADCs. Lupartumab amadotin is a LYPD3-targeting ADC with an auristatin payload; however, a phase I clinical trial in patients with advanced solid tumors (including prostate cancer) has been terminated due to insufficient participant accrual (NCT02134197).
TAG-72

Tumor-associated glycoprotein 72 (TAG-72) is a cell surface mucin-like glycoprotein expressed in a high proportion of human prostatic adenocarcinomas, particularly those with a Gleason grade of six or higher. Expression is predominantly localized to the cytoplasm and cell membrane of malignant cells, with minimal or absent staining in benign prostatic epithelium. TGW101, an MMAE-based, TAG-72-targeting ADC is currently being explored in a phase I clinical trial in patients with advanced solid tumors, including CRPC.
TM4SF1

TM4SF1 is a direct AR target gene that is overexpressed in prostate cancer tissues compared to benign prostatic hyperplasia. TM4SF1 is highly expressed by both tumor cells and tumor-associated vascular endothelial cells, and has been implicated in cancer progression, angiogenesis, metastasis, and chemoresistance. Delivery of TM4SF1-directed ADCs to both the vascular and cancer cell compartments of a tumor may be able to activate tumor immune surveillance, deprive the tumor of its blood supply, and directly kill tumor cells. AGX101, whose anti-TM4SG1 antibody delivers its maytansinoid payload directly to the target cell nucleus, is currently undergoing a phase I trial in patients with advanced solid tumors, including prostate cancer (NCT06440005).
ROR1

Receptor tyrosine kinase-like orphan receptor 1 (ROR1) is overexpressed in prostate cancer and associated with worse prognosis and more aggressive disease biology. ROR1 mediates oncogenic signaling through the Wnt5a/ROR1 axis, activating pathways such as the PI3K/AKT, MAPK, NF-kappaB, STAT3, and Hippo pathways to promote cancer cell survival, proliferation, invasion, metastasis, and resistance to apoptosis. Moreover, ROR1 has been shown to be reactivated in a subset of bone-metastatic prostate cancer cells, highlighting ROR1 as a potential therapeutic target in mCRPC. CS5001 is a ROR1-targeting ADC carrying a PBD dimer payload currently undergoing a phase I clinical trial in patients with advanced solid tumors and lymphomas, including prostate cancer; preliminary results have shown encouraging antitumor activity and no dose-limiting toxicities so far (NCT05279300).

passages.text: P-cadherin (CDH3)

Upregulation of P-cadherin (CDH3), a cell-to-cell adhesion molecule, has been observed and implicated in the development and progression of various solid tumors, including prostate cancer. In particular, CDH3 expression can promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition and increase invasion and metastasis of tumor cells, whereas reduced metastasis burden has been seen with anti-CDH3 ADCs in mouse models of prostate cancer. BC3195, which carries an MMAE payload, is the only CDH3-targeting ADC in clinical trials for patients with advanced solid malignancies (NCT05957471).
Prostate-specific cancer antigen (PSCA)

Prostate-specific cancer antigen (PSCA) is a cell surface protein frequently overexpressed in primary, metastatic, and castration-resistant prostate cancer, with limited expression in normal tissue. PSCA expression level is correlated with tumor progression, higher Gleason score, and worse prognosis, and is particularly elevated with more advanced prostate cancers such as those with bone metastases or neuroendocrine differentiation. PSCA-targeted modalities, including radiolabeled antibodies and CAR T cell therapy, have shown encouraging antitumor activity in both the preclinical and clinical settings, indicating the feasibility of PSCA as a target for ADCs. While there have been no PSCA-targeting ADCs in clinical development to date, the first reported ADC based on a fully human anti-PSCA antibody has shown efficient internalization and antitumor efficacy with its MMAE payload in a xenograft mouse model of prostate cancer.
Future perspectives
Future advancements in ADC development to improve safe and sufficient payload delivery and increase antitumor efficacy.

Improvements in linker, antibody, and payload technology, the utilization of precision medicine to identify markers of sensitivity and resistance in tumors, and combination therapy with radioligands all represent avenues for the future of ADCs.

The clinical development of ADCs for the treatment of mCRPC has been challenged by off-tumor toxicity as well as limitations in payload delivery related to target antigen selection and the histological features of mCRPC. In particular, the histological architecture of mCRPC:characterized by dense stroma, low vascularity, and high between-tumor heterogeneity:has limited ADC penetration and distribution within tumor tissue. However, optimization of antigen targets, along with exploration of new linker, antibody, and payload technologies, holds promise in amplifying the benefit of the next generation of ADCs (Fig. 2).

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: While linker instability is a common characteristic of currently-approved ADCs and may actually contribute to antitumor activity and decreased normal tissue metabolism of ADCs, off-tumor toxicity from payload release in the systemic circulation has been a limiting factor in the development of prostate cancer ADCs, especially PSMA-based ADCs plagued with problems of peripheral neuropathy. Thus, novel linker strategies have been under investigation. For example, linkers that release payloads independently of endogenous enzyme-mediated cleavage, such as those incorporating a click-to-release system upon administration of a subsequent exogenous chemical activator, have shown promising preclinical efficacy. These ADCs can be applied to a greater breadth of non-internalizing tumor antigens and stroma proteins, expanding the number and specificity of ADC targets. Extracellular cleavage of the ADCs may also result in more homogenous drug distribution throughout the tumor, enhancing the bystander effect and even potentially reaching cancer stem cells. Moreover, temporally controlling drug delivery with a separate activator administered after the ADCs have arrived at the target site may reduce off-target toxicity. Other strategies include tandem-cleavage linkers:where requiring two sequential enzymatic cleavage events for payload delivery has been shown to improve ADC stability and tolerability.

passages.text: Another obstacle to ADC approval in mCRPC remains in target selection, with heterogenous target antigen expression a main driver of ADC failure. The most studied targets in mCRPC:PSMA, STEAP1, TROP2, CD46, and B7H3:are not exclusive to nor uniformly or highly expressed across all tumor cells, impairing ADC binding and internalization, reducing effective payload delivery, and increasing the risk of on-target, off-tumor toxicity. Heterogenous and often low antigen density may be overcome with bispecific ADCs; for example, STEAP1 expression is often sustained in PSMA-low tumors, suggesting the utility of dual PSMAxSTEAP1-targeting ADCs. Bispecific ADCs have increased selectivity and internalization, as well as may limit ADC binding to normal tissue, reducing on-target off-tumor toxicity. For example, ABBV-969 is a novel PSMAxSTEAP1-directed bispecific ADC carrying a TOPI inhibitor payload with broader activity than ADCs targeting only PSMA or STEAP1 in preclinical mCRPC models, and is undergoing a phase I trial in mCRPC patients (NCT06318273). DXC-008, which carries a tubulysin B payload, is another PSMAxSTEAP1-directed ADC with potent dual-target antitumor activity in preclinical studies, currently undergoing a phase I trial in patients with prostate cancer and other solid tumors (NCT06926283). GenSci143 is a novel PSMAxB7H3-directed bispecific ADC carrying a TOPI inhibitor that has shown superior antitumor efficacy, pharmacokinetic control, and therapeutic index than single-target ADCs in in vivo models of mCRPC. DXC014, another PSMAxB7H3-directed bispecific ADC carrying a TOPI inhibitor, has also demonstrated a similar favorable antitumor efficacy and safety profile in preclinical PCa models.

passages.text: ADCs with dual payloads represent another strategy to improve anti-tumor activity. The combination of MMAE, with superior cell permeability and bystander effect, and MMAF, with less susceptibility to multidrug resistance (MDR) efflux pumps, may promote a synergistic cytotoxic effect and reduce the risk of drug resistance. Combining payloads with different mechanisms of action may also overcome resistance: for example, preclinical studies of an ADC carrying both TOPI and tubulin inhibitor payloads have demonstrated potent antitumor activity in TOPI inhibitor-resistant tumors. However, combining payloads may also increase the toxicity profile, and care must be taken to reconcile the effective and toxic doses of the drugs incorporated. Two dual payload ADCs have entered clinical development: KH815 and IBI3020. KH815, a TROP2-directed ADC conjugated to both a TOPI inhibitor and RNA polymerase II inhibitor, simultaneously inhibits RNA synthesis and induces DNA double-stranded breaks (DSB). KH815 has been shown to produce a more potent antitumor effect than single TOPI inhibitor-TROP2-targeting ADCs as well as the ability to overcome drug resistance in preclinical cancer models, and is currently being investigated in a phase I clinical trial in patients with advanced solid tumors (NCT06885645). IBI3020, a CEACAM5-targeting ADC with an undisclosed dual payload, has also shown robust antitumor activity, notable bystander effect, and a manageable safety profile in preclinical tumor models, and has just entered a phase I clinical trial in patients with unresectable, locally advanced, or metastatic solid tumors (NCT06946446).

passages.text: In recent years, ADC targets have also gradually expanded from antigens overexpressed on tumor cells to include antigens in the tumor microenvironment, such as components of the neovascular system, subendothelial extracellular matrix, and tumor matrix. By reducing angiogenesis and the concentration of growth factors produced by the tumor matrix, ADCs targeting the tumor microenvironment may increase cancer cell apoptosis, broadening their efficacy in heterogenous tumors. Moreover, non-cancerous matrix cells may have more stable genomes, reducing the risk of drug resistance towards ADCs. Recent preclinical studies investigating huB12-MMAE, an ADC targeting cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAPs) implicated in promoting cancer growth and survival, angiogenesis, drug resistance, and immunosuppression, in a prostate cancer model have found that targeting and eliminating CAPs with huB12-MMAE induces both proinflammatory and antitumor immune responses. PYX-201, an auristatin-carrying ADC targeting the extra-domain B splice variant of fibronectin (EDB + FN, an extracellular matrix protein abundantly expressed in the tumor microenvironment), is currently being evaluated in a phase I monotherapy trial (NCT06795412) and a phase I/II combination trial with pembrolizumab (NCT05720117) in patients with advanced solid tumors. Preliminary data from the phase I trial demonstrated clinical responses with an acceptable tolerability profile in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), ovarian cancer, NSCLC, HR + /HER2- breast cancer, triple negative breast cancer, and sarcoma, and PYX-201 monotherapy was granted FDA fast-track designation for patients with metastatic or recurrent HNSCC. Thus, ADCs that target stromal components may be particularly effective against cancers with high stromal-tumor ratios, such as prostate cancer.

passages.text: Another consideration for ADC use in patients is the sequencing of therapies, particularly in the context of ADCs that employ payloads with mechanisms of action shared by chemotherapeutics that are standard-of-care in treating prostate cancer. Prior exposure to taxanes during treatment of mCRPC can induce resistance mechanisms, including upregulation of efflux pumps or mutations in tubulin, that may compromise the efficacy of microtubule inhibitor-based ADCs. Thus, the timing of ADC administration, ideally before the emergence of resistance to analogous cytotoxics, may significantly impact therapeutic outcomes. Furthermore, the increasing availability of multiple ADCs within a single disease space also necessitates strategic sequencing based on payload diversity to mitigate cross-resistance and optimize efficacy. For example, in patients with metastatic breast cancer, TOPI mutations have emerged as a mechanism of acquired resistance after treatment TOPI inhibitor-based ADCs, conferring resistance to a second ADC with a similar TOPI inhibitor payload. On the other hand, switching to an ADC with a different payload class has been shown to overcome resistance and increase antitumor efficacy: in patients with HER2+ metastatic breast cancer, switching from a TOPI inhibitor-based ADC to a microtubule inhibitor-based ADC or vice versa yielded significantly higher objective response rates and progression-free survival than sequencing two ADCs with the same payload class. Further investigation into expanding payload diversity to overcome resistance mechanisms is also warranted:especially since current ADC payloads primarily fall into three main classes while many other classes of cytotoxic agents still remain. As novel payloads are explored for various cancers, future clinical trial designs should incorporate sequencing hypotheses and consider the utility of ADCs in earlier lines of therapy.

Factoring in tumor biomarkers when selecting ADC payloads may also play a role in enhancing therapeutic precision. For example, ADCs armed with TOPI inhibitors, which induce double-stranded DNA breaks that BRCA2-deficient cancer cells cannot effectively repair, may lead to enhanced cytotoxicity in prostate tumors with the BRCA2 mutation. This rationale is supporting clinical trials investigating the safety and anti-cancer activity of T-DXd or Dato-DXd with the PARPi AZD5305 in patients with advanced solid malignancies, including prostate cancer (NCT 04644068). In B7H3-targeting ADCs armed with a PBD payload that disrupts replication forks, loss-of-function alterations in RB1 and TP53:which promote replication stress:have been identified as predictors of therapeutic response. Other genomic and phenotypic markers positively predicting sensitivity to B7H3-PBD-ADCs include loss of/mutations in DNA repair proteins CHD1 and ATR, as well as expression of SLFN11, a DNA/RNA helicase that inhibits stressed replication fork repair. Beyond assessment of HRD status and other molecular vulnerabilities, tumor profiling to assess for antigen expression should also be considered, especially since the efficacy of ADCs may be highly dependent on the presence and density of the antigen target on tumor cells, with heterogenous or low expression liming therapeutic benefit. Thus, evaluation of tumor antigen target expression:by immunohistochemistry or molecular imaging:could be considered before patient selection. For example, use of PSMA-PET, which is already standard for staging, restaging, and eligibility assessment for PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy, can be extended to PSMA-targeting ADCs. Radiolabeled antibodies against STEAP1 in development can potentially guide patient selection for ADCs targeting STEAP1. Ultimately, genomic and molecular profiling along with evaluation of tumor antigen expression when selecting patients for ADCs may optimize the precision and impact of ADCs in prostate cancer.

passages.text: The role of radioligand therapies in mCRPC expanded with the approval of 177Lu-PSMA-617, which delivers beta-particle radiation to PSMA-expressing cells and the surrounding microenvironment. Both radioligands and ADCs can deliver their cytotoxic effects via selective targeting of PSMA, with possible synergy if used in combination. Radiation-induced DNA double-strand breaks could sensitize tumors to ADCs with DNA-damaging payloads, while ADCs may potentiate death in radioresistant tumor cells and induce immune cell filtration of tumors. Moreover, combination therapy with non-PSMA-targeting ADCs may be able to overcome resistance to 177Lu-PSMA-617. Disease progression on 177Lu-PSMA-617 is inevitable even in patients who are strongly PSMA-positive on imaging, with patients either having no response or progressing long-term despite having an excellent initial response. One possible mechanism for this primary and acquired resistance may be the presence of PSMA-negative disease, which may proliferate and become the predominant clone after elimination of PSMA-expressing cancer cells with 177Lu-PSMA-617. Thus, a therapeutic opportunity may lie in that these PSMA-negative clones may be sensitive to ADCs that target other antigens expressed on their cell surface, such as STEAP1. However, despite the potential for an increased antitumor response, there may also be increased risk of toxicity in healthy tissues with combination therapy. Thus, maximizing the safety profile must be considered when designing combination strategies. Overall, the current challenges faced in ADC development and strategies to address them emphasize the importance of choosing the right combination of specific target antigen, active linker, and appropriate payload for optimal efficacy in the tumor environment.

passages.text: Conclusion

As the field of oncology continues to advance towards personalized and targeted approaches, ADCs hold promise as a therapeutic strategy against prostate cancer. This manuscript reviewed some of the most relevant cytotoxic payloads, molecular targets, and ADCs that have demonstrated therapeutic potential in prostate cancer. These ADCs combine potent microtubule disruptors, topoisomerase inhibitors, and DNA alkylators to antibodies targeting antigens overexpressed on the surface of prostate cancer cells, including PSMA, B7H3, STEAP1, TROP2, CD46, TF, DLL3, SLC44A4, HER2, HER3, Nectin-4, 5T4, KAAG1, ASCT2, LYPD3, Tag-72, TM4SF1, CDH3, ROR1, and PSCA. However, due to issues with safety and specificity, no ADCs have yet been approved for the treatment of prostate cancer. Thus, further development and innovation are needed, both to refine current ADCs in the pipeline as well as develop novel ADCs with optimal targets, linkers, and/or payloads. As ADC technology continues to advance in the realm of prostate cancer, ADCs offer renewed hope for improved clinical outcomes and enhanced quality of life for patients battling this prevalent malignancy.

passages.text: Key genes and associated mechanisms of PCOS and EC comorbidity: A bioinformatics analysis

Endometrial cancer (EC) is a major reproductive system tumor and a common cancer in women. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is one of the most prevalent female reproductive endocrine disorders. The incidence of EC is significantly higher in individuals with PCOS. This study seeks to elucidate the organic correlations and interaction mechanisms between the 2 diseases through series of exploration of key genes with a bioinformatics analysis. The PCOS sample data and the EC single-cell dataset were downloaded from the gene expression omnibus database. The EC sample data were retrieved from the cancer genome atlas public database. The random survival forest method was employed to identify key genes associated with the prognosis of PCOS and EC comorbidity. Corresponding analyses on functional pathway enrichment, regulatory networks, and immune micro-environment are conducted. From a bioinformatics perspective, the association and interaction mechanisms between PCOS and EC comorbidity were explored to provide research and development references for the prevention and control of PCOS and EC comorbidity. Five key genes associated with the prognosis of PCOS and EC comorbidity were identified using the random survival forest method. The identified genes are SYTL1, PARVG, ID4, IL1RN, and S100A9. The abnormal expression of these key genes has impacted various enrichment pathways, including the TGF-beta signaling-pathway, motif regulatory networks (such as motif cisbp__M4556), and miRNA regulatory networks, which encompass genes such as ATM, BARD1 and BRCA1. Furthermore, these also influence the immune cell microenvironment, such as T cells regulatory. Collectively, these key genes play a significant role in the occurrence and progression of comorbidities through the pathways mentioned above. The dysregulation of key genes (SYTL1, PARVG, ID4, IL1RN, S100A9) in the context of PCOS-EC comorbidities, along with their associated enrichment pathways, including the TGF-beta signaling-pathway and immune microenvironment, plays a significant role in the occurrence and progression of EC.
1. Introduction

Bioinformatics is defined as an interdisciplinary set of tools that integrates computer science, mathematics, and statistics for the classification and analysis of biological information. This toolset can be applied in various areas, including genome annotation and comparison, expression data analysis, protein structure prediction, and the study of biological networks. Bioinformatics research offers substantial advantages in elucidating the occurrence and developmental pathways of these diseases, identifying biomarkers, and facilitating the development of new drugs.

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is one of the most prevalent female reproductive endocrine disorders, yet its etiology remains incompletely understood. Existing literature has identified various interactions among genes, as well as between genes and proteins, genes and environmental factors, highlighting the significance of genetic susceptibility in the onset and progression of PCOS. Furthermore, numerous studies have sought to elucidate the pathogenesis of PCOS through different omics approaches, including genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics, leading to the discovery of several candidate biomarkers that may be utilized for the diagnosis or prognostic evaluation of PCOS.

Endometrial carcinoma (EC) is a major reproductive system tumor and a common cancer in women. The mechanisms underlying their occurrence and development remain unclear. Numerous multi-omics studies on EC have yielded extensive information regarding pathogenesis, molecular markers, therapeutic targets, treatment efficacy, and prognosis.

To date, while bioinformatics has made significant strides in the research and analysis of PCOS and EC, there has been a lack of thematic bioinformatics research focusing on the comorbidity between these conditions. Both PCOS and EC are characterized by high heterogeneity and complexity, and there exists a notable correlation between them. For instance, the incidence of EC is significantly higher in individuals with PCOS, being approximately 2 to 6 times greater than in those without PCOS. This specialized study aims to conduct a bioinformatics comorbidity analysis of EC within the context of PCOS. This analysis seeks to elucidate the organic correlations and interaction mechanisms between the 2 diseases through series of exploration of relative key genes, thereby providing valuable insights for related prevention and control efforts.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Database resources
This study is a bioinformation analysis, the ethical review is not required.

The cancer genome atlas (TCGA) database is currently the largest repository of cancer genetic information, encompassing a diverse array of data types. The gene expression omnibus (GEO) database formally known as a comprehensive gene expression database.
2.2. Differential expression analysis

This study utilized the package "Limma" to conduct differential expression analysis of comorbidity-related expression profiles, aiming to identify genes with significant differential expression between PCOS and EC samples, and to perform an accompanying molecular mechanism analysis. In screening for differentially expressed genes, the criteria established were a P-value of <.05 and llogFCl >1. The results of the analysis were visualized through the generation of volcano plots and heat maps depicting the differential genes.
2.3. Gene function annotation

This study utilizes the Metascape database to perform functional annotation and analysis of gene sets, including gene ontology pathway analysis, thereby comprehensively exploring the primary biological functions of these differential gene. Results with a minimum overlap of >=3 and a P-value of <=.01 were deemed statistically significant.
2.4. Random survival forest analysis

The random survival forest (RSF) is a variant of the survival forest algorithm that integrates concepts from both survival analysis and random forests. This method predicts survival time or survival probability by constructing multiple decision trees, thereby enhancing model performance through the introduction of randomness. In this study, the package "randomForestSRC" is utilized to perform decision tree feature selection on the differential genes analyzed in the preceding step. Subsequently, the RSF algorithm is employed to rank the importance of prognosis-related genes. Genes with a relative importance >0.3 are identified and selected as the final marker genes.
2.5. Gene set enrichment analysis

Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) is a method employed to interpret high-throughput gene expression data, revealing underlying biological processes and pathways. In this specific study, GSEA will be utilized to compare the differences in signaling pathways between the high gene expression group and the low-expression group, aiming to explore the core gene pathway molecular mechanisms related to the prognosis of the comorbidity between PCOS and EC. The number of permutations is set to 1000, and the replacement type is phenotypic.
2.6. Gene set variation analysis

Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA) is a nonparametric, unsupervised method that evaluates the biological functions of a sample by comprehensively scoring the gene set of interest and converting gene-level changes into pathway-level alterations. In this study, gene sets derived from PCOS and EC samples will be obtained from the Molecular Signatures Database (version 7.0). The GSVA algorithm will be employed to comprehensively score the core gene sets associated with the prognosis of the comorbidity between PCOS and EC, thereby evaluating potential biological function changes of core genes in samples originating from these 2 disease sources.
2.7. Motif regulatory network analysis

This study utilizes the package "RcisTarget.hg19.motifDBs.cisbpOnly.500bp" to develop a Gene-motif rankings database pertinent to the comorbidity between PCOS and EC. The analysis focuses on motifs associated with genes and transcription factors within the database, along with their respective normalized enrichment scores. Beyond the annotated motifs present in the source data, additional inferences were drawn based on motif similarities and gene sequences, leading to the creation of supplementary annotation files.
2.8. MicroRNA regulatory network analysis

MicroRNA (miRNA) is a type of small noncoding RNA that regulates gene expression by promoting the degradation of mRNA or inhibiting its translation. In this study, we will obtain miRNA information related to key genes by querying the miRcode database. This information will be visualized using Cytoscape software to construct a hub gene-miRNA relationship network diagram, illustrating the interactions between genes and miRNAs. Furthermore, we will analyze the corresponding key genes and their miRNA regulatory networks, along with the relevant transcription and degradation processes, to elucidate the specific molecular mechanisms and interactive relationships associated with the comorbidity between PCOS and EC.
2.9. Immune cell infiltration

The CIBERSORT method is a widely utilized approach for assessing immune cell types within the microenvironment, capable of distinguishing 22 distinct human immune cell phenotypes, including T cells, B cells, plasma cells, and various myeloid cell subsets. In this study, the CIBERSORT algorithm was employed to analyze data related to the comorbidity of PCOS and EC, aiming to infer the relative proportions of the 22 types of immune infiltrating cells. Additionally, a correlation analysis was performed to examine the relationship between the expression of key genes and the abundance of immune cells, thereby enhancing our understanding of the immune status in cases of the comorbidity between PCOS and EC.
2.10. Single-cell analysis

This special study will first utilize the package "Seurat" to read EC single-cell data sets obtained from public databases, filtering out low-expression genes. Next, the data will be standardized and homogenized, followed by the application of the t-SNE algorithm to visualize the positional relationships of various cell groups in 2-dimensional space. This approach will facilitate the subsequent screening of single-cell group clustering based on the expression of key genes. Subsequently, the cell groups will be annotated using the annotation files provided by the package "celldex" to ascertain the cell type, state, or characteristics of each cell group. Finally, the localization of key EC progression genes (TP53, MSH6, MLH1) within EC single-cell populations will be analyzed, and the location and co-expression of these key EC progression genes alongside key genes of the comorbidity between PCOS and EC within EC single-cell populations will be discussed.
2.11. Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were conducted using the R program (version 4.2), with a significance level set at P <.05.
3. Results
3.1. Differential gene of PCOS and EC

The PCOS sample data utilized in this study was downloaded from the NCBI GEO public database, specifically the GSE 34526 dataset. This dataset comprises a total of 10 samples, including 3 cases from the normal control group and 7 cases from the PCOS disease group. Additionally, the EC sample data were retrieved from the TCGA public database, specifically the UCEC dataset, which contains a total of 589 samples, including 35 cases from the normal control group and 554 cases from the EC disease group. The EC single-cell dataset was also sourced from the NCBI GEO public database, specifically the GSE 203612 dataset, which includes a total of 3 EC disease samples.

A total of 1704 differential genes were identified in the PCOS-related GSE 34526 data set, comprising 1125 up-regulated genes and 579 down-regulated genes (Fig. 1A and B). In the EC-related TCGA-UCEC data set, 2451 differential genes were identified, including 1071 up-regulated genes and 1380 down-regulated genes (Fig. 1C and D). The intersections of both up-regulated and down-regulated genes from the PCOS and EC data sets were analyzed, resulting in 127 differential intersection genes. Specifically, there were 67 up-regulated gene intersections (Fig. 1E) and 60 down-regulated gene intersections (Fig. 1F).

(A) Volcano plot illustrating differential genes associated with PCOS; (B) Heat map depicting differential genes in PCOS; (C) Volcano plot for differential genes related to EC; (D) Heat map of differential genes in EC; (E) Venn diagram showing up-regulated differential intersection genes between PCOS and EC; (F) Venn diagram depicting down-regulated differential intersection genes in PCOS and EC; (G) Schematic representation of functional enrichment for differential intersection genes in PCOS and EC; (H) Ranking of key intersection genes pertinent to the survival of patients with PCOS-EC comorbidity. EC = endometrial cancer, PCOS = polycystic ovary syndrome.
3.2. Differential gene function enrichment

Pathway enrichment analysis was conducted on the 127 differentially intersecting genes associated with the comorbidity between PCOS and EC. The results indicated that these differentially intersecting genes were predominantly enriched in pathways such as the regulation of transforming growth factor beta receptor signaling and the regulation of hormone biosynthetic processes (Fig. 1G).
3.3. Key gene of the comorbidity between PCOS and EC
RSF analysis identified a total of 7 candidate key genes with significant importance in comorbid survival. The order of importance is illustrated in Fig. 1H.

Survival analysis revealed that 5 genes were significantly associated with the survival of the comorbidity between PCOS and EC (P <.05). These 5 genes are: Synaptotagmin-like protein 1 gene (SYTL1) (Fig. 2A), parvin gamma (actin-binding protein) gene (PARVG) (Fig. 2A and B), inhibitor of DNA binding 4 gene (ID4) (Fig. 2C), interleukin 1 receptor antagonist gene (IL1RN) (Fig. 2D), and S100 calcium-binding protein A9 gene (S100A9) (Fig. 2E).

The survival curves related to key genes associated with PCOS-EC comorbidity are as follows: (A) SYTL1; (B) PARVG; (C) ID4; (D) IL1RN; (E) S100A9. The GSEA pathway enrichment of key genes is represented by: (F) SYTL1; (G) PARVG; (H) ID4; (I) IL1RN; (J) S100A9. The GSVA pathway enrichment for the key genes includes: (K) SYTL1; (L) PARVG; (M) ID4; (N) IL1RN; (O) S100A9. EC = endometrial cancer, GSEA = gene set enrichment analysis, GSVA = gene set variation analysis, ID4 = inhibitor of DNA binding 4, IL1RN = interleukin 1 receptor antagonist, PARVG = parvin gamma, PCOS = polycystic ovary syndrome, S100A9 = S100 calcium-binding protein A9, SYTL1 = synaptotagmin-like protein 1.
3.4. Key genes set enrichment

The GSEA results indicate that the enriched pathways associated with the SYTL1 gene include the KEGG-ERBB-SIGNALING-PATHWAY and KEGG-TGF-BETA-SIGNALING-PATHWAY, among others (Fig. 2F). For the PARVG gene, the enriched pathways encompass the KEGG-INSULIN-SIGNALING-PATHWAY and KEGG-TGF-BETA-SIGNALING-PATHWAY, among others (Fig. 2G). The ID4 gene is linked to enriched pathways such as KEGG-FRUCTOSE-AND-MANNOSE-METABOLISM and KEGG-PENTOSE-PHOSPHATE-PATHWAY, among others (Fig. 2H). The enriched pathways related to the IL1RN gene include the KEGG-GNRH-SIGNALING-PATHWAY and KEGG-WNT-SIGNALING-PATHWAY, among others (Fig. 2I). Lastly, the S100A9 gene is associated with enriched pathways including the KEGG-GNRH-SIGNALING-PATHWAY and KEGG-OOCYTE-MEIOSIS, among others (Fig. 2J).
3.5. Key genes set variation

The GSVA results indicate that high expression of SYTL1 enriches the P53 pathway and the IL6-JAK-STAT3 signaling-pathway, among others, thereby triggering corresponding functional changes (Fig. 2K). Similarly, high expression of PARVG enriches the P53 pathway and the IL2-STAT5 signaling-pathway, leading to analogous functional changes (Fig. 2L). Furthermore, high expression of ID4 enriches the TGF-beta signaling-pathway and the IL2-STAT5 signaling-pathway, resulting in corresponding functional changes (Fig. 2M). Additionally, high expression of IL1RN integrates the IL6-JAK-STAT3 signaling-pathway and the IL2-STAT5 signaling-pathway, triggering related functional changes (Fig. 2N). Lastly, high expression of S100A9 enriches the P53 pathway and the IL2-STAT5 signaling-pathway, thereby inducing corresponding functional changes (Fig. 2O).
3.6. Key genes motifs regulatory network

Motif enrichment analysis revealed that these 5 key genes are jointly regulated by multiple transcription factors. We conducted Motif-TF annotation and cumulative recovery curve enrichment analysis on these transcription factors. The findings indicated that the Motif cisbp__M4556 exhibited the highest normalized enrichment score (normalized enrichment scores: 5.06). Figure 3A illustrates the primary transcription factors and their corresponding relationships with the key genes regulated by these transcription factors. Figure 3B presents the main transcription factors identified through motif enrichment analysis of the 5 key genes.

(A) Diagram illustrating the key gene motifs enrichment; (B) Main transcription factors involved in key gene motifs enrichment; (C) Prediction of hub gene-miRNA pairs in reverse direction for PCOS-EC comorbidity; (D) Key regulatory genes associated with endometrial cancer; (E) Schematic representation of the correlation between the expression levels of key genes and the expression levels of disease regulatory genes. EC = endometrial cancer, PCOS = polycystic ovary syndrome.
3.7. MicroRNA regulatory network

By querying the Mircode database, we obtained miRNA information related to 5 key genes associated with the comorbidity between PCOS and EC, which included 69 miRNAs and 135 hub gene-miRNA relationship pairs. The network relationship was constructed using Cytoscape software, as illustrated in Figure 3C. Based on these 135 hub gene-miRNA relationship pairs, we further identified regulatory genes linked to the onset of the comorbidity between PCOS and EC through the GeneCards database. After analyzing the expression levels of the top 20 genes based on relevance scores, we found that the expression of these regulatory genes, such as ATM, BARD1, BRCA1, and BRCA2, exhibited significant changes in patients with PCOS and EC (Fig. 3D). Furthermore, the expression levels of these disease-regulated genes were significantly correlated with the expression levels of 5 key genes. For instance, ID4 and PTEN demonstrated a significant positive correlation (R = 0.256), while SYTL1 and MSH6 showed a significant negative correlation (r = -0.431) (Fig. 3E). For specific relevant information, please refer to Figure S1, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/Q611.
3.8. Key genes influence the immune micro-environment

The immune infiltration micro-environment primarily consists of immune cells, extracellular matrix, various growth factors, inflammatory factors, and distinct physical and chemical characteristics. These components can significantly influence the occurrence, progression, and clinical outcomes of the disease.

Figure 4A illustrates the proportion of 22 types of immune cells in PCOS-EC comorbid patients, as analyzed using the CIBERSORT method. Figure 4B depicts the correlations among various immune cell categories in PCOS-EC comorbid patients. Figure 4C presents the comparative analysis of the proportions and differences of these 22 immune cell types between PCOS-EC comorbid patients and the control group. Figure 4D-H detail the specific relationships between 5 key genes associated with the comorbidity between PCOS and EC and the immune cell infiltration micro-environment.

(A) Proportion of immune cell content in PCOS-EC comorbid patients; (B) correlation matrix depicting the relationships between immune cells in PCOS-EC comorbid patients; (C) proportion of immune cell categories in PCOS-EC comorbid patients compared to the corresponding control group, including ratio and comparative analysis; (D-H) Correlation analysis between key genes and immune cells, specifically: (D) SYTL1; (E) PARVG; (F) ID4; (G) IL1RN; (H) S100A9. EC = endometrial cancer, ID4 = inhibitor of DNA binding 4, IL1RN = interleukin 1 receptor antagonist, PARVG = parvin gamma, PCOS = polycystic ovary syndrome, S100A9 = S100 calcium-binding protein A9, SYTL1 = synaptotagmin-like protein 1.

As shown in Figure 4B, the immune cells in PCOS-EC comorbid patients, such as CD4 resting memory T cells, exhibit significant relationships with CD8 T cells, CD4 memory-activated T cells, and T cell follicular helper cells. Additionally, M0 macrophages show a strong correlation with CD8 T cells, while activated NK cells are significantly correlated with resting mast cells.

As illustrated in Figure 4C, the proportion of M0 macrophages, M1 macrophages, plasma cells, T follicular helper cells, and regulatory T cells (Tregs) in the immune cell profiles of PCOS-EC comorbid patients is significantly higher than that of the control group.

Figure 4D-H demonstrate that the 5 key genes show strong correlations with immune cell infiltration in the micro-environment. Notably, SYTL1 exhibits a significant positive correlation with Tregs and a significant negative correlation with resting mast cells. Similarly, PARVG shows a significant positive correlation with Tregs and a significant negative correlation with resting mast cells. ID4 is positively correlated with CD4 resting memory T cells and negatively correlated with M0 macrophages. IL1RN demonstrates a significant positive correlation with neutrophils while showing a significant negative correlation with resting mast cells. Lastly, S100A9 is significantly negatively correlated with neutrophils and significantly positively correlated with resting mast cells.
3.9. Single-cell data analysis and validation
